chapters.ar: أَوۡجُهُ وَرۡشٍ فِي مَدِّ الۡبدَلِ مَع ذوَاتِ اليَاءِ عَنۡ طَرِيۡقِ الشَّاطِبِيَّةِ
chapters.en: The Wujūh of Warsh When Mad al-Badal Meets Dhāt al-Yā', via the Shāṭibiyyah
chapters.desc: In the riwāyah of Warsh through the Shāṭibiyyah, mad al-badal and dhāt al-yāʾ each have their own permitted lengths or vowel qualities. When the two meet, only four of the possible pairings are transmitted, and which four depends on which comes first.

verses.ajuz: فِي بَدَلٍ مَعۡ ذَاتِ يَاءٍ فَاقۡبَلَا

ajuzW.g: a dhāt al-yā' (a word whose alif is from yāʾ)

verses.tr: The wujūh of Warsh, according to Ḥirz, are four, where mad al-badal meets dhāt al-yā'; so, accept this.

exp.en:
Background

In the riwāyah of Warsh from Nāfiʿ, through Ḥirz al-Amānī (the Shāṭibiyyah), there are two independent features of recitation, each carrying its own range of permitted lengths or vowel qualities.

Mad al badal, the lengthening that occurs where a hamzah is followed by a mad letter substituting an original hamzah, may be read with qaṣr (the shortest length), tawassuṭ (a middle length), or ishbā' (the fullest length), e.g. ءامنوا.

Dhawāt al yā' refers to words whose final alif maqṣūrah originates from a yā'. These words may be read with fatḥ (fully open, without imālah) or taqlīl (a lighter, intermediate vowel quality, sometimes called tanqīl), e.g. أَبىٰ.

When these two features occur adjacent to one another within the same reading segment, they cannot be combined in every possible way. Only four of the possible pairings are transmitted, and these depend on which feature comes first.

Explanation

The poet opens by stating the scope and the count directly: four permitted wujūh, specifically for Warsh's riwāyah as transmitted through Ḥirz al Amānī, apply whenever mad al badal and dhāt al yā' occur together.

verses.sadr: إِنۡ ذَاتُ ياءٍ قبلَ مَدِّكَ الۡبَدَلۡ
verses.tr: If dhāt al-yā' comes before your mad al-badal, then its fatḥ comes with qaṣr, then with full length.

exp.en:
Abyāt 2–3

These two verses set out the first of the two cases: where dhāt al yā' precedes mad al badal within the segment. The order of the four wujūh is: fatḥ paired with qaṣr, fatḥ paired with ishbā', taqlīl paired with tawassuṭ, and taqlīl paired with ishbā'.

Case One: Dhāt al-Yā' Before Mad al-Badal

  1. Fatḥ of dhāt al-yā' + qaṣr of mad al-badal
  2. Fatḥ of dhāt al-yā' + ishbā' (full length) of mad al-badal
  3. Taqlīl of dhāt al-yā' + tawassuṭ of mad al-badal
  4. Taqlīl of dhāt al-yā' + ishbā' (full length) of mad al-badal

Example:

﴿فَتَلَقَّىٰ آدَمُ مِنْ رَبِّهِ كَلِمَاتٍ فَتَابَ عَلَيْهِ ۚ إِنَّهُ هُوَ التَّوَّابُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾

al-Baqarah 2:37

verses.tr: Its taqlīl comes with tawassuṭ, then with full length; and in the other case, qaṣr of the badal comes first.
With its fatḥ comes tawassuṭ of the badal, then its taqlīl; and lengthen it fully, with fatḥ and with taqlīl.

exp.en:
The closing verse, together with the final hemistich of the previous one, sets out the second case: where mad al badal precedes dhāt al yā' within the segment.

Here the order is: qaṣr paired with fatḥ, tawassuṭ paired with taqlīl, ishbā' paired with fatḥ, and ishbā' paired with taqlīl.

Case Two: Mad al-Badal Before Dhāt al-Yā'

  1. Qaṣr of mad al-badal + fatḥ of dhāt al-yā'
  2. Tawassuṭ of mad al-badal + taqlīl of dhāt al-yā'
  3. Ishbā' (full length) of mad al-badal + fatḥ of dhāt al-yā'
  4. Ishbā' (full length) of mad al-badal + taqlīl of dhāt al-yā'

Example:

﴿وَإِذْ قُلْنَا لِلْمَلَائِكَةِ اسْجُدُوا لِآدَمَ فَسَجَدُوا إِلَّا إِبْلِيسَ أَبَىٰ وَاسْتَكْبَرَ وَكَانَ مِنَ الْكَافِرِينَ﴾

al-Baqarah 2:34

A Note on Verse Endings and Words Containing Hā'

This scheme of four wujūh does not apply to ru'ūs al āy, the words that fall at the end of verses, in eleven particular sūrahs. In those places, dhāt al yā' is read exclusively with taqlīl, regardless of whether the accompanying mad al badal is read with qaṣr, tawassuṭ, or ishbā'.

Where a verse ending contains a hā', as in wa ḍuḥāhā, the reciter may choose to treat it either as an ordinary verse ending, reading taqlīl across all three lengths of the badal, or as an ordinary non-ending word, applying the full four wajh scheme above: fatḥ with qaṣr or ishbā', and taqlīl with tawassuṭ or ishbā'.

Conclusion

Not everything is possible.

Dhawāt al-yā' before mad al-badal

  1. Fatḥ + Qaṣr
  2. Fatḥ + Ishbā'
  3. Taqlīl + Tawassuṭ
  4. Taqlīl + Ishbā'

Mad al-badal before dhawāt al-yā'

  1. Qaṣr + Fatḥ
  2. Tawassuṭ + Taqlīl
  3. Ishbā' + Fatḥ
  4. Ishbā' + Taqlīl

ليس كُل مُمْكِنٍ مَرويًا

Not everything possible is transmitted.

chapters.ar: أَبوابُ الۡفَلاحِ في أَحكامِ الأَصۡبَهَانِي عن طرِيۡقِ المِصۡبَاحِ
chapters.en: Abwāb al Falāḥ fī Aḥkām al Aṣbahānī min Ṭarīq al Miṣbāḥ
chapters.desc: Nine abyāt on the riwāyah of Warsh ʿan Nāfiʿ as transmitted through Abū Bakr al-Aṣbahānī, by the route recorded in the book al-Miṣbāḥ. The poem gathers twenty-two matters, grouping words and expressions that share the same ruling so that they can be held in a short, memorable poem.

verses.tr: Praise be to Allah for this success, and for the blessing of teaching recitation from al Miṣbāḥ.

exp.en:
Background

This poem addresses a highly specialized point of qirā'āt: the recitation rulings specific to the riwāyah of Warsh 'an Nāfi', as transmitted through Abū Bakr al Aṣbahānī, by the particular route recorded in the book al Miṣbāḥ.

Warsh's reading reaches later generations through two main students, al Azraq and al Aṣbahānī, and al Aṣbahānī's own transmission branches further into several routes. Sources on this tradition record that the route underlying al Miṣbāḥ passes through Hibatullāh and, from him, through al Ḥammāmī.

The poem consists of nine verses and brings together twenty-two matters relating to the transmission of al Aṣbahānī through this route. Rather than arranging them simply according to their occurrence in the Qur'ān, the poet groups together words and expressions that share the same ruling, beginning with matters of addition and omission, followed by tawassuṭ, tas-hīl, naql, ibdāl, ḥadhf, iẓhār, taqlīl, idghām, tafkhīm, ishmām, fatḥ, and taḥqīq.

At the same time, the poem follows a broader arrangement of the uṣūl of recitation. It begins with matters relating to isti'ādhah and basmalah, followed by the mudūd, the rulings of the hamzah, idghām al ṣaghīr, and then matters relating to fatḥ, imālah and taqlīl. Within this structure, the poet identifies the specific Qur'ānic words and expressions to which each ruling applies, allowing a large number of detailed matters to be gathered into a short and memorable poem.

A Map of the Poem's Rulings

  1. Addition (زيادة) Addition to the istiʿādhah
  2. Addition (زيادة) Addition of takbīr
  3. Omission (ترك) Leaving the additional lengthening of mad al-munfaṣil
  4. Omission (ترك) Leaving ghunnah
  5. Tawassuṭ (توسط) Mad al-muttaṣil
  6. Tawassuṭ (توسط) The letter ʿAyn
  7. Tas-hīl (تسهيل) أَئِمَّة
  8. Tas-hīl (تسهيل) بَابُ: يَشَاءُ إِلَى
  9. Naql (نقل) مِلْء
  10. Ibdāl (إبدال) ءالذَّكَرَيْن
  11. Ḥadhf (حذف) The alif in هَأَنْتُمْ
  12. Iẓhār (إظهار) مَالِيَهْ هَلَكَ
  13. Iẓhār (إظهار) يَلْهَثْ ذَلِكَ
  14. Taqlīl (تقليل) The yāʾ in يس
  15. Idghām (إدغام) The nūn of يس وَالْقُرْآن
  16. Idghām (إدغام) The qāf in نَخْلُقْكُمْ
  17. Tafkhīm (تفخيم) The rāʾ in فِرْق
  18. Ishmām (إشمام) The nūn in تَأْمَنَّا
  19. Fatḥ (فتح) The opening of Sūrat Maryam; the hāʾ of Maryam; the opening of Sūrat Ṭā Hā
  20. Taḥqīq (تحقيق) Taḥqīq of hamzah in the word بِأَيِّ
  21. Taḥqīq (تحقيق) Taḥqīq of hamzah in the word تَأَذَّنَ in Surah Ibrahim
  22. Taḥqīq (تحقيق) Taḥqīq of hā of كِتَابِيَهْ when connected

Explanation

The poet opens with praise to Allah for the completion of this work and for the blessing of being able to teach recitation according to al Miṣbāḥ, naming the source text at the outset.

Among the various routes of transmission recorded in al Nashr and derived from the book al Miṣbāḥ are two of the routes of al Aṣbahānī from Warsh, from Imām Nāfiʿ al Madanī. One is through Hibatullāh ibn Jaʿfar, while the other is through al Muṭṭawwiʿī.

The poet refers to both of these routes in the second verse.

verses.tr: From Hibah and Muṭṭawwi'ī, both of them, they transmitted from al Aṣbahānī, excellently.

exp.en:
The poet names the transmitters standing between al Aṣbahānī and the reader: Hibah, that is Hibatullāh, and a second figure referred to as Muṭṭawwiʿī, both reporting from al Aṣbahānī.

The poet now moves on to the first two matters of disagreement for al Aṣbahānī through the route of al Miṣbāḥ: the addition to the istiʿādhah and the permissibility of takbīr at the end of the sūrahs.

verses.tr: For the isti'ādhah, extend it with 'inna Allāha...', and say the takbīr, if you wish, at the end of it.

exp.en:
This verse contains two matters:

1. Addition to the Istiʿādhah

The standard istiʿādhah read by the reciters is:

أَعُوذُ بِاللَّهِ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ الرَّجِيمِ

I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shayṭān.

Through the route of al Miṣbāḥ, however, al Aṣbahānī is also transmitted with an addition to this:

أَعُوذُ بِاللَّهِ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ الرَّجِيمِ، إِنَّ اللَّهَ هُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْعَلِيمُ

I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shayṭān. Indeed, Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.

Thus, when reciting through this route, the additional words إِنَّ اللَّهَ هُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْعَلِيمُ may be added to the istiʿādhah.

2. The Permissibility of Takbīr

The second matter mentioned in the verse is takbīr at the end of the sūrahs.

Through the route of al Miṣbāḥ, the reader may recite اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ at the end of the sūrahs, beginning from the end of Sūrat al-Ḍuḥā and continuing until the end of Sūrat al-Nās.

When joining two sūrahs, the takbīr is recited after completing the first sūrah and before the basmalah of the following sūrah. Thus, if the reader begins takbīr at the end of Sūrat al-Ḍuḥā, he continues with it at the end of each sūrah until he reaches Sūrat al-Nās.

verses.tr: Shorten the mad al munfaṣil, and do not apply ghunnah; lengthen the mad al muttaṣil and give the letter 'ayn a moderate length.

exp.en:
This verse deals with four matters relating to the lengthening of the recitation and the pronunciation of certain letters: qaṣr of mad al-munfaṣil, leaving ghunnah in idghām into the lām and rāʾ, tawassuṭ of mad al-muttaṣil, and tawassuṭ of the yāʾ in ʿAyn.

  • Qaṣr of mad al-munfaṣil A mad letter (ا / و / ي) at the end of a word → a hamzah (ء) at the start of the next word.
  • Leaving ghunnah into lām and rāʾ A nūn sākinah or tanwīn before lām or rāʾ (ل / ر).
  • Tawassuṭ of mad al-muttaṣil A mad letter (ا / و / ي) and a hamzah (ء) in the same word.
  • Tawassuṭ of the yāʾ of ʿAyn The yāʾ in ʿAyn (عَيْن) at the beginning of two sūrahs.

3. Qaṣr of Mad al-Munfaṣil

Mad al-munfaṣil occurs when a mad letter comes at the end of one word and a hamzah occurs at the beginning of the following word.

Through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, it is read with qaṣr, meaning that the mad is kept to its shortest length.

For example: يَا أَيُّهَا

4. Leaving Ghunnah in Idghām into the Lām and Rāʾ

The second matter concerns a nūn sākinah or tanwīn when it is followed by a lām or rāʾ. In these cases, the nūn or tanwīn is merged into the following letter.

Through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, this idghām is performed without ghunnah.

Examples include: مِن رَّبِّهِمْ ، هُدًى لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ

5. Tawassuṭ of Mad al-Muttaṣil

Mad al-muttaṣil occurs when a mad letter and a hamzah occur within the same word.

Through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, it is read with tawassuṭ, giving the connected mad a moderate length.

An example is: جَاءَ

6. Tawassuṭ of the Yāʾ in ʿAyn

The final matter concerns the letter ʿAyn, which occurs among the disjointed letters at the beginning of two sūrahs:

كهيعص Maryam 19:1 and حم عسق al-Shūrā 42:1–2

The yāʾ in ʿAyn is a madd līn and, through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, is read with tawassuṭ, giving it a moderate length.

verses.tr: Ease [tas-hīl] the hamzah in أَئِمَّةً and in يَشَاءُ إِلَى; in al dhakarayn apply ibdāl and apply Naql in مِلْءُ.

exp.en:
This verse moves on to four matters relating to the hamzah in the recitation of al-Aṣbahānī through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ:

  1. Tas-hīl of the second hamzah in أَئِمَّةً
    ﴿فَقَاتِلُوا أَئِمَّةَ الْكُفْرِ﴾ al-Tawbah 9:12
  2. Tas-hīl of the second hamzah in يَشَاءُ إِلَى and similar expressions
    ﴿يَهْدِي مَنْ يَشَاءُ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾ al-Baqarah 2:142
  3. Ibdāl in the words of the آلذكرين (bāb al-dhakarayn)
    ﴿ءَآللَّهُ أَذِنَ لَكُمْ﴾ Yūnus 10:59
  4. Naql in مِلْءُ
    ﴿مِلْءُ الْأَرْضِ ذَهَبًا﴾ Āl ʿImrān 3:91

7. Tas-hīl of the Second Hamzah in أَئِمَّةً

The first matter concerns the word أَئِمَّةً, in which two hamzahs occur within the same word. Through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, al-Aṣbahānī reads the second hamzah with tas-hīl wherever this word appears in the Qurʾān.

Tas-hīl means to soften the pronunciation of the hamzah, making its articulation easier and lighter.

The word occurs in five places in the Qurʾān, and in each occurrence the second hamzah is treated with tas-hīl according to this route.

8. Tas-hīl in يَشَاءُ إِلَى and Similar Expressions

The second matter concerns expressions such as يَشَاءُ إِلَى. Here, two hamzahs of qaṭʿ occur in succession across two words: the first hamzah is preceded by a ḍammah, while the second hamzah carries a kasrah.

Through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, the second hamzah is read with tas-hīl.

This ruling applies not only to يَشَاءُ إِلَى, but to every occurrence in which two hamzahs of qaṭʿ meet across two words, with the first preceded by ḍammah and the second carrying kasrah. There are twenty-eight such occurrences in the Qurʾān according to the reading of Nāfiʿ.

9. Ibdāl in the Words of the Bāb al-Dhakarayn

The third matter is referred to by the poet as آلذَّكَرَيْنِ. This refers to a specific group of words in which the hamzah is read with ibdāl through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ.

Ibdāl means substituting the hamzah with another letter, according to the transmitted rule.

This occurs in six places, involving three specific expressions:

  • آلذَّكَرَيْنِ 2 occurrences in Sūrat al-Anʿām
    ﴿قُلْ ءَآلذَّكَرَيْنِ حَرَّمَ أَمِ الْأُنْثَيَيْنِ﴾ al-Anʿām 6:143
    ﴿قُلْ ءَآلذَّكَرَيْنِ حَرَّمَ أَمِ الْأُنْثَيَيْنِ أَمَّا اشْتَمَلَتْ…﴾ al-Anʿām 6:144
  • آلْآنَ 2 occurrences in Sūrat Yūnus
    ﴿ءَآلْآنَ وَقَدْ كُنْتُمْ بِهِ تَسْتَعْجِلُونَ﴾ Yūnus 10:51
    ﴿ءَآلْآنَ وَقَدْ عَصَيْتَ قَبْلُ وَكُنْتَ مِنَ الْمُفْسِدِينَ﴾ Yūnus 10:91
  • ءَآللَّهُ 2 occurrences: Yūnus and al-Naml
    ﴿ءَآللَّهُ أَذِنَ لَكُمْ﴾ Yūnus 10:59
    ﴿ءَآللَّهُ خَيْرٌ أَمَّا يُشْرِكُونَ﴾ al-Naml 27:59

10. Naql in مِلْءُ

The final matter is the word مِلْءُ, which occurs in:

﴿مِلْءُ الْأَرْضِ ذَهَبًا﴾

“…the full amount of the earth in gold.” Āl ʿImrān 3:91

Through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, the ruling is naql.

Naql means transferring the vowel of the hamzah to the preceding consonant, while omitting the hamzah in pronunciation.

In مِلْءُ:

  • the hamzah is omitted,
  • its ḍammah is transferred to the preceding lām.
  • Thus, it is read as مِلُ

The beauty of this verse is that the poet has compressed four separate rules of the hamzah into a single memorable couplet.

verses.tr: Omit the alif in هَأَنْتُمْ, and make Iẓhār in the hāʾ of مَالِيَهْ, and the thāʾ of يَلْهَثْ make it clear, and apply Taqlīl.

exp.en:
The poet now turns to three matters relating to the pronunciation of particular words and letters in the recitation of al-Aṣbahānī through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ:

  1. The omission of the alif in هَأَنْتُمْ
    ﴿هَا أَنْتُمْ هَؤُلَاءِ حَاجَجْتُمْ…﴾ Āl ʿImrān 3:66
  2. The iẓhār of the hāʾ in مَالِيَهْ هَلَكَ
    ﴿مَالِيَهْ ۜ هَلَكَ عَنِّي سُلْطَانِيَهْ﴾ al-Ḥāqqah 69:28–29
  3. and the iẓhār of the thāʾ in يَلْهَثْ ذَلِكَ
    ﴿أَوْ تَتْرُكْهُ يَلْهَث ذَّلِكَ﴾ al-Aʿrāf 7:176

11. Omission of the Alif in هَأَنْتُمْ

The first matter concerns the word هَأَنْتُمْ.

Through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, al-Aṣbahānī reads this word with the alif after the hāʾ omitted, while retaining the tas-hīl of the second hamzah, which occurs in four places in the Qurʾān.

For example:

﴿هَا أَنْتُمْ هَؤُلَاءِ حَاجَجْتُمْ فِيمَا لَكُمْ بِهِ عِلْمٌ…﴾

“Here you are, arguing about that of which you have knowledge...” Āl ʿImrān 3:66

Through al-Miṣbāḥ, the alif following the hāʾ is omitted, while the second hamzah is read with tas-hīl.

12. Iẓhār of the Hāʾ in مَالِيَهْ هَلَكَ

The second matter concerns the meeting of two hāʾs in مَالِيَهْ هَلَكَ. This occurs in Sūrat al-Ḥāqqah:

﴿مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّي مَالِيَهْ ۜ (٢٨) هَلَكَ عَنِّي سُلْطَانِيَهْ (٢٩)﴾

“My wealth has not benefited me. My authority has perished from me.” al-Ḥāqqah 69:28–29

The hāʾ in مَالِيَهْ is known as a hāʾ al-sakt. It is pronounced when stopping on the word.

When مَالِيَهْ is joined to هَلَكَ, two hāʾs come together. Through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, the ruling is iẓhār: the two hāʾs are kept distinct rather than being merged. To achieve this iẓhār, a brief pause is made on مَالِيَهْ, creating a slight separation between the two hāʾs before continuing: مَالِيَهْ ۜ هَلَكَ. Thus, the two hāʾs remain clearly audible.

13. Iẓhār of the Thāʾ in يَلْهَثْ ذَلِكَ

The third matter concerns the meeting of ثْ + ذ in the words يَلْهَثْ ذَلِكَ.

Allah تعالى says:

﴿أَوْ تَتْرُكْهُ يَلْهَث ذَّلِكَ﴾

“Or you leave him, he continues to pant. That is...” al-Aʿrāf 7:176

Here, the thāʾ of يَلْهَثْ is followed by the dhāl of ذَلِكَ.

Through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, the ruling is iẓhār: the thāʾ is pronounced clearly and distinctly, rather than being assimilated into the following dhāl.

The final word of this poetic line is قَلِّلَنْ, which indicates the ruling of taqlīl. It has not been discussed under this verse, however, because the word to which it relates appears in the following line, and its ruling will therefore be explained there.

verses.tr: (Apply taqlīl to) يٰس, together with idghām; in نَخْلُقْكُمْ, make the idghām complete; and in فِرْقٍ, pronounce the rāʾ with tafkhīm.

exp.en:
The poet now turns to three words containing four related matters in the recitation of al-Aṣbahānī through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ:

  1. Taqlīl of the yāʾ in يٰسٓ
    ﴿يٰسٓ﴾ Yā Sīn 36:1
  2. Idghām of the nūn of سِين into وَالْقُرْآنِ
    ﴿يٰسٓ (١) وَالْقُرْآنِ الْحَكِيمِ﴾ Yā Sīn 36:1–2
  3. Complete idghām of the qāf in نَخْلُقْكُمْ
    ﴿أَلَمْ نَخْلُقكُّمْ مِنْ مَاءٍ مَهِينٍ﴾ al-Mursalāt 77:20
  4. Tafkhīm of the rāʾ in فِرْقٍ
    ﴿فَكَانَ كُلُّ فِرْقٍ كَالطَّوْدِ الْعَظِيمِ﴾ al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:63

14. Taqlīl of the Yāʾ in يٰسٓ

﴿يٰسٓ﴾

“Yā Sīn.” Yā Sīn 36:1

Through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, the yāʾ of يٰسٓ is read with taqlīl.

Taqlīl, also known as al-imālah al-ṣughrā, is a pronunciation between fatḥ and full imālah. Thus, the yāʾ is not pronounced with completely open fatḥ, but is inclined slightly towards imālah.

15. Idghām in يٰسٓ وَالْقُرْآنِ

The second matter concerns joining the end of يٰسٓ to the beginning of ﴿وَالْقُرْآنِ﴾. At the end of the letter سِين, there is a nūn sākinah, which meets the wāw of وَالْقُرْآنِ.

Through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, the nūn is read with idghām into the following wāw, while retaining the ghunnah.

The poet therefore combines both rulings in the phrase يٰس مع إدغامه, meaning: Yā Sīn, together with its idghām. This is important because the taqlīl of يٰسٓ and the idghām of its nūn occur together in this route.

16. Complete Idghām in نَخْلُقْكُمْ

The third matter concerns the word نَخْلُقْكُمْ. Allah تعالى says:

﴿أَلَمْ نَخْلُقكُّمْ مِنْ مَاءٍ مَهِينٍ﴾

“Have We not created you from a humble fluid?” al-Mursalāt 77:20

Here, the qāf sākinah in نَخْلُقْ is followed by the kāf of كُمْ. Through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, the qāf is assimilated into the following kāf with complete idghām. This means that the qāf loses its independent pronunciation and the resulting sound is a pure, strengthened kāf.

17. Tafkhīm of the Rāʾ in فِرْقٍ

The final matter concerns the word فِرْقٍ. Allah تعالى says:

﴿فَانْفَلَقَ فَكَانَ كُلُّ فِرْقٍ كَالطَّوْدِ الْعَظِيمِ﴾

“Then the sea split, and each part became like a huge mountain.” al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:63

Here, the rāʾ in فِرْقٍ is followed by the letter qāf, which is a letter of istiʿlāʾ. Through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, the rāʾ is read with tafkhīm, meaning that it is pronounced heavily.

Thus, although the rāʾ itself carries a kasrah, the presence of the following letter of istiʿlāʾ, qāf, leads to its tafkhīm according to this route.

verses.ajuz: يَا مَرۡيَمٍ هَا مَرۡيَمٍ طَهَ اعۡرِفِ
verses.tr: In تَأْمَنَّا, apply ishmām; and apply fatḥ to the yāʾ of كهيعص, and to the hāʾ of كهيعص and طه.

exp.en:
The poet now mentions two matters relating to the recitation of al-Aṣbahānī through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ:

  1. Ishmām in تَأْمَنَّا
    ﴿مَا لَكَ لَا تَأْمَنَّا﴾ Yūsuf 12:11
  2. Fatḥ of the yāʾ and hāʾ in the opening letters of Sūrat Maryam and the hāʾ of Sūrat Ṭā Hā
    ﴿كٓهيعٓصٓ﴾ ﴿طه﴾

18. Ishmām in تَأْمَنَّا

The first matter concerns the word تَأْمَنَّا. Allah تعالى says:

﴿قَالُوا يَا أَبَانَا مَا لَكَ لَا تَأْمَنَّا عَلَىٰ يُوسُفَ وَإِنَّا لَهُ لَنَاصِحُونَ﴾

“They said, ‘O our father, why do you not trust us with Joseph, while we are truly sincere to him?’” Yūsuf 12:11

The original form of the word is تَأْمَنُنَا. It contains two nūns: the first has a ḍammah and the second has a fatḥah. The two nūns are assimilated, producing تَأْمَنَّا.

The important point for us is what happens to the first nūn when the two nūns are merged. Through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, the nūn is read with ishmām. This means that while the two nūns are fully assimilated, there is an indication of the original ḍammah of the first nūn through the lips.

Thus, the reading is تَأْمَنَّا with ishmām, not rūm.

19. Fatḥ of the Yāʾ and Hāʾ in كهيعص and طه

The second matter concerns the letters found at the beginning of Sūrat Maryam and Sūrat Ṭā Hā. Allah تعالى says:

﴿كٓهيعٓصٓ﴾

Maryam 19:1

and:

﴿طه﴾

Ṭā Hā 20:1

There are three letters mentioned by the poet:

  • the yāʾ of كهيعص
  • the hāʾ of كهيعص
  • the hāʾ of طه

Through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, these are read with fatḥ, rather than taqlīl.

verses.tr: Pronounce the hamzah of بِأَيِّ clearly wherever it occurs, together with تَأَذَّنَ; and in كِتَابِيَهْ إِنِّي, pronounce the hāʾ clearly. Always say: My Lord, guide us.

exp.en:
The poet now concludes his discussion of the matters relating to al-Aṣbahānī through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, by mentioning three matters concerning hamzah and the hāʾ of sakt:

  1. Taḥqīq of the hamzah in بِأَيِّ
    ﴿بِأَيِّ أَرْضٍ تَمُوتُ﴾ Luqmān 31:34
  2. Taḥqīq of the hamzah in تَأَذَّنَ in Sūrat Ibrāhīm
    ﴿وَإِذْ تَأَذَّنَ رَبُّكَ﴾ al-Aʿrāf 7:167
  3. Taḥqīq of the hāʾ in كِتَابِيَهْ إِنِّي when joining
    ﴿فَيَقُولُ هَاؤُمُ اقْرَءُوا كِتَابِيَهْ (١٩) إِنِّي ظَنَنْتُ…﴾ al-Ḥāqqah 69:19–20

20. Taḥqīq of the Hamzah in بِأَيِّ

The first matter concerns the word بِأَيِّ. The word occurs in several places in the Qurʾān, such as:

﴿بِأَيِّ أَرْضٍ تَمُوتُ﴾

“In which land you will die...” Luqmān 31:34

and:

﴿بِأَيِّكُمُ الْمَفْتُونُ﴾

“Which of you is afflicted with madness.” al-Qalam 68:6

Through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, the hamzah in بِأَيِّ is read with taḥqīq, meaning that the hamzah is pronounced clearly and fully.

This is specifically concerning بِأَيِّ when it occurs without the preceding fāʾ. This distinction is important because when the word occurs preceded by fāʾ, as in:

﴿فَبِأَيِّ آلَاءِ رَبِّكُمَا تُكَذِّبَانِ﴾

“So, which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?” al-Raḥmān 55:13

the hamzah is treated differently.

The ruling mentioned in this verse is therefore for the standalone بِأَيِّ, where the hamzah is pronounced clearly, rather than being replaced with a yāʾ.

21. Taḥqīq of the Hamzah in تَأَذَّنَ

The second matter concerns the word تَأَذَّنَ, which occurs in two places in the Qurʾān.

In Sūrat al-Aʿrāf, Allah تعالى says:

﴿وَإِذْ تَأَذَّنَ رَبُّكَ لَيَبْعَثَنَّ عَلَيْهِمْ إِلَىٰ يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ﴾

“And when your Lord proclaimed that He would surely send upon them...” al-Aʿrāf 7:167

And in Sūrat Ibrāhīm:

﴿وَإِذْ تَأَذَّنَ رَبُّكُمْ لَئِنْ شَكَرْتُمْ لَأَزِيدَنَّكُمْ﴾

“And when your Lord proclaimed: If you are grateful, I will surely increase you.” Ibrāhīm 14:7

There is no disagreement regarding the reading in al-Aʿrāf for al-Aṣbahānī: the hamzah is read with tashīl, between a hamzah and an alif.

The point of this verse concerns the occurrence in Sūrat Ibrāhīm. Through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, the hamzah in تَأَذَّنَ is read with taḥqīq.

Thus, unlike the occurrence in al-Aʿrāf, the hamzah here is pronounced clearly and fully, rather than being read with tashīl.

22. Taḥqīq of the Hāʾ in كِتَابِيَهْ إِنِّي

The final matter concerns the words كِتَابِيَهْ إِنِّي. Allah تعالى says:

﴿فَيَقُولُ هَاؤُمُ اقْرَءُوا كِتَابِيَهْ (١٩) إِنِّي ظَنَنْتُ أَنِّي مُلَاقٍ حِسَابِيَهْ﴾

“He will say, ‘Here, read my record. Indeed, I was certain that I would meet my reckoning.’” al-Ḥāqqah 69:19–20

The hāʾ in كِتَابِيَهْ is a hāʾ al-sakt. Its original ruling is sukūn. When the word is joined to إِنِّي, the hamzah of إِنِّي comes after the hāʾ: كِتَابِيَهْ إِنِّي.

There is a question here concerning whether the vowel of the hamzah should be transferred onto the hāʾ through naql, or whether the hāʾ should remain sākin and the hamzah should be pronounced clearly.

Through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, the reading taken for al-Aṣbahānī is taḥqīq without naql. In other words, the hāʾ remains clearly pronounced with its original sukūn.

The poet concludes: دَائِمًا رَبِّ اهْدِنَا “Always, [say:] My Lord, guide us.”

This final phrase serves as a beautiful conclusion to the poem. After guiding the reader through the precise details of the recitation, the poet reminds us that correct recitation is ultimately a gift from Allah.

The reader may study the rules, learn the routes, memorise the differences and perfect the pronunciation, but the ability to recite the Qurʾān correctly is itself a tawfīq from Allah.

chapters.ar: بَهجَةُ الأَرۡوَاح: أحۡكَام رِوايَةِ حَفۡص عَن طَرِيقِ المصبَاح
chapters.en: Bahjat al-Arwāḥ: A Versification of the Rulings of the Riwāyah of Ḥafṣ via the Route of al-Miṣbāḥ
chapters.desc: The ten matters in which the riwāyah of Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim, by the route recorded in al-Shahrazūrī’s al-Miṣbāḥ and also found within Ibn al-Jazarī’s Ṭayyibat al-Nashr, differs from the standard route of the Shāṭibiyyah (Ḥirz al-Amānī).

verses.sadr: لَكَ الۡحَمۡدُ يَارَبِي عَلَى النِّعَمِ الۡعُلا
verses.tr: To You is praise, my Lord, for the sublime blessings, and the purest prayer upon the Messenger, beginning with the Basmalah.

exp.en:
Background

The riwāyah of Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim → following a particular route recorded in al-Miṣbāḥ → a work compiled by al-Shahrazūrī → also found within Ibn al-Jazarī’s Ṭayyibat al-Nashr

The chain of transmission: al-Fīl (route associated with) → al-Walī (narrating from) → al-Ḥammāmī (passing through)

This poem addresses a specialized point of qirāʾāt: the recitation rulings specific to the riwāyah of Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim, following a particular route recorded in al-Miṣbāḥ, a work compiled by al-Shahrazūrī, and also found within Ibn al-Jazarī’s Ṭayyibat al-Nashr.

The poem’s second verse names a chain of transmission passing through al-Ḥammāmī, from a figure referred to as al-Walī, narrating in turn from a route associated with al-Fīl.

The poem’s fourth verse states plainly that this route differs from the standard route of Ḥirz al-Amānī (the Shāṭibiyyah) in ten specific matters, which the remaining verses then enumerate one after another.

The following table summarises these ten points of difference, contrasting the reading transmitted through al-Miṣbāḥ with the corresponding route of al-Shāṭibiyyah.

Comparison between the routes of al-Miṣbāḥ and al-Shāṭibiyyah

  • Mad al-Munfaṣil and the Madd al-Taʿẓīm
    al-Miṣbāḥ: Qaṣr, two ḥarakāt
    al-Shāṭibiyyah: Four or five ḥarakāt, and the first is more well-known
  • يَبْصُطُ / بَصْطَةً
    al-Miṣbāḥ: With ṣād
    al-Shāṭibiyyah: With sīn
  • الْمُصَيْطِرُونَ
    al-Miṣbāḥ: With sīn
    al-Shāṭibiyyah: With ṣād or sīn, with ṣād being the preferred reading
  • آلئن / آللَّهُ / الذَّكَرَيْنِ
    al-Miṣbāḥ: Ibdāl only
    al-Shāṭibiyyah: Both ibdāl and tas-hīl are permitted
  • تَأْمَنَّا
    al-Miṣbāḥ: Ishmām only
    al-Shāṭibiyyah: Ishmām or ikhtilās
  • ʿAyn in كهيعص and عسق
    al-Miṣbāḥ: Four ḥarakāt
    al-Shāṭibiyyah: Four or six ḥarakāt
  • The yāʾ in آتانِ
    al-Miṣbāḥ: Omit the yāʾ and stop with a nūn sākinah
    al-Shāṭibiyyah: Retain the yāʾ, or omit it while retaining the nūn sākinah
  • فِرْقٍ
    al-Miṣbāḥ: Tafkhīm of the rāʾ
    al-Shāṭibiyyah: Tafkhīm or tarqīq, with tarqīq being the preferred reading
  • ضَعْفٍ
    al-Miṣbāḥ: Fatḥ of the ḍād
    al-Shāṭibiyyah: Fatḥ or ḍamm, with fatḥ being the preferred reading
  • The alif in سَلَاسِلا
    al-Miṣbāḥ: Omit the alif and make the lām sākin
    al-Shāṭibiyyah: Retain the alif, or omit it
  • Takbīr
    al-Miṣbāḥ: Takbīr at the end of the sūrahs
    al-Shāṭibiyyah: No takbīr

Explanation

The poet opens with praise to Allah and prayer upon the Prophet, then names the chain of transmission for this route and its two written sources, al-Miṣbāḥ and Ṭayyibat al-Nashr, in the next verse, before turning to the substantive rulings.

verses.tr: And thereafter: al-Ḥammāmī transmits from al-Walī, with the qaṣr of the Madd al-Taʿẓīm, relaying from the route of al-Fīl.

exp.en:
The poet mentions two matters in this verse:

  1. The chain of transmission
  2. The shortening of the Madd al-Taʿẓīm

1. The chain of transmission

The recitation of Ḥafṣ through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ reaches us through:

al-Ḥammāmī → al-Walī → al-Fīl

The poet mentions only these transmitters and does not continue the chain back to ʿĀṣim.

2. Qaṣr of the Madd al-Taʿẓīm

Madd al-Taʿẓīm is read with qaṣr, meaning two ḥarakāt, through this route.

Madd al-Taʿẓīm, also called Madd al-Mubālaghah, occurs in the lā of negation in the statement of tawḥīd:

﴿لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا أَنتَ سُبْحَانَكَ إِنِّي كُنتُ مِنَ الظَّالِمِينَ﴾

“There is no deity except You. Glory be to You! Indeed, I was among the wrongdoers.” al-Anbiyāʾ 21:87

Thus, through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, the lā is elongated for two ḥarakāt only.

sadrW.g: of Shahrazū-r, i.e. al-Shahrazūrī (the name runs on)

verses.tr: And that is gathered in al-Miṣbāḥ of al-Shahrazūrī and also transmitted in the sublime Ṭayyibah.
So, for mad al-muttaṣil, apply tawassuṭ, and shorten what is munfaṣil, differing from their Ḥirz in ten matters.

exp.en:
The poet announces the count directly: this route diverges from the Shāṭibiyyah in ten specific rulings, the first two of which are given here:

1. Mad al-muttaṣil

Where the mad letter and hamzah occur in the same word, it is read with a moderate length (tawassuṭ).

2. Mad al-munfaṣil

When the mad letter and hamzah occur across two words, read it with qaṣr (shortened).

verses.ajuz: وَإِنۡ شِئۡتَ كَبِّرۡ فِي أَوَاخِرِهَا الۡحُلا
verses.tr: In يَبْصُطُ, read the word with a ṣād, and likewise بَصْطَةُ. And if you wish, recite takbīr at the ends of the concluding sūrahs.

exp.en:
The poet now mentions two matters concerning the recitation of Ḥafṣ through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ:

  1. Reading يَبْصُطُ and بَصْطَةُ with ṣād
  2. The optional takbīr at the ends of the concluding sūrahs

3. Ṣād in يَبْصُطُ and بَصْطَةُ

The first matter concerns the two words: يَبْصُطُ and بَصْطَةُ

Allah تعالى says:

﴿وَاللَّهُ يَقْبِضُ وَيَبْصُطُ وَإِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾

“Allah withholds and grants abundantly, and to Him you will be returned.” al-Baqarah 2:245

And:

﴿وَزَادَكُمْ فِي الْخَلْقِ بَصْطَةً﴾

“And He increased you in stature and strength.” al-Aʿrāf 7:69

Through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, both words are read with ṣād.

4. Takbīr at the ends of the sūrahs

The second matter concerns takbīr, اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ, at the conclusion of the sūrahs.

Through this route, takbīr is permissible at the ends of the concluding sūrahs.

verses.tr: But read الْمُصَيْطِرُونَ with a sīn, and apply ishmām to تَأْمَنَّا, and disregard rawm for it.

exp.en:
The poet now mentions the next two matters concerning the recitation through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ:

  1. Reading الْمُصَيْطِرُونَ with sīn
  2. Ishmām in تَأْمَنَّا, without rawm

5. Reading الْمُصَيْطِرُونَ with sīn

The first matter concerns the word: الْمُصَيْطِرُونَ

Allah تعالى says:

﴿أَمْ عِندَهُمْ خَزَائِنُ رَبِّكَ أَمْ هُمُ الْمُصَيْطِرُونَ﴾

“Or do they possess the treasuries of your Lord, or are they the ones in control?” al-Ṭūr 52:37

Through this route, the word is read with a sīn.

6. Ishmām in تَأْمَنَّا and leaving rawm

The second matter returns to the word: تَأْمَنَّا

Allah تعالى says:

﴿قَالُوا يَا أَبَانَا مَا لَكَ لَا تَأْمَنَّا عَلَىٰ يُوسُفَ وَإِنَّا لَهُ لَنَاصِحُونَ﴾

“They said, ‘O our father, why do you not trust us with Joseph, while we are truly sincere to him?’” Yūsuf 12:11

As mentioned previously, through the route of al-Miṣbāḥ, تَأْمَنَّا is read with ishmām.

Ishmām is performed by briefly rounding the lips after the sukūn of the letter, as though preparing to pronounce a ḍammah, without an audible vowel being produced.

verses.tr: And أَللَّه, with أَلْآنَ and أَلذَّكَرَيْنِ, do not read it with tashīl; rather, substitute it with a fully lengthened mad.

exp.en:
7. Ibdāl of the second hamzah

The poet now highlights the reading of the second hamzah in certain words where two hamzahs come together. In this route, the second hamzah is not read with tashīl. Instead, it is changed into an alif of madd, resulting in a prolonged madd.

This occurs in the following three words across the Qurʾān:

1. أَللَّه

﴿قُلْ آللَّهُ أَذِنَ لَكُمْ أَمْ عَلَى اللَّهِ تَفْتَرُونَ﴾

“Say: Has Allah permitted you, or do you fabricate lies against Allah?” Yūnus 10:59

2. ءَآلْآنَ

﴿ءَآلْآنَ وَقَدْ عَصَيْتَ قَبْلُ وَكُنتَ مِنَ الْمُفْسِدِينَ﴾

“Now? Yet you disobeyed before and were of the corrupters.” Yūnus 10:91

3. ءَآلذَّكَرَيْنِ

﴿قُلْ ءَآلذَّكَرَيْنِ حَرَّمَ أَمِ الْأُنثَيَيْنِ﴾

“Say: Is it the two males that He has forbidden, or the two females?” al-Anʿām 6:143

In all three examples, the second hamzah is changed into an alif of madd, rather than being read with tashīl.

verses.tr: When stopping on آتَانِ, omit the yāʾ; and omit the alif of سَلَاسِلَا, both when stopping and when continuing.

exp.en:
The poet now mentions two matters concerning the omission of letters in specific words:

  1. Omitting the yāʾ in آتَانِ when stopping
  2. Omitting the alif in سَلَاسِلَا both when stopping and when continuing

8. Omitting the yāʾ in آتَانِ when stopping

The first matter concerns the word: آتَانِ

Allah تعالى says:

﴿فَمَا آتَانِيَ اللَّهُ خَيْرٌ مِمَّا آتَاكُم﴾

“What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you.” al-Naml 27:36

When stopping on the word آتَانِ, the yāʾ is omitted, and the word is read: آتَانْ

9. Omitting the alif in سَلَاسِلَا

The second matter concerns the word: سَلَاسِلَا

Allah تعالى says:

﴿إِنَّا أَعْتَدْنَا لِلْكَافِرِينَ سَلَاسِلَا وَأَغْلَالًا وَسَعِيرًا﴾

“Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers chains, shackles, and a blazing fire.” al-Insān 76:4

The alif at the end of سَلَاسِلَا is omitted both when stopping and when continuing.

verses.sadr: وفِي عَينِ وَسِّطۡ ثُمَّ فِرۡقٍ فَفَخِّمَنۡ
verses.tr: And for عَيْن, apply tawassuṭ; then read فِرْقٍ with a heavy rāʾ. Read ضَعْفٌ with a fatḥah, and the poem has now come to an end, so proclaim the tahlīl.

exp.en:
The poet concludes the poem by mentioning the tenth and final point, which gathers three smaller rulings together:

  1. Madd of عَيْن to four ḥarakāt
  2. Tafkhīm of the rāʾ in فِرْقٍ
  3. Fatḥ of the ḍād in ضَعْفٌ

10.1. Madd of عَيْن

The first matter concerns the letter عَيْن in the two openings:

﴿كهيعص﴾

Maryam 19:1

and:

﴿عسق﴾

al-Shūrā 42:2

The letter عَيْن is read with tawassuṭ.

10.2. Tafkhīm of the rāʾ in فِرْقٍ

The second matter concerns the word: فِرْقٍ

Allah تعالى says:

﴿فَانفَلَقَ فَكَانَ كُلُّ فِرْقٍ كَالطَّوْدِ الْعَظِيمِ﴾

“Then it split, and each portion became like a huge mountain.” al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:63

The rāʾ in فِرْقٍ is read with tafkhīm, despite the preceding kasrah, because of the presence of the letter qāf, which is a letter of istiʿlāʾ.

10.3. Fatḥ of the ḍād in ضَعْفٌ

The third matter concerns the word: ضَعْفٍ

Allah تعالى says:

﴿اللَّهُ الَّذِي خَلَقَكُم مِّن ضَعْفٍ ثُمَّ جَعَلَ مِن بَعْدِ ضَعْفٍ قُوَّةً﴾

“Allah is the One who created you from weakness, then after weakness gave you strength.” al-Rūm 30:54

And later in the same āyah:

﴿ثُمَّ جَعَلَ مِن بَعْدِ قُوَّةٍ ضَعْفًا وَشَيْبَةً﴾

“Then after strength He brought weakness and old age.” al-Rūm 30:54

The ḍād in all three occurrences is read with fatḥah.

The poet concludes:

وَتَمَّتْ فَهَلِّلَا

This means that the poem has now been completed. The reader or listener should therefore conclude by making tahlīl: لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ

Thus, the final words of the poem are not merely announcing its completion but directing the reader to remember Allah by proclaiming His oneness.

chapters.ar: أَقۡسَامُ الكَلِمَاتِ المَخۡتومَةِ بحرفِ مَدٍّ مِنۡ جِهةِ الرَّسۡمِ والنُّطقِ وَصلًا ووَقفًا
chapters.en: The Categories of Words Ending in a Madd Letter, by Rasm and by Pronunciation in Waṣl and Waqf
chapters.desc: Words ending in a madd letter (alif, wāw or yāʾ) sorted by two separate questions: is the letter written in the Uthmānī rasm or omitted from it, and is it pronounced in both waṣl and waqf, in neither, or in only one of them?

verses.tr: Words whose endings are madd letters: these are their categories.

exp.en:
Background

This poem addresses a point of qirāʾāt that combines two separate questions about words ending in a madd letter: alif, wāw, or yāʾ:

1. Is the madd letter written in the Uthmānī rasm or omitted from the rasm?

This gives the two major sections:

  • إذا كان حرف المد ثَابتا رسما: the madd letter is present in the rasm.
  • إذا كان حرف المد محذوفًا رسما: the madd letter is omitted from the rasm.

2. How is that madd letter actually pronounced?

The pronunciation is divided into four possibilities:

  • ثابتًا نطقًا في الحالين Pronounced in both waṣl and waqf
  • محذوفًا نطقًا في الحالين Not pronounced in either waṣl or waqf
  • ثابتًا في النطق وصلًا لا وقفًا Pronounced in waṣl, but omitted in waqf
  • ثابتًا في النطق وقفًا لا وصلًا Pronounced in waqf, but omitted in waṣl

Thus, a madd letter can be written but not pronounced, or omitted from the rasm but still pronounced, and its pronunciation can also change depending on whether you stop or continue.

The concept is further illustrated as follows:

  • 1. The rasm: whether the letter (alif, wāw or yāʾ) is written in the rasm (the standard Uthmanic script) or omitted from it.
  • 2. The pronunciation: how the letter is actually pronounced, which may differ from the rasm and may also differ between waṣl (continuous recitation) and waqf (when stopping).

Explanation

The poet opens by announcing the topic directly: words ending in one of the madd letters, such as يَدْعُوْا and ثَمُوْدَا, are about to be sorted into a set of categories.

verses.sadr: مِنۡ جِهَةِ الرَّسۡمِ ثُبُوتٌ أَوۡ فَلَا

sadrW.g: from the side of the rasm

verses.tr: From the perspective of the rasm, the madd letter is either present or absent; and both categories are further divided according to their pronunciation.

exp.en:
Having introduced the words that end with a letter of madd, the poet now begins to classify them.

The first division is by rasm: a word’s final madd letter may or may not actually appear in the standard Uthmanic script, regardless of how the word is pronounced.

The poet then signals that these two rasm categories divide further according to how the letter is pronounced.

verses.tr: They are either omitted in both cases or pronounced in both; or they are pronounced only when continuing, or only when stopping. So, understand this.

exp.en:
The poet now completes the classification mentioned in the previous verse.

Whether the madd letter is present in the rasm or omitted from the rasm, its pronunciation falls into four possibilities:

  1. محذوف نطقًا في الحالين: omitted in both waṣl and waqf
  2. ثابت نطقًا في الحالين: pronounced in both waṣl and waqf
  3. ثابت نطقًا وصلًا فقط: pronounced in waṣl but omitted in waqf
  4. ثابت نطقًا وقفًا فقط: pronounced in waqf but omitted in waṣl

verses.ajuz: وَصِلۡ لَهُ وَعِنۡدَ بَصۡرٍ أَيُّهَ الۡ

sadrW.g: yasri: (its yāʾ read in both states)

ajuzW.g: ayyuha al-… (its alif read in waqf)

verses.tr: For al-Makkī, يَسْرِ is read with the yāʾ in both waṣl and waqf; فَتَوَلَّ (the alif) is omitted in pronunciation for everyone. The ṣilah of لَهُ is pronounced in waṣl only. While أَيُّهَ, according to al-Baṣrī (the alif in أيهَ) is pronounced when stopping.

exp.en:
The poet now begins giving examples of the different ways in which a final letter of madd may be treated in recitation, as outlined in the previous verses.

  • He first mentions the word يَسْرِ. Although the yāʾ is omitted from the Uthmanic rasm, Ibn Kathīr al-Makkī nevertheless pronounces it in both situations, whether continuing (waṣl) or stopping (waqf), even though it is not present in the rasm.
  • The poet then mentions فَتَوَلَّ. Here, the alif is not pronounced in either case, neither in waṣl nor in waqf, and this reading applies to all the reciters.
  • The poet then says وَصِلْ لَهُ, referring to the ṣilah of the pronoun هُ in لَهُ, as in the āyah لهُ الْملكُ. The ṣilah is not represented in the rasm, yet it is established in pronunciation when the recitation continues.
  • Finally, the poet turns to أَيُّهَ. Here, the treatment differs according to the reciter. For the Baṣriyyeen, the alif is pronounced when stopping, but not when continuing.

verses.tr: In دَعَا, the alif is established in both cases, while ثَمُودَا is an example where the alif, although written, is not pronounced in either case. Ibn Dhakwān has فَلَا تَسْأَلْنِي, where the yāʾ is pronounced when continuing but omitted when stopping. The eighth example is قَالَا. Understand and apply these examples carefully.

exp.en:
The poet continues to illustrate the different categories mentioned in the previous verses by giving further Qurʾānic examples.

  • He first mentions دَعَا. The alif is written in the Uthmanic rasm and pronounced in both waṣl and waqf.
  • He then gives ثَمُودَا. Here, the alif is written in the rasm, but it is not pronounced in either waṣl or waqf.
  • The poet then gives the example connected to the reading of Ibn Dhakwān: فَلَا تَسْأَلْنِي. The yāʾ in تَسْأَلْنِي is pronounced when continuing, but is omitted when stopping, in one of the transmitted ways of Ibn Dhakwān.
  • Finally, the poet says وَالثَّامِنُ فِي قَالَا, referring to قَالَا in:

﴿وَقَالَا الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ﴾

al-Naml 27:15

Here, the alif is written in the rasm, but it is pronounced only when stopping, and it is not pronounced when continuing.

The closing word اعْقِلَا is a reminder to the reader: understand these examples carefully, connect each example to its rule, and apply the classification intelligently rather than merely memorising the examples.

The pronunciation and writing of words ending in a madd letter (alif, wāw or yāʾ)

Written in the rasm مكْتُوب في الرَّسْم

  • Pronounced in both waṣl and waqf ثابتًا نطقًا في الحالين: دَعا, alif written and pronounced in both.
  • Not pronounced in either waṣl or waqf محذوفا نطقًا في الحالين: ثَمُودَا, alif written but not pronounced in either waṣl or waqf.
  • Pronounced in waṣl only ثابتًا نطقًا وصلًا فقط: تَسْأَلْنِي, yāʾ written and pronounced in waṣl only, according to one reading of Ibn Dhakwān.
  • Pronounced in waqf only ثابتًا نطقًا وقفًا فقط: قَالَا, alif written and pronounced in waqf only.

Omitted from the rasm مَحْذُوف في الرَّسْم

  • Pronounced in both: يَسْرِ, yāʾ omitted from the rasm but pronounced in both by al-Makkī.
  • Pronounced in neither: فَتَوَلَّ, alif omitted from the rasm and not pronounced in either.
  • Pronounced in waṣl only: لَهُ, the ṣilah is not written, yet it is pronounced in waṣl only.
  • Pronounced in waqf only: أَيُّهَ, alif omitted from the rasm but pronounced in waqf according to al-Baṣrī.

chapters.ar: حكم ياءات الزوائد عند حفص في سورة الكهف
chapters.en: The Yāʾāt al-Zawāʾid Dropped by Ḥafṣ in Sūrat al-Kahf
chapters.desc: Ḥafṣ omits the Yāʾāt al-Zawāʾid, the additional yāʾs not written in the Uthmānic rasm, in both waṣl and waqf. These lines gather the nine places in Sūrat al-Kahf where he omits them, in a concise and memorable form.

verses.tr: من يَهدِ، فَهُوَ الْمُهْتَدِ، تُعَلِّمَنِ، تَرَنِ، نَبْغِ، يَهْدِيَنِ، يُؤْتِيَنِ

exp.en:
Background

This poem addresses a point of qirāʾāt concerning the Yāʾāt al-Zawāʾid: the additional yāʾs found at the ends of certain Qurʾānic words which are not written in the Uthmānic rasm.

The term Yāʾāt al-Zawāʾid refers to those occurrences of the letter yāʾ that come at the end of words, and which are read by some of the Qurrāʾ when reading waṣlan, or when reading either waṣlan or waqfan, despite them not being written according to the rasm of the Qurʾān, e.g. كيدُونِ, الدَّاع.

The Qurrāʾ treat these yāʾs differently. Ibn Kathīr establishes them in both waṣl and waqf, while Hishām has both options: reading and omission. Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah, and al-Kisāʾī read them in waṣl and omit them in waqf.

As for Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim, the general rule is that the Yāʾāt al-Zawāʾid are omitted in both waṣl and waqf. One exception to this general rule is آتَانِيَ in Sūrah al-Naml, where the yāʾ is established in waṣl. At waqf, Ḥafṣ has both the options of omission and reading, with reading being the preferred option.

With this principle in mind, the poet beautifully captures the nine occurrences in Sūrah al-Kahf in which the additional yāʾ is omitted according to Ḥafṣ, presenting them together in a concise and memorable form for ease of memorisation and recall.

Abyāt 1–2

In these three lines, the poet beautifully gathers the nine occurrences in Sūrah al-Kahf in which the additional yāʾ is omitted according to the recitation of Ḥafṣ. Rather than mentioning the full verses, he carefully identifies the words themselves, allowing the nine places to be easily memorised:

1. يَهْدِ — Sūrah al-Kahf: 17

﴿مَن يَهْدِ اللَّهُ فَهُوَ الْمُهْتَدِ﴾

“Whoever Allah guides is the rightly guided.” al-Kahf 18:17

2. الْمُهْتَدِ — Sūrah al-Kahf: 17

﴿مَن يَهْدِ اللَّهُ فَهُوَ الْمُهْتَدِ﴾

“Whoever Allah guides is the rightly guided.” al-Kahf 18:17

These are the first two occurrences, appearing together in the same āyah.

3. تُعَلِّمَنِ — Sūrah al-Kahf: 66

﴿هَلْ أَتَّبِعُكَ عَلَىٰ أَن تُعَلِّمَنِ مِمَّا عُلِّمْتَ رُشْدًا﴾

“May I follow you so that you may teach me some of what you have been taught of right guidance?” al-Kahf 18:66

4. تَرَنِ — Sūrah al-Kahf: 39

﴿إِن تَرَنِ أَنَا أَقَلَّ مِنكَ مَالًا وَوَلَدًا﴾

“If you see me as having less wealth and children than you…” al-Kahf 18:39

5. نَبْغِ — Sūrah al-Kahf: 64

﴿قَالَ ذَٰلِكَ مَا كُنَّا نَبْغِ﴾

“He said, ‘That is what we were seeking.’” al-Kahf 18:64

6. يَهْدِيَنِ — Sūrah al-Kahf: 24

﴿عَسَىٰ أَن يَهْدِيَنِ رَبِّي لِأَقْرَبَ مِنْ هَٰذَا رَشَدًا﴾

“Perhaps my Lord will guide me to something closer to right guidance than this.” al-Kahf 18:24

7. يُؤْتِيَنِ — Sūrah al-Kahf: 40

﴿فَعَسَىٰ رَبِّي أَن يُؤْتِيَنِ خَيْرًا مِّن جَنَّتِكَ﴾

“Perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden.” al-Kahf 18:40

8. تَسْتَفْتِ — Sūrah al-Kahf: 22

﴿فَلَا تُمَارِ فِيهِمْ إِلَّا مِرَاءً ظَاهِرًا وَلَا تَسْتَفْتِ فِيهِم مِّنْهُمْ أَحَدًا﴾

“Do not dispute concerning them except with an obvious argument, nor ask any of them concerning them.” al-Kahf 18:22

9. تُمَارِ — Sūrah al-Kahf: 22

﴿فَلَا تُمَارِ فِيهِمْ إِلَّا مِرَاءً ظَاهِرًا﴾

“Do not dispute concerning them except with an obvious argument.” al-Kahf 18:22

Thus, the nine words are:

يَهْدِ — الْمُهْتَدِ — تُعَلِّمَنِ — تَرَنِ — نَبْغِ — يَهْدِيَنِ — يُؤْتِيَنِ — تَسْتَفْتِ — تُمَارِ

All nine are read by Ḥafṣ with the additional yāʾ omitted, in accordance with the established rule for Yāʾāt al-Zawāʾid.

verses.tr: تَسْتَفْتِ، لَا تُمَارِ: nine occurrences, so preserve them carefully.

chapters.ar: مَوَاضِعُ تَفۡخِيۡمِ الرَّاءِ عِنۡدَ وَرۡشٍ بِغَيۡرِ خُلۡفِ
chapters.en: The Words Where Warsh Reads the Rāʾ with Tafkhīm, without Disagreement
chapters.desc: A riddle the poet found in a manuscript on the qirāʾāt, set in verse with its answer: the words in which Warsh reads the rāʾ with tafkhīm without any alternative while most reciters read it with tarqīq, because the words themselves are vocalised differently.

verses.ajuz: وَرۡشٌ بِهَا فِي الرَّاءِ قُلۡ لِي مَا هِيَهۡ
verses.tr: Without any disagreement, there are words in which Warsh reads the rāʾ with tafkhīm; tell me, what are they?

exp.en:
Background

The poet mentions that he came across a riddle in a manuscript on Qirāʾāt, concerning some words in which Warsh reads the rāʾ with tafkhīm without any alternative, while most other reciters read it with tarqīq. He then composed the riddle into verse, preserving its question-and-answer form: the first verses pose the riddle, while the following verse gives its answer.

This is among the finer points of Warsh’s recitation from Nāfiʿ, where his reading of the rāʾ differs from that of most other reciters. The distinction here is not simply a difference in the ruling of the rāʾ itself, but results from the different vocalisations transmitted for these particular words. Warsh’s reading gives a context in which the rāʾ is pronounced with tafkhīm, while the reading of most reciters gives a context in which it is pronounced with tarqīq.

The poet identifies three words in the original riddle, بَرَقَ، مَرْفِقًا، وَقَرْنَ, and then adds يُغْفَرْ لَكُمْ as another example.

Abyāt 1–3

The poet is referring to four words in which Warsh reads the rāʾ with tafkhīm, without any alternative reading, while most of the other reciters read it with tarqīq.

The distinction becomes clear when the vocalisation of each word is considered. In each case, the reading transmitted from Warsh differs from that of the majority, and this difference in vocalisation directly affects the ruling of the rāʾ.

The four occurrences are as follows:

1. بَرَقَ

Allah تعالى says:

﴿فَإِذَا بَرِقَ الْبَصَرُ﴾

al-Qiyāmah 75:7

  • Warsh reads the word as: بَرَقَ. With the fatḥah on the rāʾ, the rāʾ is read with tafkhīm.
  • Most reciters read: بَرِقَ. With the kasrah on the rāʾ, it is read with tarqīq.

Thus, the difference in the vocalisation of the word results in a difference in the treatment of its rāʾ.

2. مَرْفِقًا

Allah تعالى says:

﴿وَيُهَيِّئْ لَكُم مِّنْ أَمْرِكُم مِّرْفَقًا﴾

al-Kahf 18:16

  • Warsh reads: مَرْفِقًا. The rāʾ is sākinah and is preceded by a fatḥah, so it is read with tafkhīm.
  • Most reciters read: مِرْفَقًا. Here, the rāʾ is sākinah and is preceded by an original kasrah, so it is read with tarqīq.

3. وَقَرْنَ

Allah تعالى says:

﴿وَقَرْنَ فِي بُيُوتِكُنَّ﴾

al-Aḥzāb 33:33

  • Warsh reads: وَقَرْنَ. The rāʾ is sākinah and is preceded by a fatḥah, giving it tafkhīm.
  • Most reciters read: وَقِرْنَ. The rāʾ is preceded by an original kasrah, giving it tarqīq.

4. يُغْفَرْ لَكُمْ

The poet adds this fourth example:

﴿نَغْفِرْ لَكُمْ خَطَايَاكُمْ﴾

al-Baqarah 2:58

  • Warsh reads: يُغْفَرْ لَكُمْ. The rāʾ is sākinah and preceded by a fatḥah, so it is read with tafkhīm.
  • Most reciters read: نَغْفِرْ لَكُمْ. The rāʾ is preceded by a kasrah, so it is read with tarqīq.

In this way, the riddle highlights a particularly distinctive feature of the reading of Warsh: the same rāʾ is treated differently because the transmitted vocalisation of the word itself differs between the readings.

verses.tr: While most reciters read them with tarqīq, the answer is: بَرَقَ، مَرْفِقًا، وَقَرْنَ.
And likewise يُغْفَرْ لَكُمْ, which I have added to them; O our Lord, we hope for the lofty gardens of Paradise.

chapters.ar: السَّبۡعُ الَّتِى زِيۡدَتۡ فِيۡهَا الۡوَاوُ وَاليَاءُ وَتَعَيَّنَ فِيۡهَا الإدغَامُ وَامۡتَنَعَ النَّقۡلُ.
chapters.en: The Seven Words Where Ḥamzah Must Use Idghām, Never Naql
chapters.desc: When stopping, Ḥamzah reads seven words whose hamzah follows an extra yāʾ or wāw of madd with idghām only, never naql; the poet builds on the well-known mnemonic verse in which an earlier scholar gathered them.

verses.sadr: أدۡغِمۡ فَقَطۡ لا تَنۡقُلَنۡ في سَبۡعَةِ
verses.tr: Make idghām only (assimilate); do not apply naql, in seven [words] in which an extra wāw or yāʾ has been added, (according to the reading of) Hamzah.

exp.en:
Background

This poem concerns a particular aspect of وقف حمزة على الهمز. Ḥamzah has several ways of dealing with a word containing hamzah when stopping. These verses, however, address a specific set of seven words in which the hamzah is preceded by an additional ياء مدية or واو مدية.

In these words, when stopping, حمزة reads the hamzah with إدغام, assimilating the two letters together with a doubling. Consequently, the usual option of نقل, transferring the hamzah’s vowel onto the preceding letter and lightening it, is not permitted.

The seven words are gathered in a well-known verse transmitted among the reciters. The poet notes that these positions had already been gathered, generations earlier, by an unnamed but brilliant scholar (حبر عبقري) into a single, well-known verse, one the poet himself heard from his own teachers some thirty years ago, who in turn had heard it from theirs:

قِفْ فِي هَنِيئًا مَعْ مَرِيئًا مَعْ بَرِي ۞ دُرِّيٍّ نَسِيءٍ قُرُوءٍ خَطِيئَةٍ حَرِّرِ

The poet, Shaykh Dr. Walīd ibn Idrīs al-Minīsī, incorporates most of this inherited mnemonic into his own verse to indicate that these words are منقول, rather than his own formulation, while honouring the earlier poet who composed it.

The first bayt

The poet begins by stating the essential rule. At the relevant occurrences, the preceding واو or ياء is an extra letter of madd, and Hamzah, when stopping, replaces the following hamzah with a matching واو or ياء and then assimilates the two letters. Thus, the resulting pronunciation has idghām with tashdīd, while naql is excluded.

verses.sadr: قَدۡ عَدَّها مِنۡ قَبۡلُ حَبۡرٌ عَبۡقَري
verses.tr: A brilliant scholar had previously counted them, arranging them in his carefully composed verse.

exp.en: The poet acknowledges that the seven words were already gathered by an earlier scholar in a single mnemonic verse. He therefore preserves the established mnemonic rather than presenting its wording as his own.

verses.tr: “They are: هَنِيئًا, with مَرِيئًا, with بَرِيء, دُرِّيء, النَّسِيء, قُرُوء, and خَطِيئَة — preserve them carefully.”
Hishām likewise agrees with him in بَرِيء, النَّسِيء, and قُرُوء, where the hamzah falls at the very end; so, remember this.

exp.en:
The poet then identifies the agreement of Hishām with Ḥamzah in three of these words: بَرِيء, النَّسِيء, and قُرُوء. In these three cases, the hamzah is متطرفة, which is the point of agreement being highlighted.

There is, however, an important distinction concerning دُرِّيء. The poet is careful to explain why دُرِّيء is not counted among the words where Hishām agrees with Ḥamzah, despite falling within the same list of seven: حمزة reads it with hamzah, so it is included among his seven words. Hishām, on the other hand, does not pronounce the hamzah in دُرِّيء, neither in waṣl nor in waqf; therefore, it is not counted among his corresponding words.

The seven words

  • هَنِيئًا all its occurrences; an-Nisāʾ 4:4, among others. Also Hishām? No.
  • مَرِيئًا a single occurrence; an-Nisāʾ 4:4. Also Hishām? No.
  • بَرِيء all its occurrences, singular and plural; al-Anʿām 6:19, among others. Also Hishām? Yes.
  • دُرِّيء a single occurrence; an-Nūr 24:35. Also Hishām? No: Hishām does not pronounce a hamzah here at all.
  • النَّسِيء a single occurrence; at-Tawbah 9:37. Also Hishām? Yes.
  • قُرُوء a single occurrence; al-Baqarah 2:228. Also Hishām? Yes.
  • خَطِيئَة all its occurrences, singular and plural; al-Baqarah 2:81, among others. Also Hishām? No.

The essential point can therefore be preserved as follows:

  • حمزة: in these seven words, when stopping, إبدال الهمز ثم إدغامه is required, and نقل is excluded.
  • هشام: he agrees with Hamzah in three words, بَرِيء، النَّسِيء، قُرُوء, because the hamzah in these is متطرفة.
  • دُرِّيء: it is counted for Hamzah because he reads the hamzah, but it is not counted for Hishām because Hishām does not read its hamzah, neither in waṣl nor in waqf.

chapters.ar: نَظۡمُ زِيَادَاتِ الدُّرَّةِ عَلَى الطَّيبَة
chapters.en: The Four Readings Where al-Durrah Adds to Ṭayyibah
chapters.desc: Four readings of Ibn Wardān found in al-Durrah but not in Ṭayyibat al-Nashr, in at-Tawbah, al-Aʿrāf and al-Isrāʾ, each signalled by a word in the verse, with praise for the transmitters who preserved them.

verses.tr: Al-Durrah added over Ṭayyibah with four [readings]; take them: suqāta, 'amarah...

exp.en:
Background

The poem discusses four reading variants mentioned in al-Durrah that are additional to those found in Ṭayyibat al-Nashr. These variants concern specific words in three different sūrahs: at-Tawbah, al-Aʿrāf, and al-Isrāʾ. The poet identifies each occurrence through concise references within the verse, highlighting the particular readings transmitted by Ibn Wardān. He concludes by praising the distinguished transmitters who preserved and conveyed these readings.

Abyāt 1–2

The poet begins by stating that al-Durrah includes four additional reading variants beyond those found in Ṭayyibat al-Nashr. He then identifies the four places through brief references to the relevant words and their locations in the Qur’an.

1. سُقَاةَ and عَمَرَةَ: Sūrah at-Tawbah

The first two additions occur in the same verse, where Allah says:

﴿أَجَعَلْتُمْ سِقَايَةَ الْحَاجِّ وَعِمَارَةَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ كَمَنْ آمَنَ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ وَجَاهَدَ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ ۚ لَا يَسْتَوُونَ عِندَ اللَّهِ ۗ وَاللَّهُ لَا يَهْدِي الْقَوْمَ الظَّالِمِينَ﴾

at-Tawbah 9:19

The two words are سِقَايَةَ and عِمَارَةَ. In the reading attributed to Ibn Wardān in al-Durrah, they are read سُقَاةَ and عَمَرَةَ, respectively. The poet signals these two places with the words سُقَاةَ عَمَرَةْ.

2. يُخْرِجُ: Sūrah al-Aʿrāf

The third addition occurs in the statement of Allah:

﴿وَالْبَلَدُ الطَّيِّبُ يَخْرُجُ نَبَاتُهُ بِإِذْنِ رَبِّهِ ۖ وَالَّذِي خَبُثَ لَا يَخْرُجُ إِلَّا نَكِدًا ۚ كَذَٰلِكَ نُصَرِّفُ الْآيَاتِ لِقَوْمٍ يَشْكُرُونَ﴾

al-Aʿrāf 7:58

The relevant phrase is لَا يَخْرُجُ إِلَّا نَكِدًا. Ibn Wardān’s reading, as identified in al-Durrah, is لَا يُخْرِجُ, with ḍammah on the yāʾ and kasrah on the rāʾ. The poet points to this occurrence with يُخْرِجُ فِي الْأَعْرَافِ.

3. تُغَرِّقَ: Sūrah al-Isrāʾ

The fourth and final addition occurs in the verse:

﴿أَمْ أَمِنتُمْ أَن يُعِيدَكُمْ فِيهِ تَارَةً أُخْرَىٰ فَيُرْسِلَ عَلَيْكُمْ قَاصِفًا مِّنَ الرِّيحِ فَيُغْرِقَكُم بِمَا كَفَرْتُمْ ثُمَّ لَا تَجِدُوا لَكُمْ عَلَيْنَا بِهِ تَبِيعًا﴾

al-Isrāʾ 17:68–69

The relevant word is فَيُغْرِقَكُم. In the reading attributed to Ibn Wardān in al-Durrah, it is read فَتُغَرِّقَكُم, with tāʾ in place of yāʾ and a doubled rāʾ. The poet identifies it through مَعْ تُغَرِّقَ الْإِسْرَا.

The poet concludes with رَوَاهَا الْبَرَرَةْ, praising the noble transmitters who conveyed and preserved these readings. Their inclusion in the poem reflects the care taken by the scholars of qirāʾāt to preserve the transmitted forms of recitation accurately.

verses.sadr: فِي تَوۡبَةٍ يُخۡرِجُ فِي الۡأَعۡرَافِ مَعۡ
verses.tr: ...in Tawbah; yukhriju in al-A'rāf, together with tughriqa in al-Isrā'. The righteous ones transmitted them.

chapters.ar: المَنۡظُومَةُ المُهَذَّبَة فِي زِيَادَاتِ فَرۡشِ الطَّيِّبَة
chapters.en: The Additional Farsh Readings Unique to Ṭayyibat al-Nashr
chapters.desc: Seventeen farsh readings found in Ṭayyibat al-Nashr but not in the routes of al-Shāṭibiyyah and al-Durrah, arranged in a compact sequence that names each word, its sūrah where needed, and its reader or transmitter.

verses.sadr: فِي سَبۡعَةٍ مِنۡ بَعۡدِ عَشۡرٍ طَيِّبَةۡ
verses.tr: Seventeen additions are found in Ṭayyibah; here they are, in order.

exp.en:
Background

Studying the ten major (العشر الكبرى) and ten minor (العشر الصغرى) readings involves more than differences in the fundamental principles of recitation; it also requires careful attention to the individual words discussed under farsh al-ḥurūf (the specific differences in the pronunciation or form of Qur’anic words, rather than general principles of recitation).

While al-Shāṭibiyyah and al-Durrah cover the ten minor readings, Ṭayyibat al-Nashr presents the ten major readings, including additional transmitted variants not found in the routes covered by the former two works.

The poem arranges these additions in a compact sequence, identifying each word, its sūrah where necessary, and the reader or transmitter associated with it. The seventeen additions are explained below.

sadrW.g: for Ibn Wardān (lit. the son of Wardān)

verses.tr: Isjudū, for Ibn Wardān, with ishmām; and baṣṭatan (read with ṣād), for Qunbul, before 'ilm.

exp.en:
1. Ishmām (الإشمام) in اسْجُدُوا: Ibn Wardān

The poet refers to the phrase لِلْمَلَائِكَةِ اسْجُدُوا, wherever it occurs. Ibn Wardān has ishmām in اسْجُدُوا.

2. بَصْطَةً: Qunbul

This addition occurs in Sūrah al-Baqarah, where Allah says:

﴿وَزَادَهُ بَسْطَةً فِي الْعِلْمِ وَالْجِسْمِ﴾

al-Baqarah 2:247

Qunbul reads بَصْطَةً with ṣād rather than the sīn.

verses.tr: The second occurrence of رُضْوَانَهُ is read with ḍammah by Shuʿbah; and the kasrah in اضْطِرِرْ is known for Ibn Wardān.

exp.en:
3. رِضْوَانَهُ: Shuʿbah

The poet specifies the second occurrence of رِضْوَانَهُ, in Sūrah al-Māʾidah:

﴿يَهْدِي بِهِ اللَّهُ مَنِ اتَّبَعَ رِضْوَانَهُ سُبُلَ السَّلَامِ وَيُخْرِجُهُم مِّنَ الظُّلُمَاتِ إِلَى النُّورِ بِإِذْنِهِ وَيَهْدِيهِمْ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ﴾

al-Māʾidah 5:16

Shuʿbah reads the initial rāʾ of this occurrence with ḍammah: رُضْوَانَهُ.

4. اضْطُرِرْتُمْ: Ibn Wardān

The relevant word occurs in Sūrah al-Anʿām:

﴿وَمَا لَكُمْ أَلَّا تَأْكُلُوا مِمَّا ذُكِرَ اسْمُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِ وَقَدْ فَصَّلَ لَكُم مَّا حَرَّمَ عَلَيْكُمْ إِلَّا مَا اضْطُرِرْتُمْ إِلَيْهِ﴾

al-Anʿām 6:119; excerpt

Ibn Wardān reads the ṭāʾ in اضْطُرِرْتُمْ with kasrah, as indicated by the poet’s phrase كَسْرُ اضْطِرِرْ.

ajuzW.g: lā yaḥsibanna (with yāʾ and kasrah on sīn)

verses.tr: In إِنَّ وَلِيَّ اللَّهُ, drop the yāʾ for as-Sūsī; their Idrīs, read for him لَا يَحْسِبَنْ (with yāʾ and kasrah on sīn).

exp.en:
Abyāt 4–5

5. إِنَّ وَلِيَّ اللَّهُ: as-Sūsī

This occurs in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf:

﴿إِنَّ وَلِيِّيَ اللَّهُ الَّذِي نَزَّلَ الْكِتَابَ وَهُوَ يَتَوَلَّى الصَّالِحِينَ﴾

al-Aʿrāf 7:196

The reading of as-Sūsī involves omitting the second yāʾ in وَلِيِّيَ in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf. The remaining yāʾ is read with tashdīd, and it may be pronounced with either fatḥah or kasrah, as indicated in the transmitted reading.

6. لَا يَحْسَبَنَّ: Idrīs

The poet refers to two occurrences, one in Sūrah al-Anfāl and the other in Sūrah an-Nūr:

﴿وَلَا يَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا سَبَقُوا إِنَّهُمْ لَا يُعْجِزُونَ﴾

al-Anfāl 8:59

﴿لَا تَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مُعْجِزِينَ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَمَأْوَاهُمُ النَّارُ وَلَبِئْسَ الْمَصِيرُ﴾

an-Nūr 24:57

Idrīs reads the relevant verb with yāʾ and a kasrah on the sīn.

7. وَيَكُونَ لَكُمَا: Shuʿbah

The reading occurs in Sūrah Yūnus:

﴿قَالُوا أَجِئْتَنَا لِتَلْفِتَنَا عَمَّا وَجَدْنَا عَلَيْهِ آبَاءَنَا وَتَكُونَ لَكُمَا الْكِبْرِيَاءُ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَمَا نَحْنُ لَكُمَا بِمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾

Yūnus 10:78

Shuʿbah reads the verb تَكُونَ with yāʾ: يَكُونَ.

verses.tr: The two occurrences are in Sūrahs al-Anfāl and an-Nūr; and for Shuʿbah, read وَيَكُونَ لَكُمَا.

verses.sadr: فِي يُوسُفٍ هِئۡتُ لَكَ قَرَا هِشَامۡ
verses.tr: In Sūrah Yūsuf, Hishām reads هِئْتُ لَكَ; and in Sūrah al-Ḥijr, Ruways reads أُدْخِلُوهَا بِسَلَامْ.

exp.en:
8. هِئْتُ لَكَ: Hishām

The word occurs in the story of Yūsuf عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ:

﴿وَرَاوَدَتْهُ الَّتِي هُوَ فِي بَيْتِهَا عَن نَّفْسِهِ وَغَلَّقَتِ الْأَبْوَابَ وَقَالَتْ هَيْتَ لَكَ ۚ …﴾

Yūsuf 12:23

Hishām reads هِئْتُ لَكَ, with kasrah on the hāʾ, a hamzah, and ḍammah on the tāʾ. This is one of the additions specifically noted in the corrected version of the poem.

9. أُدْخِلُوهَا بِسَلَامٍ: Ruways

The word occurs in Sūrah al-Ḥijr:

﴿ادْخُلُوهَا بِسَلَامٍ آمِنِينَ﴾

al-Ḥijr 15:46

Ruways reads أُدْخِلُوهَا with kasrah on the khāʾ, as indicated by the poem.

verses.tr: In Sūrah al-Kahf, read لَدْنِي with ikhtilās for Shuʿbah; and in Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ, establish the yāʾ in يَصِفُونَ.

exp.en:
10. لَدُنِّي: Shuʿbah

The particular occurrence is:

﴿قَالَ قَدْ بَلَغْتَ مِن لَّدُنِّي عُذْرًا﴾

al-Kahf 18:76

Shuʿbah reads لَدُنِّي in Sūrah al-Kahf with ikhtilās of the ḍammah on the dāl, pronouncing only part of the vowel rather than giving it its full duration.

11. يَصِفُونَ: Ibn Dhakwān

The word occurs in Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ:

﴿قَالَ رَبِّ احْكُم بِالْحَقِّ ۗ وَرَبُّنَا الرَّحْمَٰنُ الْمُسْتَعَانُ عَلَىٰ مَا تَصِفُونَ﴾

al-Anbiyāʾ 21:112

Ibn Dhakwān reads the verb with yāʾ: يَصِفُونَ, rather than tāʾ.

verses.sadr: ذَا لابۡنِ ذَكۡوَانَ وَقُلۡ بِهِ الرِّيَاحۡ
verses.tr: This is for Ibn Dhakwān; and say بِهِ الرِّيَاحْ, in al-Ḥajj, success will come to you.

exp.en:
12. الرِّيَاحِ: Abū Jaʿfar

The relevant occurrence is in Sūrah al-Ḥajj:

﴿حُنَفَاءَ لِلَّهِ غَيْرَ مُشْرِكِينَ بِهِ ۚ وَمَن يُشْرِكْ بِاللَّهِ فَكَأَنَّمَا خَرَّ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ فَتَخْطَفُهُ الطَّيْرُ أَوْ تَهْوِي بِهِ الرِّيحُ فِي مَكَانٍ سَحِيقٍ﴾

al-Ḥajj 22:31

Abū Jaʿfar reads the word in the plural, الرِّيَاحِ, rather than the singular الرِّيحِ.

verses.tr: In Sūrah al-Furqān, Qunbul reads with yāʾ in يَقُولْ; and Shuʿbah reads يِخِصِّمُونَ, O seeker of knowledge.

exp.en:
13. بِمَا يَقُولُونَ: Qunbul

This occurs in Sūrah al-Furqān:

﴿فَقَدْ كَذَّبُوكُم بِمَا تَقُولُونَ فَمَا تَسْتَطِيعُونَ صَرْفًا وَلَا نَصْرًا ۚ وَمَن يَظْلِم مِّنكُمْ نُذِقْهُ عَذَابًا كَبِيرًا﴾

al-Furqān 25:19

Qunbul has a reading with yāʾ in يَقُولُونَ, rather than the tāʾ in تَقُولُونَ.

14. يِخِصِّمُونَ: Shuʿbah

The word occurs in Sūrah Yā-Sīn:

﴿مَا يَنظُرُونَ إِلَّا صَيْحَةً وَاحِدَةً تَأْخُذُهُمْ وَهُمْ يَخِصِّمُونَ﴾

Yā-Sīn 36:49

Shuʿbah reads يِخِصِّمُونَ, with kasrah on the yāʾ as well as the khāʾ, and a doubled ṣād. This is the form identified in the poem.

verses.tr: Qunbul reads لِتْنَاهُم in Sūrah aṭ-Ṭūr, together with رَءَافَةَ in al-Ḥadīd for him, so listen.

exp.en:
15. أَلَتْنَاهُمْ: Qunbul

The relevant word occurs in Sūrah aṭ-Ṭūr:

﴿وَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَاتَّبَعَتْهُمْ ذُرِّيَّتُهُم بِإِيمَانٍ أَلْحَقْنَا بِهِمْ ذُرِّيَّتَهُمْ وَمَا أَلَتْنَاهُم مِّنْ عَمَلِهِم مِّن شَيْءٍ﴾

aṭ-Ṭūr 52:21

Qunbul reads the word أَلَتْنَاهُمْ with a kasrah on the lām, on the pattern of أَفْعِلْنَاهُمْ, while the remaining Qurrāʾ read it with a fatḥah on the lām.

16. رَأْفَةً: Qunbul

The word occurs in Sūrah al-Ḥadīd:

﴿ثُمَّ قَفَّيْنَا عَلَىٰ آثَارِهِم بِرُسُلِنَا وَقَفَّيْنَا بِعِيسَى ابْنِ مَرْيَمَ وَآتَيْنَاهُ الْإِنجِيلَ وَجَعَلْنَا فِي قُلُوبِ الَّذِينَ اتَّبَعُوهُ رَأْفَةً وَرَحْمَةً وَرَهْبَانِيَّةً ابْتَدَعُوهَا﴾

al-Ḥadīd 57:27; excerpt

Qunbul has two ways of reading the word رَأْفَةً in Sūrah al-Ḥadīd: the first, with a sākin hamzah, which is the well-known reading; and the second, through certain routes in the kubrā, by replacing the hamzah with an alif of madd: رَآفَةً.

verses.ajuz: صَلَّى عَلَيۡكَ اللهُ يَا نُورَ الۡحَدَقۡ
verses.tr: Ruways reads النَّافِثَاتِ in Sūrah al-Falaq. May Allah send blessings upon you, O light of the eye.

exp.en:
17. النَّافِثَاتِ: Ruways

The final addition occurs in Sūrah al-Falaq:

﴿وَمِن شَرِّ النَّفَّاثَاتِ فِي الْعُقَدِ﴾

al-Falaq 113:4

Ruways has two ways of reading in Sūrah al-Falaq: the first, with an alif after the nūn and a kasrah on the fāʾ without tashdīd: النَّافِثَاتِ; and the second, with a fatḥah and tashdīd on the fāʾ, followed by an alif: النَّفَّاثَاتِ, as read by the other Qurrāʾ.

The poet ends with a prayer for blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ, bringing the poem to a close after arranging all seventeen additions into a sequence that can be memorised and revisited.

The value of this منظومة lies in its precision: it brings together readings that might otherwise be overlooked when a student studies only the routes of al-Shāṭibiyyah and al-Durrah. By identifying each word and its associated reader, it serves as a compact guide to the additional farsh material found in Ṭayyibat al-Nashr.

chapters.ar: وَقف يعقوب بهاء السكتِ من طرِيۡقِ الدرّة
chapters.en: Yaʿqūb’s Waqf with Hāʾ al-Sakt via Durrah
chapters.desc: The eight words in which the kāf of address is followed by the nūn of the feminine plural: Yaʿqūb stops on them with hāʾ al-sakt by the route of al-Durrah, while by the route of al-Ṭayyibah the hāʾ may be affirmed or omitted.

verses.ajuz: جَا فِي ثَمَانٍ وَقۡفُنَا فِيهَا بِهَاءۡ

sadrW.g: the nūn of the feminine plural

verses.tr: The kāf of address is followed by the nūn of the feminine plural in eight words; when stopping on them, we do so with a hāʾ.

exp.en:
Background

This poem addresses eight words in which the كاف الخطاب (the kāf of address) is followed by نون النسوة (the nūn indicating the feminine plural). These words have a specific ruling concerning هاء السكت when stopping on them in the recitation of Yaʿqūb al-Ḥaḍramī.

The ruling must be understood according to the route of transmission: through الدُّرَّة, the hāʾ is affirmed when stopping on these eight words; through الطَّيِّبَة, it may either be affirmed or omitted.

The poet identifies all eight words in the following lines.

Abyāt 1–2

The eight words in their Qur’anic contexts

1. كَيْدِكُنَّ

﴿إِنَّهُ مِن كَيْدِكُنَّ ۖ إِنَّ كَيْدَكُنَّ عَظِيمٌ﴾

Yūsuf 12:28

2. فَذَٰلِكُنَّ

﴿قَالَتْ فَذَٰلِكُنَّ الَّذِي لُمْتُنَّنِي فِيهِ﴾

Yūsuf 12:32

3. خَطْبُكُنَّ

﴿قَالَ مَا خَطْبُكُنَّ إِذْ رَاوَدتُّنَّ يُوسُفَ عَن نَّفْسِهِ﴾

Yūsuf 12:51

4. أُمَتِّعْكُنَّ

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ قُل لِّأَزْوَاجِكَ إِن كُنتُنَّ تُرِدْنَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا وَزِينَتَهَا فَتَعَالَيْنَ أُمَتِّعْكُنَّ﴾

al-Aḥzāb 33:28

5. وَأُسَرِّحْكُنَّ

﴿وَأُسَرِّحْكُنَّ سَرَاحًا جَمِيلًا﴾

al-Aḥzāb 33:28

6. بُيُوتِكُنَّ

﴿وَقَرْنَ فِي بُيُوتِكُنَّ وَلَا تَبَرَّجْنَ تَبَرُّجَ الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ الْأُولَىٰ﴾

al-Aḥzāb 33:33

7. طَلَّقَكُنَّ

﴿عَسَىٰ رَبُّهُ إِن طَلَّقَكُنَّ أَن يُبْدِلَهُ أَزْوَاجًا خَيْرًا مِّنكُنَّ﴾

al-Taḥrīm 66:5

8. مِنْكُنَّ

﴿أَزْوَاجًا خَيْرًا مِّنكُنَّ مُسْلِمَاتٍ مُّؤْمِنَاتٍ قَانِتَاتٍ تَائِبَاتٍ عَابِدَاتٍ سَائِحَاتٍ ثَيِّبَاتٍ وَأَبْكَارًا﴾

al-Taḥrīm 66:5

The central point is that eight specific words share a particular structure: the كاف الخطاب is followed by نون النسوة. The ruling concerning هاء السكت when stopping on these words differs according to the route of transmission.

The Ruling According to the Route

Through الدُّرَّة

For Yaʿqūb al-Ḥaḍramī, هاء السكت is affirmed when stopping on these eight words.

Ibn al-Jazarī cited كَيْدِكُنَّ as an example of a position involving هاء السكت in التحبير. The other seven words are treated as corresponding examples of the same pattern.

Through الطَّيِّبَة

The hāʾ may either be affirmed or omitted when stopping on these words. The same rule applies to words such as عَلَيْهِنَّ, and other positions in which نون النسوة is preceded by هاء الغيبة.

Words That Must Not Be Included

The author then cautions against extending this ruling to words that merely appear similar.

كُنَّ and يَكُنَّ

In these forms, the kāf is an original root letter (فاء الكلمة), not كاف الخطاب. The doubled nūn consists of two nūns: one is the original final root letter of the verb, and the other is نون النسوة.

Therefore, these words do not fall under the pattern discussed in the poem. The author compares them with يُؤْمِنَّ, in which there is no هاء السكت.

رَاوَدْتُنَّ and كُنْتُنَّ

The author also excludes words in which نون النسوة is preceded by تاء, such as رَاوَدْتُنَّ and كُنْتُنَّ. His stated reason is that none of the authorities whose views are relied upon used a feminine plural nūn preceded by tāʾ as an example of this ruling.

The distinction is therefore not simply whether a word ends in نون النسوة. The structure preceding that nūn matters, and the ruling must remain restricted to the pattern established.

verses.tr: The poet mentions the eight words through shortened portions of each expression, allowing the relevant pattern to be identified. The eight words are: خَطْبُكُنَّ، أُمَتِّعْكُنَّ، وَأُسَرِّحْكُنَّ، كَيْدِكُنَّ، طَلَّقَكُنَّ، مِنْكُنَّ، بُيُوتِكُنَّ، فَذَٰلِكُنَّ.

chapters.ar: المواضِعُ الخمسةُ التي يُفخِّم فيها ورشٌ الراءَ لتكرارها في كلمة
chapters.en: The Five Rā's Warsh Gives Tafkhīm Because of Repetition, With No Tarqīq at All
chapters.desc: A single line gathering the five Qurʾānic words in which Warsh reads the rāʾ with tafkhīm, against his general rule of tarqīq, because the rāʾ is repeated within the same word.

verses.tr: (Read) the rā' with tafkhīm in ضِرَارًا, إِسْرَارا, مِدْرَارً, الْفِرَارُ, together with فِرَارا.

exp.en:
Background

A general rule governing Warsh’s reading of the الرَّاء (ر) is that when the rāʾ carries a fatḥah or ḍammah and is preceded by a kasrah or a sākin yāʾ, it is read with tarqīq (تَرْقِيق), a light pronunciation.

However, there is a specific exception to this rule when the letter rāʾ occurs twice within the same word. In these instances, Warsh reads the relevant rāʾ with tafkhīm (تَفْخِيم), a heavy pronunciation, even where the first rāʾ carries a fatḥah and is preceded by a kasrah—a configuration that would ordinarily call for tarqīq according to his general rule. The repetition of rāʾ within the same word therefore gives rise to this exceptional ruling.

The poet gathers the five Qurʾānic words in which this occurs into a single line, making the exception easier to remember.

Explanation

The poet simply names the five words in a single line, with no further explanation needed once the underlying rule, tafkhīm wherever a rāʾ repeats within one word, has been understood. The five are ḍirāran, isrāran, midrāran, al-firār, and firāran, the last two being two separate Qurʾānic occurrences of the same root.

The five words are found in the following āyahs:

1. ضِرَارًا

﴿وَلَا تُمْسِكُوهُنَّ ضِرَارًا لِتَعْتَدُوا﴾

al-Baqarah 2:231

It also occurs in Sūrat al-Tawbah (9:107):

﴿وَالَّذِينَ اتَّخَذُوا مَسْجِدًا ضِرَارًا وَكُفْرًا وَتَفْرِيقًا بَيْنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾

al-Tawbah 9:107

2. إِسْرَارًا

﴿ثُمَّ إِنِّي أَعْلَنْتُ لَهُمْ وَأَسْرَرْتُ لَهُمْ إِسْرَارًا﴾

Nūḥ 71:9

3. مِدْرَارًا

﴿يُرْسِلِ السَّمَاءَ عَلَيْكُمْ مِدْرَارًا﴾

Nūḥ 71:11; Hūd 11:52

And in Sūrat al-Anʿām (6:6):

﴿وَأَرْسَلْنَا السَّمَاءَ عَلَيْهِمْ مِدْرَارًا﴾

al-Anʿām 6:6

4. الْفِرَار

﴿قُلْ لَنْ يَنْفَعَكُمُ الْفِرَارُ إِنْ فَرَرْتُمْ مِنَ الْمَوْتِ أَوِ الْقَتْلِ﴾

al-Aḥzāb 33:16

5. فِرَارًا

﴿لَوَلَّيْتَ مِنْهُمْ فِرَارًا وَلَمُلِئْتَ مِنْهُمْ رُعْبًا﴾

al-Kahf 18:18

chapters.ar: الحُرُوفُ الزَّوَائِدُ التِّسۡعَةُ الۡمُتَّصِلَةُ بِهَمۡزَةِ الۡقَطۡعِ عِنۡدَ حَمۡزَةَ
chapters.en: The Nine Additional Connected Letters Affecting Hamzat al-Qaṭʿ in the Recitation of Ḥamzah
chapters.desc: Two lines in al-Baḥr al-Mutadārik that gather, in the mnemonic sawfa abkī lahu, the nine letters which, when they come before a word beginning with hamzat al-qaṭʿ, allow Imām Ḥamzah a change in that hamzah when stopping.

verses.tr: Ḥamzah changes a hamzah before which comes one of سَوْفَ أَبْكِيْ لَهُ; سَأُرِي is given as an example.

exp.en:
Background

Among the distinctive rulings of Imām Ḥamzah is the treatment of Hamzat al-Qaṭʿ (هَمْزَةُ الْقَطْعِ) when stopping (الوقف). When a word begins with Hamzat al-Qaṭʿ and is preceded by one of nine letters, Imām Ḥamzah has a ruling that permits a change in the initial hamzah when stopping.

The poet gathers these nine letters into the mnemonic سَوْفَ أَبْكِي لَهُ (and also لَسَوْفَ أَبْكِيهِ) to make them easier to memorise. The letters are: س، و، ف، ء، ب، ك، ي، ل، ه.

Abyāt 1–2

The two lines, composed in al-Baḥr al-Mutadārik, gather the letters that may precede a word beginning with Hamzat al-Qaṭʿ and affect its treatment when stopping according to the recitation of Imām Ḥamzah.

The mnemonic سَوْفَ أَبْكِي لَهُ contains the nine letters, each illustrated by an example:

Qurʾānic Examples of the Nine Letters

1. سَأُرِيكُمْ — السِّين (س)

﴿سَأُرِيكُمْ دَارَ الْفَاسِقِينَ﴾

al-Aʿrāf 7:145

2. وَإِذَا — الْوَاو (و)

﴿وَإِذَا مَرِضْتُ فَهُوَ يَشْفِينِ﴾

ash-Shuʿarāʾ 26:80

3. فَإِذَا — الْفَاء (ف)

﴿فَإِذَا هِيَ ثُعْبَانٌ مُبِينٌ﴾

ash-Shuʿarāʾ 26:32

4. أَئِذَا — الْهَمْزَة (ء)

﴿أَئِذَا مِتْنَا وَكُنَّا تُرَابًا وَعِظَامًا أَئِنَّا لَمَبْعُوثُونَ﴾

aṣ-Ṣāffāt 37:16

5. بِأَخٍ — الْبَاء (ب)

﴿وَلَمَّا جَهَّزَهُمْ بِجَهَازِهِمْ قَالَ ائْتُونِي بِأَخٍ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَبِيكُمْ﴾

Yūsuf 12:59

6. كَأَنْ — الْكَاف (ك)

﴿كَأَنْ لَمْ يَغْنَوْا فِيهَا﴾

Hūd 11:68

7. يَا أُولِي — الْيَاء (ي)

﴿وَلَكُمْ فِي الْقِصَاصِ حَيَاةٌ يَا أُولِي الْأَلْبَابِ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَّقُونَ﴾

al-Baqarah 2:179

8. لَأَنْتُمْ — اللَّام (ل)

﴿لَأَنْتُمْ أَشَدُّ رَهْبَةً فِي صُدُورِهِمْ مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾

al-Ḥashr 59:13

The lām of the definite article is also included in this category, as in الْأَرْضِ, for example in Sūrat al-Baqarah (2:22):

﴿الَّذِي جَعَلَ لَكُمُ الْأَرْضَ فِرَاشًا﴾

al-Baqarah 2:22

9. هَؤُلَاءِ — الْهَاء (ه)

﴿إِنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ لَشِرْذِمَةٌ قَلِيلُونَ﴾

ash-Shuʿarāʾ 26:54

There are several mnemonic phrases used to remember these letters, including لَسَوْفَ أَبْكِيهِ, سَوْفَ أَبْكِي لَهُ, أَيُّوبُ كَفَّهُ سَلَا, and فُلُوسٌ بِأَيْكَةٍ.

The essential point is that the ruling concerns the initial hamzah of a word when stopping, provided it is preceded by one of these specified letters.

The mnemonic helps the student recall the letters, while the examples illustrate their occurrence.

verses.tr: Wa-idhā, fa-idhā, a-idhā, bi-akhin, wa-ka'an, yā-ūlī, wa-la-an, hā'ulā'.

chapters.ar: التَّخَلُّصُ مِنِ الۡتِقَاءِ السَّاكِنَيۡنِ لَدَى الفعلِ المَبدوءِ بهمزةِ الوصلِ الذيۡ ثالثُه مضمومٌ ضمًا لازمًا
chapters.en: Resolving the Meeting of Two Sākin Letters, before a Verb Beginning with Hamzat al-Waṣl Whose Third Letter Carries a Fixed Ḍammah
chapters.desc: How the readers resolve the meeting of two sākin letters when a word ending in a sākin letter is followed by a verb beginning with hamzat al-waṣl whose third letter carries a fixed ḍammah, summarised in three mnemonics: tanud, ltanud and litanūda.

verses.tr: For Ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, apply kasrah to the letters gathered in تَنُدْ; and for Yaʿqūb, apply kasrah to those gathered in لْتَنُدْ. (For ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah), apply kasrah to the letters gathered in لِتَنُودَ.

exp.en:
Background

Two consecutive sākin letters may meet when one word is joined to the next; this is known as التقاء الساكنين, the meeting of two letters that carry no vowel.

While reciting waṣlan, the reciter must resolve this meeting so that the two sākin letters are not pronounced consecutively. The method used depends on the letters involved and the transmitted reading of each qāriʾ.

This poem discusses a situation that occurs when a word ends with a sākin letter and is followed by a verb beginning with همزة الوصل, whose third letter carries an obligatory ḍammah. When the hamzat al-waṣl drops, the reciter must resolve the meeting of the two sākin letters. The difference discussed in these verses concerns whether the preceding letter is given a kasrah or a ḍammah.

Shaykh Waleed al-Meneese summarises these differences through three memorable expressions: تَنُدْ، لْتَنُدْ، لِتَنُودَ. Each mnemonic gathers the letters for which a particular group of readers uses kasrah.

Abyāt 1–2

1. Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ — تَنُدْ
