Abū ʿAmr resolves the meeting of two sākin letters with kasrah on the letters gathered in the mnemonic تَنُدْ:

  • ت — تاء التأنيث الساكنة
  • ن — نون أَنْ
  • ن — نون مَنْ
  • د — دال قَدْ

These letters occur before verbs beginning with hamzat al-waṣl whose third letter carries an obligatory ḍammah.

For example,

﴿فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ بِمَكْرِهِنَّ أَرْسَلَتْ إِلَيْهِنَّ وَأَعْتَدَتْ لَهُنَّ مُتَّكَأً وَآتَتْ كُلَّ وَاحِدَةٍ مِنْهُنَّ سِكِّينًا وَقَالَتِ اخْرُجْ عَلَيْهِنَّ …﴾

Yūsuf 12:31

The tāʾ of قَالَتْ is originally sākin. When joined to اخْرُجْ, the hamzat al-waṣl drops, and the two sākin letters would meet. Abū ʿAmr therefore reads the tāʾ with kasrah: قَالَتِ اخْرُجْ.

The other letters in تَنُدْ follow the same principle in their respective locations.

2. Yaʿqūb — لْتَنُدْ

Yaʿqūb also uses kasrah for the letters gathered in تَنُدْ, but his mnemonic adds another letter: لْتَنُدْ. The additional letter is:

  • ل — لام قُلْ

Thus, Yaʿqūb applies kasrah to the letters covered by Abū ʿAmr’s mnemonic, as well as the lām of قُلْ when it is followed by a word beginning with hamzat al-waṣl in the relevant context.

For example:

﴿قُلِ ادْعُوا الَّذِينَ زَعَمْتُمْ مِنْ دُونِهِ فَلَا يَمْلِكُونَ كَشْفَ الضُّرِّ عَنْكُمْ وَلَا تَحْوِيلًا﴾

al-Isrāʾ 17:56

Here, the lām of قُلْ receives kasrah when joined to ادْعُوا.

The mnemonic لْتَنُدْ therefore reminds the student that Yaʿqūb’s rule includes the additional lām, alongside the letters already covered by تَنُدْ.

3. ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah — لِتَنُودَ

ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah use kasrah for the letters gathered in لِتَنُودَ. This mnemonic includes the letters covered by the previous two groups, together with an additional letter:

  • و — واو أَوْ

The additional wāw occurs in three locations, where أَوْ is followed by a word beginning with hamzat al-waṣl in the relevant context: أَوِ اخْرُجُوا, أَوِ ادْعُوا الرَّحْمَٰنَ, أَوِ انْقُصْ.

The mnemonic لِتَنُودَ thus gathers the letters for which ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah use kasrah in this rule.

4. The Remaining Readers — الضم

The remaining readers generally resolve the meeting of two sākin letters with ḍammah in the letters gathered in لِتَنُودَ.

There are two important details to retain:

  • The two Basran readers, Abū ʿAmr and Yaʿqūb, agree with this group in using ḍammah on the و of أَوْ.
  • Abū ʿAmr also agrees with them in using ḍammah on the ل of قُلْ.

These are specific points of agreement within the rule. They do not mean that the readers abandon their other established differences.

Note: The rule above concerns resolving the meeting of two sākin letters when a word ending in a sākin letter is followed by a word beginning with hamzat al-waṣl. التنوين قبل همزة الوصل is a separate case and should not be confused with the mnemonics تَنُدْ، لْتَنُدْ، لِتَنُودَ.

When tanwīn precedes a verb beginning with hamzat al-waṣl whose third letter carries an obligatory ḍammah, the tanwīn is given kasrah in the routes of الشاطبية والدرة for ʿĀṣim, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah and Yaʿqūb. Ibn Dhakwān has an option (khulf) in the two words رَحْمَةٍ and خَبِيثَةٍ.

The mnemonic تَنُودَ is an Arabic word associated with swaying or nodding, including movement caused by drowsiness. The letters may also be remembered through the rearranged expression تَدْنُو, meaning “it draws near.”

The key is to remember the progression:

تَنُدْ Abū ʿAmr, with a kasrah → لْتَنُدْ Yaʿqūb, with a kasrah → لِتَنُودَ ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah, with a kasrah → الضَّمّ the remaining readers, with a ḍammah

Each reader has a different way of resolving the meeting of the two sākin letters, while maintaining the correct pronunciation of the hamzat al-waṣl and the ḍammah.

These mnemonics make it easier to identify which letters receive kasrah and which are read with ḍammah when resolving التقاء الساكنين.

verses.tr: As for the remaining readers, apply ḍammah to these letters, so verify it.

chapters.ar: مَا زَادَهُ الشَّاطِبِيُّ عَلَى التَّيۡسِيرِ وَلَمۡ يَصِحّ
chapters.en: What al-Shāṭibī Added to al-Taysīr That Was Not Authenticated
chapters.desc: Of the 135 additions al-Shāṭibī made in Ḥirz al-Amānī beyond al-Dānī’s al-Taysīr, the poem counts and names the nine that Ibn al-Jazarī did not authenticate and that are not recited through the route of al-Shāṭibiyyah.

verses.sadr: قَدۡ زادَ فِي الۡحَرۡزِ عَلَى التَّيۡسِيۡرِ
verses.tr: Al-Shāṭibī added to al-Taysīr in al-Ḥirz; count them using قُلْهُ, and give preference to my taḥrīr.

exp.en:
Background

Imām al-Shāṭibī’s Ḥirz al-Amānī, commonly known as al-Shāṭibiyyah, is based on Imām al-Dānī’s al-Taysīr. In composing his poem, al-Shāṭibī included additional points of recitational detail beyond those explicitly presented in al-Taysīr. These are known as زيادات الشاطبي على التيسير.

Imām ash-Shāṭibī added 135 masāʾil in Ḥirz al-Amānī beyond what is found in al-Taysīr. Of these 135 additions, 126 are sound, and reciting by them is not prohibited, according to the rājiḥ, the preferred verification of the poet's own teacher, Shaykh Dr. Īhāb Fikrī, in Taqrīb ash-Shāṭibiyyah.

Only nine of the additions are impermissible to recite; the issue is not simply whether a particular reading has been reported somewhere; rather, it concerns whether it is established and may be transmitted through this specific route.

Imām Ibn al-Jazarī did not authenticate these nine additions or teach them through the route of al-Shāṭibiyyah. Consequently, the scholars who followed his position refrained from teaching them through that route.

Note: Scholars in the Maghrib continued to teach many of these readings, since their chains of transmission to al-Shāṭibiyyah do not pass through Ibn al-Jazarī.

The poem gathers the nine disputed additions into a sequence, allowing students to identify each one and understand the basis for its exclusion from the preferred transmission through al-Shāṭibiyyah.

Explanation

The first hemistich contains the mnemonic قُلْهُ, whose letters are counted using abjad letter values:

  • ق = 100
  • ل = 30
  • ه = 5

The total is 135. This is the number of additions that al-Shāṭibī included beyond al-Taysīr, according to the poem’s explanation.

Of these, 126 are accepted. This poem addresses the remaining nine additions.

verses.tr: Of these, nine were not authenticated; their chains of transmission were cut off, and al-Jazarī forbade them.

exp.en:
Abyāt 2–6

The Nine Additions — الزيادات التسع

1. The additional lengthening in يُؤَاخِذُ

The first addition concerns Warsh and the two additional lengthening options, tawassuṭ and ishbāʿ, in:

﴿لَا يُؤَاخِذُكُمُ اللَّهُ بِاللَّغْوِ فِي أَيْمَانِكُمْ وَلَٰكِنْ يُؤَاخِذُكُمْ بِمَا كَسَبَتْ قُلُوبُكُمْ وَاللَّهُ غَفُورٌ حَلِيمٌ﴾

al-Baqarah 2:225

The poem indicates that these two additional options are not to be transmitted through the route of al-Shāṭibiyyah according to the preferred taḥrīr.

2. Applying Fatḥ to a Munawwan letter when stopping

The second addition concerns Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī, who apply fatḥ instead of Imālah when stopping on words ending in tanwīn, such as هُدًى.

An example of the word هُدًى occurs in:

﴿ذَٰلِكَ الْكِتَابُ لَا رَيْبَ فِيهِ هُدًى لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾

al-Baqarah 2:2

The point concerns the manner of stopping on the word, not its pronunciation when continuing.

3. Idghām in وَجَبَتْ

The third addition concerns Ibn Dhakwān and the idghām associated with وَجَبَتْ in the Ayah:

﴿فَإِذَا وَجَبَتْ جُنُوبُهَا فَكُلُوا مِنْهَا وَأَطْعِمُوا الْقَانِعَ وَالْمُعْتَرَّ كَذَٰلِكَ سَخَّرْنَاهَا لَكُمْ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَشْكُرُونَ﴾

al-Ḥajj 22:36

The additional mode of idghām mentioned in the poem is among the nine not accepted through the route under discussion.

4. Imālah of يَا

The fourth addition concerns as-Sūsī and the Imālah of يَا at the beginning of Sūrah Maryam:

﴿كهيعص﴾

Maryam 19:1

The poem identifies this additional mode of pronunciation as one that is not accepted through the route of al-Shāṭibiyyah according to the position being presented.

5. Imālah of the rāʾ in رَأَى

The fifth addition concerns as-Sūsī and the imālah of the rāʾ in رَأَى, whether it occurs before a sākin or a vowelled letter.

6. Imālah of the hamzah in نَأَى

The sixth addition concerns as-Sūsī and the imālah of the hamzah in نَأَى.

An example occurs in:

﴿وَإِذَا أَنْعَمْنَا عَلَى الْإِنْسَانِ أَعْرَضَ وَنَأَىٰ بِجَانِبِهِ وَإِذَا مَسَّهُ الشَّرُّ كَانَ يَئُوسًا﴾

al-Isrāʾ 17:83

The poem excludes the additional imālah of the hamzah in this word through the route being discussed.

7. Imālah of the hamzah in رَأَى before a sākin letter

The seventh addition concerns Shuʿbah and the imālah of the hamzah in رَأَى when it occurs before a sākin letter.

This is distinct from the previous item: the fifth concerns the rāʾ in رَأَى for Sūsī, whereas this item concerns the hamzah in رَأَى for Shuʿbah in the specified context.

8. Imālah of يُوَارِي and أُوَارِي

The eighth addition concerns al-Dūrī from al-Kisāʾī and the imālah of the two forms يُوَارِي and أُوَارِي.

An example of يُوَارِي occurs in:

﴿فَبَعَثَ اللَّهُ غُرَابًا يَبْحَثُ فِي الْأَرْضِ لِيُرِيَهُ كَيْفَ يُوَارِي سَوْءَةَ أَخِيهِ قَالَ يَا وَيْلَتَا أَعَجَزْتُ أَنْ أَكُونَ مِثْلَ هَٰذَا الْغُرَابِ فَأُوَارِيَ سَوْءَةَ أَخِي فَأَصْبَحَ مِنَ النَّادِمِينَ﴾

al-Māʾidah 5:31

The additional imālah of these forms is among the nine additions excluded from transmission through the route under discussion.

9. Omission of the yāʾ in كيْدُونِ when joining

The ninth addition concerns Hishām and the omission of the yāʾ in كيْدُونِ when continuing recitation.

The relevant verse is:

﴿فَكِيدُونِي جَمِيعًا ثُمَّ لَا تُنْظِرُونِ﴾

Hūd 11:55

The poem specifies retaining the yāʾ when joining: وَالْيَاءَ فِي كيْدُونِ أَثْبِتْ إِنْ تَصِلْ. The additional mode of omitting it is not accepted through the route of al-Shāṭibiyyah according to this taḥrīr.

The following are the nine additional modes mentioned in the poem:

  1. يُؤَاخِذُ The additional lengthening in يُؤَاخِذُ (Warsh – tawassuṭ and ishbāʿ).
  2. هُدًى Applying fatḥ to a munawwan letter when stopping (Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī).
  3. وَجَبَتْ Idghām in وَجَبَتْ (Ibn Dhakwān).
  4. يَا Imālah of يَا (as-Sūsī).
  5. رَأَى Imālah of the rāʾ in رَأَى (as-Sūsī).
  6. نَأَى Imālah of the hamzah in نَأَى (as-Sūsī).
  7. رَأَى Imālah of the hamzah in رَأَى (Shuʿbah).
  8. يُوَارِي / أُوَارِي Imālah of يُوَارِي and أُوَارِي (al-Dūrī from al-Kisāʾī).
  9. كيْدُونِ Omission of the yāʾ in كيْدُونِ (Hishām).

These nine additions are not accepted through the route of al-Shāṭibiyyah according to the preferred taḥrīr.

verses.ajuz: نَحۡوَ هُدًى فِي وَقۡفِهِمۡ ٣ كَذَا امۡنَعَنۡ

sadrW.g: (2) do not apply fatḥ (to the munawwan)

verses.tr: 1: yu'ākhidhu, forbid its lengthening; 2: do not apply Fatḥ to the Munawwan, as in هُدًى at their pause; 3: likewise forbid

verses.ajuz: ٥ إمَالَةَ الرَّا فِي رَأَى ٦ هَمۡزِ نَأَى
verses.tr: 4: their idghām in wajabat; the imālah of yā'; 5: the imālah of the rā' in رَأَى; 6: and the hamzah of نَأَى.
7: and in رَأَى, do not apply imālah to the hamzah before a sākin letter, [this being] a reading of Shu'bah.

verses.sadr: ٨ ثُمَّ يُوَارِي مَعۡ أُوَارِي لَا تُمِلۡ
verses.ajuz: ٩ وَالۡيَاءَ فِي كِيۡدُوۡنِ أَثۡبِتۡ إنۡ تَصِلۡ
verses.tr: 8: then يُوَارِي together with أُوَارِي, do not apply imālah; 9: and retain the yāʾ in كيْدُونِ when joining in recitation.

chapters.ar: أَوۡجُهُ لَفۡظِ التَّوۡرَاةِ لِقَالُونَ مَعَ الۡمَدِّ الۡمُنۡفَصِلِ وَمِيمِ الۡجَمۡعِ
chapters.en: The Options for al-Tawrāh in Qālūn’s Recitation with Madd Munfaṣil and Mīm al-Jamʿ
chapters.desc: The options for the word al-tawrāh in Qālūn’s recitation when it occurs with madd munfaṣil and mīm al-jamʿ: five according to the well-known position, and eight according to a second position, which the poet notes has been preferred.

verses.tr: For Qālūn, in التوراة, there are five Awjuh, when madd munfaṣil and mīm al-jamʿ occur together in recitation.

exp.en:
Background

This poem discusses the options available to Qālūn when the word التوراة occurs alongside madd munfaṣil and mīm al-jamʿ in the same recited passage. It examines how the length of the madd munfaṣil, the reading of mīm al-jamʿ with either iskān or ṣilah, and the reading of التوراة with either fatḥ or taqlīl combine to produce the different options. The poet first outlines the five options according to the well-known position, then presents a second position that permits eight options.

Abyāt 1–4

The poet first explains the five options for Qālūn when التوراة occurs with madd munfaṣil and mīm al-jamʿ in the same passage as in the ayah:

﴿وَلَوْ أَنَّهُمْ أَقَامُوا التَّوْرَاةَ وَالْإِنْجِيلَ وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْهِمْ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ …﴾

al-Māʾidah 5:66

1. Qaṣr with iskān

When madd munfaṣil is read with qaṣr and mīm al-jamʿ is read with iskān, the word التوراة is read with taqlīl.

2. Qaṣr with ṣilah

When madd munfaṣil is read with qaṣr and mīm al-jamʿ is read with ṣilah, the word التوراة is read with fatḥ.

3 & 4. Tawassuṭ with iskān

When madd munfaṣil is read with tawassuṭ and mīm al-jamʿ with iskān, both fatḥ and taqlīl are permitted in التوراة.

5. Tawassuṭ with ṣilah

When madd munfaṣil is read with tawassuṭ and mīm al-jamʿ with ṣilah, the word التوراة is read with taqlīl.

These combinations yield five options according to the well-known position, adopted by scholars including al-Ṭabbākh, al-Mutawallī, al-Abyārī and al-Khalījī.

The poet then refers to the second position, which permits eight options. This is the position adopted by Ibn al-Qāṣiḥ, al-Ḍabbāʿ in his commentary on al-Jawhar al-Maknūn, and al-Qāḍī in al-Budūr al-Zāhirah.

According to this position, both fatḥ and taqlīl are permitted in التوراة with either iskān or ṣilah of mīm al-jamʿ. Each of these four combinations may then be read with either qaṣr or tawassuṭ of madd munfaṣil, giving eight options in total. The combinations are summarised below:

  • Mīm al-jamʿ: iskān · التوراة: fatḥ · madd munfaṣil: qaṣr or tawassuṭ
  • Mīm al-jamʿ: iskān · التوراة: taqlīl · madd munfaṣil: qaṣr or tawassuṭ
  • Mīm al-jamʿ: ṣilah · التوراة: fatḥ · madd munfaṣil: qaṣr or tawassuṭ
  • Mīm al-jamʿ: ṣilah · التوراة: taqlīl · madd munfaṣil: qaṣr or tawassuṭ

Thus, each of the four combinations allows two options for madd munfaṣil, giving eight options in total.

The poet concludes by stating وَفُضِّلَا, indicating that this second position was preferred by verifying scholars, who considered it consistent with the unrestricted wording of both the Shāṭibiyyah and the Ṭayyibah.

verses.sadr: فَفِي الۡقَصۡرِ وَالإِسۡكَانِ قَلِّلۡهُ يَا فَتَى
verses.tr: With qaṣr and iskān, apply taqlīl to it O young man; But if you read with qaṣr while reading waṣlan, then apply fatḥ.

verses.sadr: مَعَ المَدِّ وَالإِسۡكَانِ قَلِّلۡ أَوِ افۡتَحَنۡ
verses.ajuz: وَفِي المَدِّ مَع وَصۡلٍ لِمِيمٍ فَقَلِّلَا
verses.tr: With madd and iskān, apply taqlīl or fatḥ; and with madd together with ṣilah of the mīm, apply taqlīl.
In another school (position), apply fatḥ or taqlīl, with sukūn or ṣilah; combine these with tawassuṭ or qaṣr. This position has been preferred.

chapters.ar: تحرِيراتُ وَرۡش: اِجتِمَاعُ مَدِّ الۡبَدَلِ ومَدِّ الليۡن
chapters.en: The Combination of Madd al-Līn al-Mahmūz and Madd al-Badal in Warsh’s Recitation
chapters.desc: The combinations permitted to Warsh when madd al-līn al-mahmūz and madd al-badal occur together: tawassuṭ of the līn goes with all three lengths of the badal, while ṭūl goes only with ṭūl.

verses.ajuz: وَالطُّولُ مَعۡ طُولٍ يَجِي يَا ذَا الۡأَمَلۡ
verses.tr: Read shayʾan with tawassuṭ, alongside the three options of madd al-badal, and full length comes with full length, O one of hope.

exp.en:
Background

These verses explain the options available to Warsh when madd al-līn and madd al-badal occur together. The poet clarifies which combinations are permitted, distinguishing between reading the madd al-līn with tawassuṭ or ṭūl and the corresponding options for madd al-badal.

Explanation

The poet outlines the four permitted combinations when madd al-līn al-mahmūz and madd al-badal occur together in the same passage, as in the Ayah:

﴿أَوَلَوْ كَانَ آبَاؤُهُمْ لَا يَعْقِلُونَ شَيْئًا وَلَا يَهْتَدُونَ﴾

al-Baqarah 2:170

1. Tawassuṭ of madd al-līn

When madd al-līn, as in شَيْئًا, is read with tawassuṭ, all three options of madd al-badal are permitted: qaṣr, tawassuṭ, and ṭūl. This gives three combinations.

2. Ṭūl of madd al-līn

When the līn is read with ṭūl, madd al-badal must also be read with ṭūl. The combination of ṭūl with qaṣr or tawassuṭ of madd al-badal is not permitted.

Thus, the poem identifies four permitted combinations in total (madd al-līn, as in شَيْئًا + madd al-badal):

  • Tawassuṭ + Qaṣr: permitted
  • Tawassuṭ + Tawassuṭ: permitted
  • Tawassuṭ + Ṭūl: permitted
  • Ṭūl + Ṭūl: permitted
  • Ṭūl + Qaṣr: not permitted
  • Ṭūl + Tawassuṭ: not permitted

chapters.ar: اِجۡتِمَاعُ لَام فِصَالا وَأَخَوَاتِهَا مَعَ مَدِّ الۡبَدَلِ عِنۡدَ وَرۡشٍ
chapters.en: The Combination of the Lām in فِصَالًا and Similar Words with Madd al-Badal in Warsh’s Recitation
chapters.desc: Warsh’s combinations of the lām in fiṣālan and similar words with madd al-badal, and of dhawāt al-yāʾ with madd al-līn al-mahmūz: in both cases the poet leaves all the options unrestricted (iṭlāq al-awjuh).

sadrW.g: in the case of fiṣālan (and the like)

verses.tr: In the case of فِصَالًا, leave all the options unrestricted; And with dhāt yāʾ alongside شَيْءٍ, likewise.

exp.en:
Background

These verses discuss two matters relating to the combinations permitted for Warsh. The first concerns words such as فِصَالًا, يَصَّالَحَا and طَالَ when they occur alongside madd al-badal in the same āyah, as in:

﴿فَإِنْ أَرَادَا فِصَالًا عَنْ تَرَاضٍ مِنْهُمَا وَتَشَاوُرٍ فَلَا جُنَاحَ عَلَيْهِمَا وَإِنْ أَرَدْتُمْ أَنْ تَسْتَرْضِعُوا أَوْلَادَكُمْ فَلَا جُنَاحَ عَلَيْكُمْ إِذَا سَلَّمْتُمْ مَا آتَيْتُمْ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ﴾

al-Baqarah 2:233

The lām in these words may be read with taghlīẓ or tarqīq, while madd al-badal may be read with qaṣr, tawassuṭ or ishbāʿ.

There are two positions regarding the combination of these options. The first permits all six combinations, allowing both taghlīẓ and tarqīq with each of the three lengths of madd al-badal. This is the position of al-Izmīrī, al-Mutawallī and those who agree with them. The poet identifies this as the more correct view.

The second position prohibits one combination: tarqīq with qaṣr of madd al-badal, leaving five permitted combinations.

The second matter concerns the combination of dhawāt al-yāʾ with madd al-līn al-mahmūz, as in شَيْءٍ, as in the āyah:

﴿وَعَسَىٰ أَنْ تَكْرَهُوا شَيْئًا وَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ …﴾

al-Baqarah 2:216

Here, the options are fatḥ or taqlīl for dhāt al-yāʾ, combined with either tawassuṭ or ṭūl for madd al-līn al-mahmūz.

The poet extends the principle of unrestricted combinations to this case, permitting all four combinations.

Explanation

The poet addresses the combination of the lām in فِصَالًا and similar words with madd al-badal, as in the āyah:

﴿فَإِنْ أَرَادَا فِصَالًا عَنْ تَرَاضٍ مِنْهُمَا وَتَشَاوُرٍ فَلَا جُنَاحَ عَلَيْهِمَا وَإِنْ أَرَدْتُمْ أَنْ تَسْتَرْضِعُوا أَوْلَادَكُمْ فَلَا جُنَاحَ عَلَيْكُمْ إِذَا سَلَّمْتُمْ مَا آتَيْتُمْ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ﴾

al-Baqarah 2:233

The word فِصَالًا may be read with either taghlīẓ or tarqīq, while آتَيْتُمْ permits the three lengths of madd al-badal. The question is whether every combination of these options is permitted.

The poet adopts the position of iṭlāq al-awjuh, unrestricted combinations, permitting all six possibilities (lām in فِصَالًا + madd al-badal in آتَيْتُمْ):

  • Tarqīq + Qaṣr
  • Tarqīq + Tawassuṭ
  • Tarqīq + Ishbāʿ
  • Taghlīẓ + Qaṣr
  • Taghlīẓ + Tawassuṭ
  • Taghlīẓ + Ishbāʿ

According to this position, no combination is excluded. The alternative position prohibits tarqīq with qaṣr, allowing only five combinations. The poet favours the unrestricted position.

The poet then extends the principle of unrestricted combinations to the meeting of dhawāt al-yāʾ with madd al-līn al-mahmūz, as in شَيْءٍ. In this case, the options for the words with yāʾ and the two lengths of madd al-līn al-mahmūz are combined without excluding any of the four possibilities:

  • Fatḥ of dhāt al-yāʾ with tawassuṭ of شَيْءٍ.
  • Fatḥ of dhāt al-yāʾ with ṭūl of شَيْءٍ.
  • Taqlīl of dhāt al-yāʾ with tawassuṭ of شَيْءٍ.
  • Taqlīl of dhāt al-yāʾ with ṭūl of شَيْءٍ.

Thus, the poet applies the principle of iṭlāq al-awjuh to both cases: the combination of فِصَالًا and similar words with madd al-badal, and the combination of dhawāt al-yāʾ with madd al-līn al-mahmūz.

chapters.ar: تَحۡرِيۡرٌ لِحَمۡزَةَ عِندَ الوَقفِ عَلَى الۡمَبدُوءِ بهمزٍ وقبلَه ساكنٌ مفصُولٌ
chapters.en: Taḥrīr on Ḥamzah's Reading: Pausing on a Disjoined Sukūn Before a Hamzah
chapters.desc: Ḥamzah’s options when pausing on a word whose final sākin letter meets a hamzah at the start of the next word, as in in anta: a single verse sums up the rulings for Khalaf and Khallād and makes naql the option to begin with.

verses.tr: For Ḥamzah, in إِنْ أَنْتَ, pause as you would connect; Add naql to that, and begin with it.

exp.en:
Background

This verse discusses the options available to حمزة when pausing on a word whose final sākin letter is followed by a hamzah at the beginning of the next word, as in إِنْ أَنْتَ, قَدْ أَفْلَحَ and أَرَاغِبٌ أَنْتَ.

The ruling is addressed in the context of two such positions occurring in the same passage, where one is read in waṣl and the other is paused upon.

For Khalaf, there are two options at waqf: naql, transferring the vowel of the hamzah to the preceding sākin letter, and the option that corresponds to his reading in waṣl.

If he reads without sakt in waṣl, he may pause with naql or without sakt. If he reads with sakt in waṣl, he may pause with naql or sakt.

For Khallād, according to the route of the Shāṭibiyyah, waṣl is read with taḥqīq, without sakt. His two options at waqf are therefore naql and taḥqīq without sakt.

The poet summarises these rulings in a single verse and indicates that naql is the preferred option to begin with.

  • Khalaf: without sakt in waṣl; at waqf, naql or without sakt.
  • Khalaf: with sakt in waṣl; at waqf, naql or sakt.
  • Khallād: taḥqīq without sakt in waṣl; at waqf, naql or taḥqīq without sakt.

Explanation

The poet uses إِنْ أَنْتَ as an example of a sākin letter at the end of one word followed by a hamzah at the beginning of the next. His instruction, قِفْ كَوَصْلِهِ, means that the reciter may pause using the same reading he employed in waṣl.

For Khalaf, this means that the option at waqf corresponds to his treatment in waṣl: if he read without sakt, he may pause without sakt; if he read with sakt, he may pause with sakt. For Khallād, the corresponding option is taḥqīq without sakt, since this is his reading in waṣl according to the Shāṭibiyyah.

The poet adds naql as a further option at waqf for both transmitters. In naql, the vowel of the hamzah is transferred to the preceding sākin letter, allowing the hamzah itself to be omitted in this treatment. The instruction وَابْدَأَنْ به indicates that naql is the preferred option to mention first.

chapters.ar: نَظۡمُ مَن لَّمۡ يُمِلۡ شَيئًا وَمَنۡ أَمَال كَلِمةً واحِدةً فَقَطۡ إِمَالةً كُبرٰى مِنَ الشَّاطِبيَّة والدُّرَّة
chapters.en: Those Who Applied No Imālah, and Those Who Applied Imālah Kubrā to Only One Word
chapters.desc: The two extremes of imālah among the qurrāʾ: Abū Jaʿfar and Ibn Kathīr, who apply no major imālah anywhere, and Qālūn, Ḥafṣ and Warsh, who each apply imālah kubrā to a single word in the entire Qurʾān.

verses.sadr: بُو جَعۡفَرٍ وَابۡنُ كَثِيرٍ يَا فَتَى
verses.ajuz: لَمۡ يُضۡجِعَا حَرۡفًا بِهِ قَدِ اشۡتَهَرۡ

ajuzW.g: for this they became well known

verses.tr: Abū Jaʿfar and Ibn Kathīr, O young man, inclined no letter for which this became well known.

exp.en:
Background

These verses summarise positions of imālah among several Qurra, and address the two extremes: reciters who apply no imālah at all anywhere in their reading, and reciters who apply imālah kubrā, the full, major form of the inclination, to exactly one single word in the entire Qur’ān.

The term الإضجاع refers to major imālah (الإمالة الكبرى), in which the fatḥah is inclined towards kasrah or the alif towards yāʾ. It is distinguished from التقليل, where the inclination of the sound is made such that it is closer to the fatḥah than the kasrah.

Explanation

The poet addresses the student of knowledge, explaining that Imām Abū Jaʿfar and Imām Ibn Kathīr do not read any position in the entire Qur’ān with major imālah (الإمالة الكبرى). Their general approach is to read with fatḥ, and this is a well-known and established feature of their recitations.

ajuzW.g: and the hāʾ of Ṭā Hā

verses.tr: Qālūn هَارٍ; Ḥafṣ, مَجرى—incline (apply imālah); And for Warsh, the hāʾ of طه is where it is confined.

exp.en:
The poet turns to specific words associated with individual reciters.

1. Qālūn and هَارٍ

Imām Qālūn, who narrates from Nāfiʿ, generally does not apply major imālah in the Qur’ān, with one exception: the word هَارٍ in Sūrat al-Tawbah, in the āyah ﴿عَلَىٰ شَفَا جُرُفٍ هَارٍ﴾ al-Tawbah 9:109, which he reads with major imālah.

2. Ḥafṣ and مَجْرَاهَا

Imām Ḥafṣ, who narrates from ʿĀṣim, has only one instance of imālah in the entire Qur’ān: the word مَجْرَاهَا in Sūrat Hūd, in the verse ﴿بِسْمِ اللَّهِ مَجْرَاهَا وَمُرْسَاهَا﴾ Hūd 11:41. In this word, he reads the rāʾ and the following alif with imālah, bringing the pronunciation closer to majrēhā.

3. Warsh and the hāʾ of Ṭā Hā

Imām Warsh, who also narrates from Nāfiʿ, is well known for using taqlīl (التقليل), or minor imālah, in words containing a yāʾ-originating alif (ذوات الياء). However, with regard to major imālah (الإمالة الكبرى, also called الإضجاع), his imālah is restricted to a single letter in the entire Qur’ān: the hāʾ at the beginning of Sūrat Ṭā Hā (طه). He reads this letter with major imālah, and this is the sole instance of major imālah attributed to him in this context.

chapters.ar: نَظۡمُ إِمَالاتِ يَعۡقُوۡب
chapters.en: The Imālah Positions of Yaʿqūb
chapters.desc: Two verses summarising the few positions of imālah in the recitation of Imām Yaʿqūb al-Ḥaḍramī through Ruways and Rawḥ: first the positions both narrators share, then what is particular to each.

verses.tr: Yaʿqūb’s imālah is confined to: The first أَعْمَى in al-Isrāʾ, and كَافِرِينَ [in al-Naml.]

exp.en:
Background

These two verses from the منظومات of Shaykh Dr Waleed summarise the positions of imālah in the recitation of Imām Yaʿqūb al-Ḥaḍramī through his two narrators, Ruways and Rawḥ. Although fatḥ is the general rule in his recitation, imālah occurs in a limited number of specific positions. The poet first mentions the positions shared by both narrators before distinguishing what is particular to each of them.

Explanation

The poet begins by establishing the general rule for Imām Yaʿqūb: his use of imālah is limited to a small number of specific positions. The verses identify these positions and distinguish between those shared by both narrators and those particular to Ruways or Rawḥ.

The first position is the word أَعْمَى in Sūrat al-Isrāʾ, in the verse:

﴿وَمَنْ كَانَ فِي هَٰذِهِ أَعْمَىٰ فَهُوَ فِي الْآخِرَةِ أَعْمَىٰ وَأَضَلُّ سَبِيلًا﴾

al-Isrāʾ 17:72

Both Ruways and Rawḥ read the first occurrence of أَعْمَى with imālah, while the second occurrence in the same verse is read with fatḥ.

The second position shared by both narrators is the word كَافِرِينَ in Sūrat al-Naml:

﴿إِنَّهَا كَانَتْ مِنْ قَوْمٍ كَافِرِينَ﴾

al-Naml 27:43

Here, both narrators read كَافِرِينَ with imālah. The poet then moves on to explain how the two narrators differ in their treatment of this word elsewhere in the Qur’ān.

verses.tr: Wherever كَافِرِينَ occurs, Ruways [inclines it]; And Rawḥ inclines the يَا of يس—so learn this and give thanks.

exp.en:
The poet explains that Ruways has a further rule: he reads الْكَافِرِينَ and كَافِرِينَ with imālah wherever they occur in the Qur’ān in the forms ending in ـِينَ, whether definite or indefinite, as in عَلَى الْكَافِرِينَ and بِالْكَافِرِينَ.

Rawḥ does not apply this general rule to these other occurrences, although he shares with Ruways the imālah of كَافِرِينَ in Sūrat al-Naml mentioned above.

The poet concludes by identifying a position particular to Rawḥ: the letter يَا at the beginning of Sūrat Yā Sīn. Rawḥ reads it with imālah, whereas Ruways reads it with fatḥ:

﴿يس ۝ وَالْقُرْآنِ الْحَكِيمِ﴾

Yā Sīn 36:1–2

The final word وَاشْكُرِ calls the student to gratitude to Allah for the blessing of learning the Qur’ānic recitations and preserving their precise modes of transmission.

Summary of Yaʿqūb’s Imālah Positions

  • أَعْمَى, first occurrence in Sūrat al-Isrāʾ (17:72): Ruways, imālah; Rawḥ, imālah.
  • كَافِرِينَ in Sūrat al-Naml (27:43): Ruways, imālah; Rawḥ, imālah.
  • الْكَافِرِينَ / كَافِرِينَ, other occurrences in the forms ending in ـِينَ: Ruways, imālah; Rawḥ, fatḥ.
  • يَا at the beginning of Sūrat Yā Sīn (36:1): Ruways, fatḥ; Rawḥ, imālah.

chapters.ar: نَظمُ مَوَاضِعِ الۡهَمزةِ المُتوسِّطةِ المضمُومةِ بَعۡدَ كَسۡرٍ
chapters.en: The Medial Ḍammah-Hamzah Preceded by Kasrah in Ḥamzah’s Waqf
chapters.desc: The words in which a medial hamzah carries a ḍammah after a kasrah, gathered into two verses, with the options open to Imām Ḥamzah when he stops on them: tashīl bayna bayn, a yāʾ carrying ḍammah, and in some words ḥadhf according to the rasm.

verses.tr: For Ḥamzah, note سَيِّئُهُ and مُسْتَهْزِئُون, Then أَنْبِئُوا, with يُطْفِئُوا and لِيُوَاطِئُوا.

exp.en:
Background

In this poem, Shaykh Dr Waleed bin Idris al-Meneese gathers the words in which the medial hamzah carries a ḍammah and is preceded by a kasrah, explaining the options available when Imām Ḥamzah stops on them. The hamzah may be read with tashīl bayna bayn, between the hamzah and the corresponding vowel, or replaced with a yāʾ carrying ḍammah, following the approach attributed to al-Akhfash. In certain words, a further option is available: ḥadhf, dropping the hamzah entirely, in accordance with the رسم of the muṣḥaf, with its ḍammah transferred to the preceding letter where applicable.

The poet organises these instances into eleven distinct root words fitting this description, some occurring only once and others recurring across many conjugated or derived forms.

Explanation

The poet begins with سَيِّئُهُ, followed by مُسْتَهْزِئُون and its related forms, such as يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ, تَسْتَهْزِئُونَ, and اسْتَهْزِئُوا. In these words, the hamzah is preceded by a kasrah and carries a ḍammah. When stopping on them, Ḥamzah has the option of tashīl bayna bayn or replacing the hamzah with a yāʾ carrying ḍammah. In words such as مُسْتَهْزِئُون, where the hamzah is followed by a wāw, ḥadhf is also among the recognised options associated with the رسم-based approach to stopping on the hamzah.

The poet next mentions أَنْبِئُوا and its related forms, including أَنْبِئُونِي, نَبِّئُونِي, يُنَبِّئُهُمْ, تُنَبِّئُهُمْ, فَيُنَبِّئُهُمْ, تُنَبِّئُونَهُ, أَتُنَبِّئُونَ, وَيَسْتَنْبِئُونَكَ, يُنَبِّئُكُمْ, وَيُنَبِّئُكُمْ, فَيُنَبِّئُكُمْ, أَنْبِئْكُمْ, أَأُنَبِّئُكُمْ, فَأُنَبِّئُكُمْ, أَفَأُنَبِّئُكُمْ, فَنُنَبِّئُكُمْ, سَأُنَبِّئُكَ, نُنَبِّئُكُمْ, and يُنَبِّئُكَ. He then mentions يُطْفِئُوا and its related form لِيُطْفِئُوا, followed by لِيُوَاطِئُوا. These examples share the relevant hamzah arrangement, and the applicable stopping options are determined by the word’s structure and the approach followed in stopping on the hamzah. Where the hamzah is followed by a wāw and the رسم-based ḥadhf applies, deletion is also permitted.

verses.tr: And الصَّابِئُون, سَنُقْرِئُكَ, and فَمَالِئُون, مُتَّكِئُون, الْمُنْشِئُون, and الْخَاطِئُون.

exp.en:
The next group consists of الصَّابِئُون, سَنُقْرِئُكَ, and فَمَالِئُون. The poet includes these because their hamzah also carries a ḍammah after a kasrah. The first and third belong to the group of words in which the hamzah is followed by a wāw, so the deletion option may apply in accordance with the relevant stopping rule.

In سَنُقْرِئُكَ, however, the hamzah is followed by a kāf, so the additional ḥadhf option associated with a following wāw does not apply.

The final group comprises مُتَّكِئُون and its related form يَتَّكِئُون, together with الْمُنْشِئُون and الْخَاطِئُون. As in the preceding examples, Ḥamzah may use tashīl bayna bayn or replace the hamzah with a yāʾ carrying ḍammah. Where the word meets the conditions for ḥadhf in accordance with the رسم, deletion is also permitted.

By gathering these examples into a single poem, the author provides the student with a practical means of recalling the relevant words and distinguishing the general options from the additional option of deletion.

chapters.ar: نَظمُ مواضعِ جوازِ إمالةِ الراءِ وصلا التي بعدها ألفٌ ممالةٌ محذوفةٌ لسكونِ ما بعدها للسوسي
chapters.en: A Poem on the Positions in Which al-Sūsī May Incline the Rāʾ Waslan, Whereby the Following Alif Is Omitted Due to a Subsequent Sukūn
chapters.desc: Al-Sūsī’s option of fatḥ or imālah of a rāʾ whose alif drops in connected recitation before a following sukūn: twenty-nine places before al-, and one in Ṭā Hā before a verb beginning with hamzah, arranged by their wording to be easy to memorise.

verses.sadr: فِي تِسۡعَةٍ مِنۡ بَعۡدِ عِشۡرِينَ أَمِلۡ
verses.ajuz: بِالۡخُلۡفِ لِلسُّوسِيِّ رَا مِنۡ قَبۡلِ أَلۡ
verses.tr: In twenty-nine [places], incline, with an option, for al-Sūsī, the rā' before al-.

exp.en:
Background

This poem addresses a specific case of imālah in the recitation of al-Sūsī from Abū ʿAmr al-Baṣrī. The case concerns a rāʾ followed by an alif that would ordinarily be inclined, but which is omitted in connected recitation (وصلا) because of the following word beginning with the definite article al-.

Al-Sūsī has two transmitted options in these positions: fatḥ and imālah of the rāʾ, with the latter indicating the alif that has been omitted in pronunciation.

This applies in twenty-nine such places in the Qur’ān, with one further, separate case at the very start of an āyah in Sūrat Ṭā Hā, occurring just before a verb beginning with hamzah rather than before al-.

Rather than naming all twenty-nine occurrences one by one, which would have made for an unwieldy verse, the poet economises by giving the nine base roots explicitly and then simply stating how many further occurrences of those same roots carry a prefixed wāw, tāʾ, or fāʾ, a natural shorthand once the reader recognises that Arabic verbs and nouns of this kind recur constantly across the Qur’ān with different leading conjunctions attached.

This is a particular rule and should not be confused with the general principles governing ذوات الياء. The poet arranges the examples according to their wording and the letters preceding them, making the positions easier to memorise.

Explanation

The poet begins by identifying the main rule: in twenty-nine positions, al-Sūsī has a choice between fatḥ and imālah of the rāʾ when it precedes an alif that is omitted in connected recitation before a following sukūn. The difference concerns the rāʾ, because the alif itself is no longer pronounced in waṣl. The imālah is retained as an indication of the omitted alif, while fatḥ reflects the absence of that alif in the connected pronunciation. This is a transmitted difference in recitation, not merely a phonetic inference.

sadrW.g: of an āyah of Ṭā Hā

verses.tr: And one place at the beginning of an āyah in Ṭā Hā, before the hamzah of the verb that follows it.

exp.en:
The poet then draws attention to a particular position at the end of an āyah in Sūrat Ṭā Hā, where the word الْكُبْرَىٰ is followed by the imperative اذْهَبْ at the beginning of the next āyah. When the two are connected, the hamzat al-waṣl of اذْهَبْ falls, producing the relevant context for this rule.

Allah says:

﴿لِنُرِيَكَ مِنْ آيَاتِنَا الْكُبْرَىٰ ۝ اذْهَبْ إِلَىٰ فِرْعَوْنَ إِنَّهُ طَغَىٰ﴾

Ṭā Hā 20:23–24

This example is singled out because the word occurs at the end of an āyah and is followed, in connected recitation, by a verb beginning with hamzat al-waṣl.

verses.sadr: وَهۡيَ نَرَى الله أَرَى الۡهُدۡهُدَ مَعۡ
verses.tr: And they are: نَرَى الله, أَرَى الْهُدْهُدَ, together with يَرَى الَّذِينَ, and وَيَرَى الَّذِينَ, so understand.

exp.en:
The poet now begins listing examples of the relevant words. Among them is نَرَى اللَّهَ, in which the rāʾ precedes an alif that is omitted when connected to the name of Allah. He also mentions أَرَى الْهُدْهُدَ, from the account of Sulaymān عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ, and examples involving يَرَى الَّذِينَ. These examples help the student recognise the rule in different verbal forms rather than memorising a single word in isolation.

Allah says:

﴿وَإِذْ قُلْتُمْ يَا مُوسَىٰ لَنْ نُؤْمِنَ لَكَ حَتَّىٰ نَرَى اللَّهَ جَهْرَةً﴾

al-Baqarah 2:55

﴿وَتَفَقَّدَ الطَّيْرَ فَقَالَ مَا لِيَ لَا أَرَى الْهُدْهُدَ أَمْ كَانَ مِنَ الْغَائِبِينَ﴾

al-Naml 27:20

﴿وَيَرَى الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْعِلْمَ الَّذِي أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْكَ مِنْ رَبِّكَ هُوَ الْحَقَّ﴾

Sabaʾ 34:6

verses.ajuz: ذِكۡرَى الۡقُرَى كَذَا النَّصَارَى قَدۡ حَصَلۡ
verses.tr: And سَيَرَى, فَسَيرَى الله عَمَلْ, ذِكْرَى الْقُرَى, likewise النَّصَارَى, has occurred.

exp.en:
The poet continues with سَيَرَى and فَسَيَرَى اللَّهُ عَمَلَكُمْ, then mentions ذِكْرَى الدَّارِ, الْقُرَى الَّتِي, and النَّصَارَى الْمَسِيحُ. These are further examples of the rāʾ-related positions discussed in this chapter. In the cases where the alif is omitted in connected recitation because of the following word, al-Sūsī has the transmitted options of fatḥ and imālah of the rāʾ. When the rāʾ is inclined before the name of Allah, the treatment of the lām in اللَّه must also be considered according to the rules governing the lām of the Divine Name.

Allah says:

﴿وَقُلِ اعْمَلُوا فَسَيَرَى اللَّهُ عَمَلَكُمْ وَرَسُولُهُ وَالْمُؤْمِنُونَ﴾

al-Tawbah 9:105

﴿إِنَّا أَخْلَصْنَاهُمْ بِخَالِصَةٍ ذِكْرَى الدَّارِ﴾

Ṣād 38:46

﴿وَجَعَلْنَا بَيْنَهُمْ وَبَيْنَ الْقُرَى الَّتِي بَارَكْنَا فِيهَا قُرًى ظَاهِرَةً﴾

Sabaʾ 34:18

﴿وَقَالَتِ الْيَهُودُ عُزَيْرٌ ابْنُ اللَّهِ وَقَالَتِ النَّصَارَى الْمَسِيحُ ابْنُ اللَّهِ﴾

al-Tawbah 9:30

verses.sadr: ذِي تِسۡعَةٌ قَدۡ أُفۡرِدَتۡ مَا كُرِّرَتۡ
verses.tr: These are nine, given individually, not repeated; and ten more you find preceded by a wāw.

exp.en:
Having introduced the examples, the poet explains how the positions are organised. Nine are treated as individual, non-repeated examples, while ten are associated with forms preceded by wāw. This division is a mnemonic aid: it groups the instances according to their wording and helps the student retrieve them systematically.

One example is:

﴿وَرَأَى الْمُجْرِمُونَ النَّارَ فَظَنُّوا أَنَّهُمْ مُوَاقِعُوهَا﴾

al-Kahf 18:53

Here, رَأَى is followed by الْمُجْرِمُونَ, and the alif is omitted in connected recitation. This illustrates the type of connection under discussion.

verses.tr: And five more you find with a tā'; and five, say, with a fā'.

exp.en:
The poet completes the numerical classification by identifying five examples associated with tāʾ and another five associated with fāʾ. These forms include expressions such as تَرَى and فَتَرَى.

Examples include:

﴿وَتَرَى النَّاسَ سُكَارَىٰ وَمَا هُمْ بِسُكَارَىٰ﴾

al-Ḥajj 22:2

﴿فَتَرَى الْوَدْقَ يَخْرُجُ مِنْ خِلَالِهِ﴾

al-Nūr 24:43

These examples demonstrate the relevant verbal patterns.

verses.tr: Ṭāhir al-Suyūṭī shared this benefit with us, the knowledgeable, skilled, and eminent reciter.

exp.en: The poet concludes by praising the learned reciter Ṭāhir al-Suyūṭī, acknowledging his contribution to preserving and transmitting the details of this subject.

chapters.ar: أَوَلَمۡ يَسِيۡروۡا وأَفَلمۡ يَسِيۡرُوۡا
chapters.en: Verbal Similarities in the Noble Qur'ān: “Awalam Yasīrū” and “Afalam Yasīrū”
chapters.desc: Awalam yasīrū and afalam yasīrū, “have they not travelled”, differ only in their opening particle. Two abyāt sort their seven occurrences: the first wording comes in three places, the second in four.

verses.ajuz: مَعۡ سُورَةِ الرُّومِ كَذَا فِي فَاطِرِ
verses.tr: Say أَوَلَمْ in the first occurrence in Ghāfir, along with Sūrat ar-Rūm, and likewise in Fāṭir.

exp.en:
Background

Among the mutashābih lafẓī in the Noble Qur'ān is the pairing of أَوَلَمْ يَسِيْرُوْا and أَفَلَمْ يَسِيْرُوْا, both meaning “have they not travelled,” differing only in their opening interrogative particle. أَوَلَمْ يَسِيْرُوْا occurs in three places, and أَفَلَمْ يَسِيْرُوْا occurs in four.

Occurrences of أَوَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا and أَفَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا

  • أَوَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا (3 occurrences): Ghāfir (the first occurrence), ar-Rūm, Fāṭir.
  • أَفَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا (4 occurrences): Ghāfir (the last occurrence), Muḥammad, al-Ḥajj, Yūsuf.

Abyāt 1–2

The poet categorizes the seven occurrences of this phrase across the two variations; أَوَلَمْ يَسِيْرُوْا accounts for three of them: the first occurrence in Sūrat Ghāfir, together with Sūrat ar-Rūm and Sūrat Fāṭir.

أَفَلَمْ يَسِيْرُوْا accounts for the remaining four: the last occurrence in Sūrat Ghāfir itself, together with Sūrat Muḥammad, Sūrat al-Ḥajj, and Sūrat Yūsuf.

verses.tr: And أَفَلَمْ in the last occurrence in Ghāfir, in Muḥammad, in al-Ḥajj, and in Yūsuf, so give thanks.

chapters.ar: مَا كَسَبَتۡ وَبِمَا كَسَبَتۡ
chapters.en: Al-Mutashābih al-Lafẓī: The pairing of “Mā Kasabat” and “Bimā Kasabat”
chapters.desc: A ḥāfiẓ asked the poet how to tell mā kasabat, without a bā’, from bimā kasabat, with one. His answer in two abyāt: the first half of the Qurʾān reads mā kasabat apart from three exceptions, and the second half reads bimā kasabat.

verses.ajuz: مِنۡ غَيۡرِ بَا إِلَّا ثَلَاثًا قَدۡ أَتۡتۡ

sadrW.g: of the two halves (of the Qurʾān)

verses.tr: In the first of the two halves, say مَا كَسَبَتْ without a bā', except for three that came differently.

exp.en:
Background

A ḥāfiẓ of the Qur'ān once asked the poet for a method to distinguish the places where the wording is مَا كَسَبَتْ, without a bā', from the places where it is بِمَا كَسَبَتْ, with a bā'.

He replied that in the first half of the Qur'ān, that is, in al-Baqarah, Āl 'Imrān, al-An'ām, ar-Ra'd, and Ibrāhīm, the wording is always mā kasabat, without a bā', except for three exceptions preceded by the words يُؤَاخِذْ, tubsala, and qā'imun. In the second half of the Qur'ān, that is in ar-Rūm, Ghāfir, ash-Shūrā, al-Jāthiyah, and al-Muddaththir, the wording is always bimā kasabat, with a bā'.

Abyāt 1–2

The poet condenses his own answer into two verses.

The first half of the Qur'ān reads مَا كَسَبَتْ throughout, except at three specific points, each identifiable by the word that comes just before it.

The second half of the Qur'ān reads بِمَا كَسَبَتْ throughout, with no exceptions given.

The concept is further illustrated below.

The wording of مَا كَسَبَتْ: with and without a bā’ in different parts of the Qur’ān

  • The first half of the Qur’ān (al-Baqarah, Āl ʿImrān, al-Anʿām, ar-Raʿd and Ibrāhīm): مَا كَسَبَتْ, without a bā’.
  • The second half of the Qur’ān (ar-Rūm, Ghāfir, ash-Shūrā, al-Jāthiyah and al-Muddaththir): بِمَا كَسَبَتْ, with a bā’.

Three exceptions. In the first half, there are three exceptions, each preceded by:

1. يُؤَاخِذُكُمْ

﴿لَا يُؤَاخِذُكُمُ اللَّهُ بِاللَّغْوِ فِي أَيْمَانِكُمْ وَلَٰكِن يُؤَاخِذُكُم بِمَا كَسَبَتْ قُلُوبُكُمْ﴾

al-Baqarah 2:225

2. تُبْسَلَ

﴿وَذَكِّرْ بِهِ أَن تُبْسَلَ نَفْسٌ بِمَا كَسَبَتْ﴾

al-Anʿām 6:70

3. قَائِمٌ

﴿أَفَمَنْ هُوَ قَائِمٌ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ نَفْسٍ بِمَا كَسَبَتْ﴾

ar-Raʿd 13:33

verses.tr: And they are yu'ākhidh, qā'imun, and tubsalu; and in the last of the two halves, a bā' adorns it.

chapters.ar: الخَائِبُوۡنَ فِي الۡقُرۡآنِ
chapters.en: The Four Who Fail in the Qur'ān: Khāba and Qad Khāba
chapters.desc: The four places where the Qurʾān describes someone with khāba, “he failed”, and the small detail that tells them apart: whether qad comes before it.

verses.tr: Those who fail in the Qur'ān are four: their tyrant, their obstinate one, so listen to it.

exp.en:
Background

This poem addresses the four places in the Qur'ān where the word خاب, meaning to fail or be disappointed, is used to describe someone, together with the small but distinguishing detail of whether the word قد precedes it.

Abyāt 1–3

The poet gathers the four places in the Qur’ān where خَابَ is used to describe one who fails. The Qur’ānic concept of failure, however, is far greater than merely losing wealth, status, or worldly possessions. A person may lose something of this world and still be successful in the sight of Allah, while true failure is the loss of eternal success. The Qur’ān therefore draws our attention to those who have fallen into true and lasting failure, so that we may take heed and not find ourselves among them.

The four described are:

  1. The obstinate tyrant
  2. The one who fabricates lies
  3. The one who bears injustice
  4. And the one who corrupts his own soul.

The poet also points out a small but distinguishing detail: قَدْ precedes خَابَ in the final three occurrences, while it does not occur in the first.

The four occurrences are:

1. جَبَّارٍ عَنِيدٍ

﴿وَخَابَ كُلُّ جَبَّارٍ عَنِيدٍ﴾

Ibrāhīm 14:15

2. مَنِ افْتَرَىٰ

﴿وَقَدْ خَابَ مَنِ افْتَرَىٰ﴾

Ṭā Hā 20:61

3. مَنْ حَمَلَ ظُلْمًا

﴿وَقَدْ خَابَ مَنْ حَمَلَ ظُلْمًا﴾

Ṭā Hā 20:111

4. مَن دَسَّاهَا

﴿وَقَدْ خَابَ مَن دَسَّاهَا﴾

ash-Shams 91:10

verses.tr: That is the first; and the second, say: whoever fabricates; and the third, whoever bears injustice and dares.
And the fourth: whoever corrupts his soul. And قَدْ occurs before خَابَ in all except the first.

chapters.ar: تَرۡتِيۡبُ ذِكۡرِ الۡجِنِّ والإِنۡسِ فِي الۡقُرۡآنِ
chapters.en: Al-Mutashābih al-Lafẓī: the Order of “al-Jinn” and “al-Ins”
chapters.desc: When does the Qurʾān mention al-jinn before al-ins, and when the reverse? Three words coming just before the pair put al-jinn first; the nominative case and the word shayāṭīn put al-ins first.

verses.ajuz: (مِنۡ) جِنُّهَا جَا قَبۡلَ إِنۡسٍ قَدۡ وَعَوۡا
verses.tr: Whatever is preceded by معشر, or خلقتُ, or مِن — its جن comes before إنس, as [the scholars] have understood.

exp.en:
Background

In the Noble Qur'ān, the word الجن precedes الإنس whenever either of three words comes just before them: معشر, خلقتُ, or مِن. Conversely, الإنس precedes الجن in two further situations: wherever both words appear in the nominative case (مرفوعا), and wherever the word شياطين (“devils”) comes just before them.

Abyāt 1–2

The two verses establish the order in which the Qurʾān mentions الْجِنّ and الْإِنْس. The poet first identifies three words which, when they precede the pair, indicate that الْجِنّ comes first: مَعْشَرَ, خَلَقْتُ and مِنْ.

The second verse gives the instances in which the order is reversed. الْإِنْس comes before الْجِنّ when both are in the nominative case, and it also comes first when preceded by شَيَاطِين.

The occurrences are therefore as follows:

1. الْجِنّ before الْإِنْس: مَعْشَرَ

Wherever the expression يَا مَعْشَرَ الْجِنِّ وَالْإِنسِ occurs, الْجِنّ is mentioned first.

﴿يَا مَعْشَرَ الْجِنِّ وَالْإِنسِ إِنِ اسْتَطَعْتُمْ أَن تَنفُذُوا مِنْ أَقْطَارِ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ فَانفُذُوا﴾

al-Raḥmān 55:33

The same order is maintained wherever the expression مَعْشَرَ الْجِنِّ وَالْإِنسِ occurs.

2. الْجِنّ before الْإِنْس: خَلَقْتُ

﴿وَمَا خَلَقْتُ الْجِنَّ وَالْإِنسَ إِلَّا لِيَعْبُدُونِ﴾

al-Dhāriyāt 51:56

Here the pair is preceded by خَلَقْتُ, so الْجِنّ comes before الْإِنْس.

3. الْجِنّ before الْإِنْس: مِنْ

Wherever the pair is preceded by مِنْ, الْجِنّ comes first.

﴿مِنَ الْجِنِّ وَالْإِنسِ﴾

4. Both in the nominative: الْإِنْس before الْجِنّ

When الْإِنْس and الْجِنّ are both in the nominative case, الْإِنْس comes first.

﴿لَئِنِ اجْتَمَعَتِ الْإِنسُ وَالْجِنُّ عَلَىٰ أَن يَأْتُوا بِمِثْلِ هَٰذَا الْقُرْآنِ لَا يَأْتُونَ بِمِثْلِهِ﴾

al-Isrāʾ 17:88

Both الْإِنْسُ and الْجِنُّ are marfūʿ, and thus the order.

Similarly:

﴿وَأَنَّا ظَنَنَّا أَن لَّن تَقُولَ الْإِنسُ وَالْجِنُّ عَلَى اللَّهِ كَذِبًا﴾

al-Jinn 72:5

5. Preceded by the word شَيَاطِين: الْإِنْس before الْجِنّ

When شَيَاطِينَ precedes the pair, الْإِنْس comes first:

﴿وَكَذَٰلِكَ جَعَلْنَا لِكُلِّ نَبِيٍّ عَدُوًّا شَيَاطِينَ الْإِنسِ وَالْجِنِّ﴾

al-Anʿām 6:112

In this way, the poet gathers the Qurʾānic occurrences according to the words and grammatical positions that determine their order. The rule can be summarised at a glance as follows:

The order of mentioning الْجِنّ and الْإِنْس in the Qurʾān

  • When الْجِنّ comes first: when one of these words precedes the pair, the order is الْجِنّ, then الْإِنْس: مَعْشَرَ (a gathering, O people), خَلَقْتُ (I created), مِنْ (from).
  • When الْإِنْس comes first: الْإِنْس comes before الْجِنّ when both are in the nominative case; and when شَيَاطِين precedes the pair, الْإِنْس comes first in the order.

In short: certain words signal that الْجِنّ comes first, while in other cases, الْإِنْس comes first, especially when both are in the nominative case or when preceded by شَيَاطِين.

verses.tr: “And الإنس [comes] before الجن wherever both are in the nominative case — or where the word شياطين precedes it. Listen!”

chapters.ar: مَوَاضِعُ ذِكۡرِ كَلِمَةِ "فِيۡهَا" مَعَ "يَشَاءُوۡنَ" فِي الۡقُرۡآنِ الۡكَرِيۡمِ
chapters.en: Al-Mutashābih al-Lafẓī: The Placement of “Fīhā” with “Yashā'ūn”
chapters.desc: The five occurrences of yashāʾūn in the Qurʾān and the three patterns of fīhā around them: after it in Qāf, before it in al-Furqān and al-Naḥl, and absent in al-Shūrā and al-Zumar.

verses.tr: The word يَشَاءُونَ occurs in five [places] — and in Sūrat Qāf, establish فِيهَا after it.

exp.en:
Background

Among the mutashābih lafẓī in the Noble Qurʾān are the five occurrences of يَشَاءُونَ, where the surrounding wording varies in three patterns. The distinction centres on whether فِيهَا is placed after يَشَاءُونَ or omitted.

  1. In Sūrat Qāf, فِيهَا comes after يَشَاءُونَ.
  2. In Sūrat al-Furqān and Sūrat al-Naḥl, فِيهَا comes before يَشَاءُونَ.
  3. In Sūrat al-Shūrā and Sūrat al-Zumar, فِيهَا does not occur at all.

Abyāt 1–2

The poet gathers five easily confused Qurʾānic expressions and distinguishes them according to the position of فِيهَا. The key is to remember the three patterns:

i. Qāf: فِيهَا comes after يَشَاءُونَ.

﴿لَهُم مَّا يَشَاءُونَ فِيهَا وَلَدَيْنَا مَزِيدٌ﴾

Qāf 50:35

This is the single occurrence in which فِيهَا follows the verb.

ii. al-Furqān and al-Naḥl: فِيهَا comes before يَشَاءُونَ.

﴿لَهُمْ فِيهَا مَا يَشَاءُونَ خَالِدِينَ كَانَ عَلَىٰ رَبِّكَ وَعْدًا مَّسْئُولًا﴾

al-Furqān 25:16

﴿لَهُمْ فِيهَا مَا يَشَاءُونَ كَذَٰلِكَ يَجْزِي اللَّهُ الْمُتَّقِينَ﴾

al-Naḥl 16:31

Thus, al-Furqān and al-Naḥl share the same arrangement.

iii. al-Shūrā and al-Zumar: فِيهَا is omitted.

﴿لَهُم مَّا يَشَاءُونَ عِندَ رَبِّهِمْ ذَٰلِكَ هُوَ الْفَضْلُ الْكَبِيرُ﴾

al-Shūrā 42:22

﴿لَهُم مَّا يَشَاءُونَ عِندَ رَبِّهِمْ ذَٰلِكَ جَزَاءُ الْمُحْسِنِينَ﴾

al-Zumar 39:34

Thus, the five occurrences are distinguished by the placement of فِيهَا: after يَشَاءُونَ in Qāf, before it in al-Furqān and al-Naḥl, and omitted altogether in al-Shūrā and al-Zumar.

verses.tr: As for فِيهَا, in al-Furqān and al-Naḥl place it before; while in al-Shūrā and al-Zumar it is omitted—so know this well.
