chapters.ar: مَوَاضِعُ تَقۡدِيۡمِ النَّفۡعِ عَلَى الضَّرِّ فِي القُرۡآنِ الكَرِيۡمِ
chapters.en: The Places Where Benefit Precedes Harm in the Noble Qur'ān
chapters.desc: A mnemonic for the places where the Qurʾān mentions benefit (al-nafʿ) before harm (al-ḍarr): an ʿayn in the sūrah’s name decides the order in the first half of the Qurʾān and a hamzah in the second, with one exception in each half.

verses.sadr: إِنَّ سُوۡرَةً فِي وَسۡمِهَا عَيۡنٌ يُرىٰ
verses.tr: “If a sūrah has an ʿayn in its name, then place النفع first and الضر after it.”

exp.en:
Background

This poem presents a concise method for remembering the places in the Qurʾān where النفع is mentioned before الضر, and where the order is reversed. The mnemonic is based on the names of the sūrahs and divides the Qurʾān into two halves, with a single exception in each.

In the first half of the Qurʾān, the rule concerns the nouns النفع and الضر: in sūrahs whose names contain the letter ع, النفع comes before الضر; in sūrahs without ع, the order is reversed. The exception is the final occurrence in Sūrah Yūnus.

In the second half, the same principle applies more broadly: whether the words occur as the nouns النفع and الضر, or as the verbs يَنْفَعُ and يَضُرُّ, the presence of a همزة in the sūrah's name indicates that النفع or يَنْفَعُ comes first. In sūrahs whose names do not contain a همزة, الضر or يَضُرُّ comes first. The exception is the second occurrence in Sūrah al-Furqān.

This mnemonic was conveyed by Shaykh ʿAbd al-Munʿim al-Maqṣabī al-Lībī during the judging of the Imām al-Shāṭibī Qurʾān Competition on 4 Muḥarram 1440 AH. At the request of Shaykh Dr. Sālim al-Zahrānī, the poet Shaykh Dr. Walīd ibn Idrīs al-Minīsī versified this benefit in the following lines.

Explanation

The poet begins with the first half of the Qurʾān. In the sūrahs whose names contain the letter ع, when the two terms occur together, النفع is mentioned before الضر. The letter ع therefore serves as the mnemonic for remembering this order.

verses.sadr: فِي أَوَّلِ الشَّطۡرَيۡنِ يَا مَنۡ يَأۡتَسِي
verses.ajuz: وَشَذَّ عَنۡ ذَا آخِرٌ مِنۡ يُوۡنسِ
verses.tr: [This applies] in the first of the two halves, O one who seeks to follow; an exception to this is the final occurrence in Surah Yūnus.

exp.en: The rule applies to the first half of the Qurʾān, but the poet immediately identifies its exception: the final occurrence in Sūrah Yūnus, where the order differs from the general pattern.

verses.ajuz: فَالنَّفۡعَ قَدِّمۡ قَبۡلَ ضَرٍّ يَا فَتَى
verses.tr: “And if a sūrah has a hamzah in its name, then place النفع before الضر, O young man.”

exp.en: The poet now moves to the second half of the Qurʾān. Here the mnemonic changes: the presence of a همزة in the name of the sūrah indicates that النفع comes before الضر.

verses.sadr: فِي آخِرِ الشَّطۡرَيۡنِ لَا فَرۡقَ بِهِ
verses.ajuz: فِي اسۡمِ أَتَى وَما أَتَى مِنۡ فِعۡلِهِ
verses.tr: In the latter half, there is no distinction between them, whether they occur as a noun or as a verb.

exp.en: The rule in the second half applies whether the words occur as the nouns النفع and الضر, or through their corresponding verbal forms, يَنْفَعُ and يَضُرُّ. Thus, the mnemonic concerns the order of meaning rather than restricting the rule to a particular grammatical form.

verses.tr: “Exclude from this the second occurrence in Surah al-Furqān; truly, successful are those who memorise the Book of our Lord.”

exp.en: The poet concludes by identifying the second exception: the second occurrence in Sūrah al-Furqān, where the order does not follow the general rule of the second half.

chapters.ar: مَا نُهِيَ عَنِ التَّشَبّه به فِي الصَّلَاة مِنَ الحيوان
chapters.en: What Is Forbidden by Way of Resembling Animals in Prayer
chapters.desc: Nine animal-like postures and movements the worshipper is warned against in prayer, gathered in three abyāt: the rooster, crow, monkey, fox, dog, camel, horse, donkey and the beast of prey.

verses.tr: We have been warned against animals; we should not resemble them in our prayers.

exp.en:
Background

These verses gather several animal-like postures and movements that the worshipper has been warned to avoid during Ṣalāh in various Ahadith. For instance, Ibn al-Qayyim, in Zād al-Ma'ād, records a set of postures and movements that the praying person is instructed to avoid, each described through a comparison to an animal's behaviour.

The poet brings together nine such examples: the rooster, crow, monkey, fox, dog, camel, horse, donkey and the predatory beast.

The purpose is not merely to avoid resembling animals, but to preserve the dignity, stillness, and attentiveness that should characterise prayer.

Abyāt 1–3

The poet gathers nine animal-like movements or postures that the worshipper is warned against in Ṣalāh.

The common thread is that Ṣalāh is not meant to be performed with careless, hurried, or undignified movements. The Sunnah repeatedly emphasises ṭumaʾnīnah, stillness, and proper composure, and in several cases the Prophet ﷺ specifically used the movements of animals to illustrate what should be avoided.

Each animal corresponds to a particular movement or posture:

نَقْرُ الدِّيك 1. The Rooster

This refers to hurrying through the prayer, particularly in rukūʿ and sujūd, without allowing sufficient time for each posture. The movement resembles the quick pecking of a rooster.

The Prophet ﷺ described such a prayer:

عَنْ أَنَسِ بْنِ مَالِكٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ: تِلْكَ صَلَاةُ الْمُنَافِقِ، يَجْلِسُ يَرْقُبُ الشَّمْسَ حَتَّى إِذَا كَانَتْ بَيْنَ قَرْنَيِ الشَّيْطَانِ قَامَ فَنَقَرَهَا أَرْبَعًا، لَا يَذْكُرُ اللَّهَ فِيهَا إِلَّا قَلِيلًا

“That is the prayer of the hypocrite: he sits watching the sun, and when it is between the two horns of Shayṭān, he gets up and pecks at it four times, hardly remembering Allah therein.” Narrated by Muslim

نَقْرُ الْغُرَاب 2. The Crow

This refers to pecking the ground during sujūd, lowering oneself quickly and rising again without proper stillness and composure.

The Prophet ﷺ explicitly prohibited:

أَمَرَنِي رَسُولُ اللهِ صَلَّى اللهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بِثَلَاثٍ، وَنَهَانِي عَنْ ثَلَاثٍ ... وَنَهَانِي عَنْ نَقْرَةِ الْغُرَابِ ... الحديث

“And he forbade me from pecking like a crow.” Narrated by Aḥmad in his Musnad

الْقِرْد 3. The Monkey

The monkey represents excessive and restless movement in Ṣalāh: unnecessary movement, fidgeting, and constantly shifting the body without need.

رَوَغَانُ الثَّعْلَب 4. The Fox

This refers to repeatedly turning and looking around during Ṣalāh, moving the face from side to side without need, like the cautious and evasive movement of a fox.

The Prophet ﷺ said:

أَمَرَنِي رَسُولُ اللهِ صَلَّى اللهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بِثَلَاثٍ، وَنَهَانِي عَنْ ثَلَاثٍ ... وَنَهَانِي عَنْ نَقْرَةِ الْغُرَابِ ... وَرَوَاغَانِ كَرَوَاغَانِ الثَّعْلَبِ

“And [he forbade] turning about like the turning of a fox.” Narrated by Aḥmad in his Musnad

إِقْعَاءُ الْكَلْبِ وَافْتِرَاشُهُ 5. The Dog

The dog is mentioned in more than one posture.

One is إقعاء الكلب, referring to a manner of sitting resembling the sitting of a dog. The Prophet ﷺ said:

أَمَرَنِي رَسُولُ اللهِ صَلَّى اللهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بِثَلَاثٍ، وَنَهَانِي عَنْ ثَلَاثٍ ... وَنَهَانِي عَنْ نَقْرَةِ الْغُرَابِ وَإِقْعَاءِ الْكَلْبِ وَرَوَاغَانِ كَرَوَاغَانِ الثَّعْلَبِ

“And he forbade me from sitting like a dog.” Narrated by Aḥmad in his Musnad

Another is افتراش الكلب, which occurs in sujūd when the worshipper spreads his forearms on the ground.

The Prophet ﷺ said:

اعْتَدِلُوا فِي السُّجُودِ، وَلَا يَبْسُطْ أَحَدُكُمْ ذِرَاعَيْهِ انْبِسَاطَ الْكَلْبِ

“Be balanced in sujūd, and none of you should spread his forearms like a dog.” Narrated by al-Bukhārī and Muslim in their Ṣaḥīḥs

بُرُوكُ الْبَعِير 6. The Camel

The comparison here concerns the manner of descending into sujūd.

The Prophet ﷺ said:

إِذَا سَجَدَ أَحَدُكُمْ فَلَا يَبْرُكْ كَمَا يَبْرُكُ الْبَعِيرُ ... الحديث

“When one of you prostrates, let him not kneel as the camel kneels down.” Narrated by Abū Dāwūd

أَذْنَابُ الْخَيْلِ الشُّمُس 7. The Horse

This refers to raising and moving the hands, in a manner resembling the movement of the tails of restless horses.

Jābir ibn Samurah رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ said:

مَا لِي أَرَاكُمْ رَافِعِي أَيْدِيكُمْ كَأَنَّهَا أَذْنَابُ خَيْلٍ شُمْسٍ؟ اسْكُنُوا فِي الصَّلَاةِ

“Why do I see you raising your hands as though they are the tails of restless horses? Remain still in the prayer.” Narrated by Muslim

رَأْسُ الْحِمَار 8. The Donkey

The donkey is associated with raising one's head before the imām, whether from rukūʿ or sujūd, thereby racing the imām.

The Prophet ﷺ warned:

أَمَا يَخْشَى أَحَدُكُمْ إِذَا رَفَعَ رَأْسَهُ قَبْلَ الْإِمَامِ أَنْ يَجْعَلَ اللَّهُ رَأْسَهُ رَأْسَ حِمَارٍ، أَوْ يَجْعَلَ اللَّهُ صُورَتَهُ صُورَةَ حِمَارٍ

“Does not one of you fear that, when he raises his head before the imām, Allah may make his head the head of a donkey, or make his form the form of a donkey?” Narrated by al-Bukhārī and Muslim

افْتِرَاشُ السَّبُع 9. The Predatory Beast

Finally, the poet mentions the sabʿ, a fierce predatory animal. This refers to spreading the arms on the ground during sujūd, resembling the manner in which a predatory animal stretches itself.

The Prophet ﷺ said:

عَنْ عَبْدِ الرَّحْمَنِ بْنِ شِبْلٍ قَالَ: نَهَى رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ عَنْ نَقْرَةِ الْغُرَابِ، وَافْتِرَاشِ السَّبُعِ ... الحديث

“The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade pecking like a crow and spreading oneself like a predatory beast.” Narrated by Abū Dāwūd

This is closely related to the prohibition of spreading the forearms on the ground like a dog. The purpose is to maintain the proper posture of sujūd rather than collapsing into a posture resembling an animal.

verses.tr: Rooster, crow, monkey, fox; the rest of the nine is what comes next.
Dog, camel, horse, donkey, and last of all a fierce beast of prey.

chapters.ar: الشُّرُوۡطُ الأَرۡبَعَة لِلعُلُوۡمِ النَّافِعَة
chapters.en: Shurūṭ al-'Ilm: The Four Conditions of Beneficial Knowledge
chapters.desc: A versification of the well-known counsel that the conditions of knowledge are four: a sincere teacher, authentic books, clear handwriting and persistent study. Its final verse adds a fifth, soundness of intellect, which some scholars appended to the list.

ajuzW.g: so here they are, take them
so that you may gather them

verses.tr: The conditions of knowledge are four. Here they are, so that you may gather them together.

exp.en:
Background

This poem versifies a well-known piece of traditional counsel on the conditions required for sound learning, usually phrased in prose as: شُرُوْطُ الْعِلْمِ أَرْبَعَةٌ, meaning the conditions of knowledge are four:

  1. شَيْخٌ نَصَّاحٌ, a sincere and advising teacher;
  2. وَكُتُبٌ صِحَاحٌ, authentic books;
  3. وَخَطٌّ وَضَّاحٌ, clear handwriting;
  4. والدَّرْسُ بِإِلْحَاحٍ, persistent, unrelenting study.

A closely related saying, phrased with slightly different wording, is also transmitted:

آلَاتُ الْعِلْمِ أَرْبَعَةٌ, meaning the tools of knowledge are four:

  1. شَيْخٌ فَتَّاحٌ, an opening, illuminating teacher;
  2. وَعَقْلٌ رَجَّاحٌ, a sound and weighty intellect;
  3. وَكُتُبٌ صِحَاحٌ, authentic books;
  4. وَمُدَاوَمَةٌ وَإِلْحَاحٌ, constancy and persistence.

The poet's final verse draws on this second saying to add a further condition beyond the first list of four.

The four conditions of beneficial knowledge

  1. شيخ نصوح A teacher whose guidance is sincere and trustworthy.
  2. كتب صحيحة ونافعة Books that are both authentic in their transmission and genuinely useful in their content.
  3. وضوح خط Clarity of handwriting or script, so that the texts themselves can be read without difficulty.
  4. إلحاح في الدرس Persistence in study, returning to the material again and again rather than a single pass.
  5. رجاح عقل Soundness or weightiness of intellect (an addition by some scholars).

Together, these conditions ensure that knowledge is authentic, beneficial, understood and acted upon, and firmly rooted in the heart and mind.

Explanation

The poet opens by announcing the topic and its structure directly: four conditions are about to be listed, and the student is invited to commit them to memory as a set.

verses.tr: A sincere teacher and books that are authentic and beneficial.

exp.en:
The first two conditions are given:

  • I. شَيْخٌ نَصُوْحٌ, a teacher whose guidance is sincere and trustworthy.
  • II. كُتُبٌ صحِيْحَةٌ وَنَافِعَةٌ, books that are both authentic in their transmission and genuinely useful in their content.

verses.tr: Clarity of script, and that you persist in studying it, and take that along with it.

exp.en:
The third and fourth conditions follow:

  • III. وضوحُ خطٍّ, clarity of handwriting or script, so that the texts themselves can be read without difficulty.
  • IV. إِلْحَاحٌ فِي الدَّرْسِ, persistence in study, returning to the material again and again rather than a single pass.

وخُذْ مَعَه, take that along with it, signals that a further addition follows in the next verse.

verses.tr: Soundness of intellect, which some of them added and appended to the list.

exp.en:
The closing verse brings in the fifth element, رَجَاحَ عَقْل, soundness or weightiness of intellect, explicitly framed as an addition made by some scholars rather than as part of the original four.

The poet thereby preserves both traditions in a single piece: the classic set of four and the scholarly addition of a fifth.

chapters.ar: رَؤُفٌ رَحِيۡمٌ: اِسۡمَانِ مِنۡ أَسۡمَاءِ اللهِ سَمَّى بِهِمَا حَبِيۡبَهُ
chapters.en: Ra'ūf, Raḥīm: The Two Names Allah Joined for His Chosen Prophet
chapters.desc: Imām al-Muntajab al-Hamadhānī observed that Allah named none of His servants with two of His own Beautiful Names joined together except the Prophet ﷺ, as Ra'ūf and Raḥīm toward the believers. Shaykh Ṭāhir al-Asyūṭī added that this joined pair occurs eight times in the Qur'ān.

verses.tr: In the Qur'ān, our Lord has joined two names for the Chosen One.

exp.en:
Background

This poem versifies a benefit shared by Shaykh Ṭāhir al-Asyūṭī, may Allah preserve him. Imām al-Muntajab al-Hamadhānī had observed that Allah never named any of His servants with two of His own Beautiful Names joined together, except our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, in the verse: بِالمؤْمنين رَؤُوفٌ رحِيْمٌ, meaning that toward the believers he is Ra'ūf (Most Kind) and Raḥīm (Most Merciful). Shaykh Ṭāhir then added a further observation: that Allah describes Himself with this very same pair of names, joined together, in eight separate places in the Qur'ān.

Explanation

The poet opens by stating the general fact: Allah joined together, for al-Muṣṭafā (the Chosen One, a title of the Prophet ﷺ), two of His Names in a single verse.

verses.tr: Toward the believers, he is Ra'ūf, Raḥīm, a gift the All-Knowing granted to none but him.

exp.en:
The poet names the two attributes directly: Ra'ūf and Raḥīm, both describing the Prophet's disposition toward the believers, drawn from the end of Sūrat at-Tawbah:

﴿لَقَدْ جَاءَكُمْ رَسُولٌ مِّنْ أَنفُسِكُمْ عَزِيزٌ عَلَيْهِ مَا عَنِتُّمْ حَرِيصٌ عَلَيْكُم بِالْمُؤْمِنِينَ رَءُوفٌ رَّحِيمٌ﴾

al-Tawbah 9:128

Al-'Alīm here refers to Allah Himself, the All-Knowing, and the verse states plainly that this joined pairing of names was never granted to any other of His creation.

verses.tr: And al-Hamadhānī, al-Muntajab, added this benefit: eight times are they joined together; take note of the count.

exp.en:
The final verse attributes the original observation to Imām al-Muntajab al-Hamadhānī, concerning the Prophet ﷺ being described by the two names رَؤُوفٌ رَحِيمٌ. Shaykh Ṭāhir al-Asyūṭī then adds that this same pairing of names occurs eight times in the Qur'ān: seven times in reference to Allah ﷻ, and once in reference to His beloved Prophet ﷺ. The following are those eight occurrences:

  1. Surah al-Baqarah 2:143 ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ بِالنَّاسِ لَرَءُوفٌ رَّحِيمٌ﴾
  2. Surah al-Tawbah 9:117 ﴿إِنَّهُ بِهِمْ رَءُوفٌ رَّحِيمٌ﴾
  3. Surah al-Tawbah 9:128 ﴿بِالْمُؤْمِنِينَ رَءُوفٌ رَّحِيمٌ﴾
  4. Surah al-Naḥl 16:7 ﴿إِنَّ رَبَّكُمْ لَرَءُوفٌ رَّحِيمٌ﴾
  5. Surah al-Naḥl 16:47 ﴿فَإِنَّ رَبَّكُمْ لَرَءُوفٌ رَّحِيمٌ﴾
  6. Surah al-Ḥajj 22:65 ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ بِالنَّاسِ لَرَءُوفٌ رَّحِيمٌ﴾
  7. Surah al-Nūr 24:20 ﴿وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ رَءُوفٌ رَّحِيمٌ﴾
  8. Surah al-Ḥadīd 57:9 ﴿وَإِنَّ اللَّهَ بِكُمْ لَرَءُوفٌ رَّحِيمٌ﴾

chapters.ar: دِرَاسَةُ عِلۡمِ الصَّرۡفِ مِنۡ غَيۡرِ عِلَلِهِ
chapters.en: Studying Ṣarf Without Its ʿIlal
chapters.desc: A single verse on the saying of Dr Ḥasan al-'Uthmān: whoever studies ṣarf (Arabic morphology) without its 'ilal, the reasons behind its changes, is like one who eats kunāfah without sugar.

verses.tr: Kunāfah without sugar grows tiresome — like the student of ṣarf who studies it without its 'ilal.

exp.en:
Background

This verse versifies a saying of Dr. Ḥasan al-'Uthmān, a scholar of ṣarf (Arabic morphology): “Whoever studies ṣarf without studying its 'ilal (underlying causes) is like one who eats kunāfah without sugar.”

Ṣarf is the study of word patterns, how verbs and nouns are inflected and altered, while its 'ilal are the morphological and phonetic reasons behind those changes (substitution, elision, assimilation, and the like): the very rationale that makes the rules make sense, rather than a set of forms to be memorized by rote.

يَا طَالِبَ عِلْمِ الصَّرْفِ ... اِحْذَرْ مِنْ تَرْكِ الْعِلَلِ

يَقُولُ فِي ذَلِكَ شَيْخُنَا الدُّكْتُورُ المنيسي حفظه الله وَرعاه مُنَبِّهًا طَالِبَ عِلْمِ الصَّرْفِ مُبَيِّنًا لَهُ أَهَمِّيَةَ الْعِلَلِ:

Explanation

The poet likens a student of ṣarf who is content to memorize word-patterns and rules without grasping their 'ilal (why a word takes a given pattern, why a substitution, elision, or assimilation occurs) to someone eating kunāfah, a dessert whose whole character depends on its sugar, when it has been served without any. Both “grow tiresome/wearisome”: the palate tires of the one, the mind tires of the other.

chapters.ar: فِي تَرۡتِيۡبِ مَنَاسِكِ الۡحَجِّ يَوۡمَ النَّحۡرِ
chapters.en: Ranḥaṭ: A Mnemonic for the Order of the Rites on the Day of Sacrifice
chapters.desc: A one-verse mnemonic for the recommended order of the four rites of the Day of Sacrifice during Ḥajj (ramy, naḥr, ḥalq and ṭawāf), whose first letters are strung together in the coined word Ranḥaṭ.

verses.tr: Order your Ḥajj, take the most cautious course — the actions of the Day of Sacrifice is in Ranḥaṭ.

exp.en:
Background

This verse addresses the recommended (most cautious) order of the rites performed on Yawm an-Naḥr (the Day of Sacrifice, the 10th of Dhū al-Ḥijjah) during Ḥajj: ramy (stoning Jamrat al-'Aqabah), naḥr (sacrificing the offering), ḥalq (shaving or trimming the head), and ṭawāf (Ṭawāf al-Ifāḍah) — in that order.

  • ر: رمي
  • ن: نحر
  • ح: حلق
  • ط: طواف

Explanation

This verse addresses a practical fiqh matter: the recommended (most cautious) order of the four rites performed on the Day of Sacrifice, ramy, naḥr, ḥalq, and ṭawāf. The poet coins an artificial word (Ranḥaṭ) that strings together the first letter of each rite, in sequence, to serve as an easily recalled key.

chapters.ar: وَصِيَّةُ الۡأَئِمَّةِ الۡأَرۡبَعَةِ فِي صِيَانَةِ الۡعُلُوۡمِ عَنِ الۡإِضَاعَةِ
chapters.en: The Counsel of the Four Imāms: Guarding Knowledge from Being Squandered
chapters.desc: The counsel of the four great Imāms of fiqh on the preservation and dignity of knowledge. Though their schools differed, their advice converges: knowledge should not be squandered through indiscriminate debate, questioning, or transmission to those not prepared to receive it.

verses.tr: The bequest of the four Imāms is the safeguarding of knowledge from being squandered.

exp.en:
Background

These verses gather the counsel of the four great Imāms of fiqh concerning the preservation and dignity of knowledge. Although their legal schools differed, their advice converges on a common principle: knowledge should not be squandered through indiscriminate debate, questioning, or transmission to those who are not prepared to receive it.

Explanation

The poet establishes the central theme of the verses: the knowledge inherited from the scholars must be protected from being diminished, misused, or placed where it will not be valued. The following verses then present the counsel of each of the four Imāms.

verses.tr: So, the master al-Nuʿmān said: ‘Avoid every debate with the common folk or the masses.’

exp.en:
Abū Ḥanīfah — النُّعْمَان

السَّيِّدُ النُّعْمَانُ refers to Imām Abū Ḥanīfah al-Nuʿmān ibn Thābit. His counsel is to avoid debate with those who are not equipped for meaningful scholarly discussion. The warning is not against conveying knowledge to ordinary people, but against debate over technical matters of knowledge, which should be reserved for those equipped to engage with it properly.

verses.tr: And the star Mālik says: ‘Whoever answers every questioner, that is a form of demeaning [knowledge].’

exp.en:
Imām Mālik ibn Anas

النَّجْمُ مَالِكٌ is Imām Mālik ibn Anas. His counsel highlights the dignity of knowledge: responding to every question indiscriminately can become a form of إِذَالَةِ: lowering and demeaning knowledge, when the answer is given without considering the questioner, the purpose of the question, or whether the matter is suited to them. Knowledge is not diminished by being shared; rather, it is demeaned when it is treated as something to be distributed without discernment.

verses.tr: “‘Do not debate everyone who wishes to debate you’ — the saying of the Imām, the author of al-Risālah.”

exp.en:
Imām ash-Shāfiʿī

صَاحِبُ الرِّسَالَةِ identifies Imām Muḥammad ibn Idrīs al-Shāfiʿī, author of the renowned الرِّسَالَةِ. His counsel reinforces the same principle expressed by Imām Abū Ḥanīfah: not every person who seeks a debate should be engaged. Debate is valuable when it seeks truth and benefit; when it is merely an invitation to dispute, engaging with it can turn knowledge into an exercise in argument rather than a means of guidance.

verses.tr: Muhannā said to Imām Aḥmad: ‘What does al-Aʿmash say to Shuʿbah:

exp.en:
Abyāt 5–6: Imām Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal

This final passage is presented as a dialogue. Muhannā ibn Yaḥyā was a close companion of Imām Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal and a transmitter of many of his sayings (recorded in the well-known Masā'il Muhannā). Here he relays to Imām Aḥmad a saying attributed to al-A'mash (Sulaymān ibn Mihrān), addressed to his student, the great ḥadīth critic Shu'bah ibn al-Ḥajjāj: “Do not dress a pig in pearls”, a vivid metaphor warning against bestowing precious knowledge (ḥadīth) on someone unworthy or unable to appreciate its value.

Imām Aḥmad then expresses the same principle positively: حَدِّثَنْ مُسْتَاهِلَ الْكَرَامَةِ, narrate to one who is worthy of honour. Thus, the counsel of the four Imāms converges on one principle: knowledge has a dignity, and that dignity is preserved by knowing when, how, and to whom it should be conveyed.

verses.tr: “Do not dress a pig in pearls”?’ He replied: ‘Narrate only to one who is worthy of honour.’

chapters.ar: نَصِيۡحَةٌ لِمَنۡ يَحۡفَظُ الۡقُرۡآنَ
chapters.en: Advice for the One Who Memorizes the Qur'ān
chapters.desc: Six short couplets that set in verse the counsel of Shaykh Dr ʿĀmir Bahjat, the Ḥanbalī jurist and teacher at al-Masjid al-Nabawī, to those seeking to master the memorisation of the Qurʾān: reduce the amount, increase the repetition, keep at it, and constantly seek forgiveness.

verses.tr: O you who aspire to memorisation, listen! May you be guided and attain success.

exp.en:
Background

This poem versifies the counsel of Shaykh Dr. ʿĀmir Bahjat, a well-known Ḥanbalī jurist and teacher at al-Masjid al-Nabawī, to those seeking to master the memorisation of the Qurʾān. His original advice centres on four essential principles:

أَنْ تُقَلِّلَ الْمِقْدَارَ، وَتُكْثِرَ التَّكْرَارَ، وَتَحْرِصَ عَلَى الْمُدَاوَمَةِ وَالِاسْتِمْرَارِ، مَعَ مُلَازَمَةِ الِاسْتِغْفَارِ لِلْوَاحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ.

“That you reduce the amount [memorised at a time], increase the repetition, remain committed to consistency and continuity, together with constantly seeking forgiveness from al-Wāḥid al-Qahhār.”

The poet, Shaykh Dr. Walīd ibn Idrīs al-Minīsī, then distilled this counsel into a short series of tightly rhymed couplets, preserving its central principles while making them easy to memorise alongside the very advice they contain.

Explanation

The poet opens with a direct address to anyone aspiring to memorise the Qurʾān. The expression هُدِيتَ functions as a short supplication embedded in the address itself, and تُحْظَى sets up the promise that follows: listening carefully to this advice is the path to attaining the goal.

sadrW.g: of Ibn Bahjat (Shaykh Dr ʿĀmir Bahjat)

verses.tr: The counsel of Ibn Bahjat, for whoever comprehends and makes it firm.

exp.en: The poet identifies the source of this advice as ابْنُ بَهْجَتٍ, referring to Shaykh Dr. ʿĀmir Bahjat, lending the poem the authority of direct attribution rather than anonymous wisdom. The expressions وَعَى and ثَبَّتَ highlight that benefiting from this counsel requires more than simply hearing it; one must understand it and firmly implement it.

verses.tr: Reduce the amount and increase the repetition.

exp.en: This is the first practical principle of the poem: memorise smaller portions and repeat them more frequently. Rather than rushing through large quantities, the emphasis is on securing what has been memorised through consistent repetition. The objective is quality and retention over sheer quantity covered.

verses.tr: Maintain continuity and hold firmly to seeking forgiveness.

exp.en: The poet combines two essential disciplines: consistency in practice (not memorizing in bursts followed by long gaps), paired directly with istighfār (seeking Allah's forgiveness). The pairing is deliberate; the practical discipline of continuous effort is placed alongside the spiritual discipline of turning to Allah, reflecting the original prose counsel's own structure.

verses.tr: And ask al-Qahhār, privately or openly.

exp.en: Having outlined the practical means, the poet turns the student's attention to Allah. The name الْقَهَّار emphasises Allah's absolute power and dominion, evoking His complete power over all affairs, including the ease or difficulty of memorization itself. The student is therefore encouraged to turn to Him in supplication, whether privately or openly, seeking His assistance in the journey of memorisation.

verses.tr: [Ask Him for] help and support, and success and happiness.

exp.en:
The final couplet completes the supplication by specifying what the student should seek from Allah: الْعَوْنَ وَالْإِمْدَادَ, help and sustaining support in the process itself, and الْفَوْزَ وَالْإِسْعَادَ, success and happiness as its fruit, tying the entire piece of practical advice back to its spiritual foundation.

The poem thus concludes by reminding the aspiring ḥāfiẓ that although disciplined effort and repetition are essential, lasting success ultimately rests upon Allah's assistance and grace.

chapters.ar: اِبۡتِلاءُ الۡقُرۡبِ وَالۡبُعۡدِ
chapters.en: The Trial of Nearness and the Trial of Distance
chapters.desc: A single verse versifying the saying attributed to Ibn Ḥazm: trial through the nearness of one you dislike is like trial through the distance of one you love.

verses.tr: Trial through nearness to one you dislike is like trial through distance from one you love.

exp.en:
Background

This verse versifies a saying attributed to Ibn Ḥazm:

مَنْ اُبْتُلِيَ بِقُرْبِ مَنْ يَكْرَهُ، كَمَنْ اُبْتُلِيَ بِبُعْدِ مَن يُحِبُّ.

“Trial through the nearness of one you dislike is like trial through the distance of one you love.” Ibn Ḥazm al-Andalusī

لَيْسَ كُلُّ قُرْبٍ نِعْمَةً، وَلَا كُلُّ بُعْدٍ نِقْمَةً، فَرُبَّ قُرْبٍ وَبَالٌ، وَرُبَّ بُعْدٍ رَاحَةٌ، وَمَا أَجْمَلَ مَا قَالَهُ ابْنُ حَزْمٍ رَحِمَهُ اللهُ: مَنْ اُبْتُلِيَ بِقُرْبِ مَنْ يَكْرَهُ، كَمَنْ اُبْتُلِيَ بِبُعْدِ مَنْ يُحِبُّ.

فَصَاغَ شَيْخُنَا الدُّكْتُورُ الْمُنَيْسِيُّ حَفِظَهُ اللهُ وَرَعَاهُ مَعْنَاهُ فِي بَيْتٍ بَدِيعٍ، فَقَالَ:

Explanation

The poet presents two seemingly opposite forms of trial: being near someone whom one dislikes and being separated from someone whom one loves. Yet both can be equally difficult tests for the heart. The verse therefore captures the wisdom of Ibn Ḥazm: nearness is not always a blessing, nor is distance always a relief; either may become a test depending on whom the heart is drawn towards or away from.

chapters.ar: مِنۡ ظَهۡرِ أَبٍ إِلٰى يَوۡمِ عَرۡضٍ
chapters.en: From a Father's Back to the Day of Standing
chapters.desc: A short poem tracing the human journey through five successive stages, from a father's back to the Day of Presentation, before concluding with a personal supplication.

verses.tr: From the back of a father to the womb of a mother, and from the womb of a mother to the surface of the earth.

exp.en:
Background

This short poem traces the human journey through five successive stages, from origin to the Hereafter, before concluding with a personal supplication.

The opening verse also contains a brief philological note: the poet doubles the ب in أَبّ as a poetic necessity (ضَرُورَةُ النَّظْم), departing from the usual أَب. He cites al-Miṣbāḥ al-Munīr, which records a rare dialect in which the ب is doubled, so one says: هُوَ الأَبُّ.

يَقُولُ الشَّيْخُ الدُّكْتُوْرُ وَلِيد المنيسي حفظه الله ورعاه في المرَاحِلِ التِي يَمُرُّ بِهَا الإِنْسَانُ، مِنْ إِنْشَائِهِ إِلَى مَمَاتِهِ، بفصَاحَةِ اللسَانِ وبَلَاغَةِ الْكَلَامِ:

Explanation

The poet begins with the first two stages of human existence: from the father's back (the origin of the seed) to the mother's womb, and from the womb to the surface of the earth, that is, birth into worldly life.

Each hemistich contains one transition, the two forming a matched pair (ẓahr/baṭn, “outside/inside”, echoed and reversed in the following verse).

verses.tr: And from the surface of the earth to the belly of the earth, and from the belly of the earth to the Day of Presentation.

exp.en:
The same pattern now continues with the earth: from its surface, where a person lives his worldly life, to its interior, where he is buried after death, and from the grave to يَوْمِ عَرْضٍ, the Day on which creation will be presented before Allah.

Thus, the two verses form one continuous journey through five stages:

The five stages: a journey through life

  1. The back of a father ظهر أب
  2. The womb of a mother بطن أم
  3. The back of a land (the earth) ظهر أرض
  4. The womb of a land (the earth) بطن أرض
  5. The Day of Presentation يوم عرض

verses.tr: So, my Lord, honour me, and after my death, may my happiness be the reward for my striving.

exp.en: Having traced the inevitable journey of the human being from his origin to the Day of Presentation, the poet now turns from description to دُعَاء. The poet turns to Allah with a personal request: to be honoured, and for his happiness after death to stand as the reward (jazā') for his رَكْض, literally “running,” referring here to his striving and exertion in the pursuit of obedience and good deeds.

chapters.ar: الوَزنُ النَّادِرُ فِي الجُمُوۡعِ
chapters.en: The Rarest Forms of Plurals
chapters.desc: A celebrated anecdote from Arabic philology about the rare plural pattern fiʿlā: al-Mutanabbī told Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī it was confined to two words, and generations later al-Damāmīnī identified a third.

verses.sadr: وَوَزۡنُ فِعۡلَى فِي الۡجُمُوعِ قَدۡ نَدَرۡ
verses.tr: The pattern فِعْلَى is rare among plurals, confined to حِجْلَى and ظِرْبَى.

exp.en:
Background

This poem relates a celebrated anecdote from Arabic philology concerning the plural pattern فِعْلَى. It was classically regarded as an exceptionally rare plural pattern, known from the two words حِجْلَى, the plural of حِجْل (partridge), and ظِرْبَى, the plural of ظِرْبَان (a small, foul-smelling animal). The poem recounts how this restricted pattern became the subject of a famous exchange between the poet أبو الطيب المتنبي and the grammarian أبو علي الفارسي, and how a third example was identified generations later by الدماميني.

Explanation

The poet begins by establishing the linguistic principle: the pattern فِعْلَى is exceptionally rare among Arabic plurals. The two words traditionally cited for the pattern are حِجْلَى and ظِرْبَى.

verses.tr: And al-Mutanabbī, in his answer to al-Fārisī: ‘There is no third; do not search and give up hope [of finding one].’

exp.en: The poet now introduces the famous exchange. When أبو علي الفارسي asked أبا الطيب المتنبي about plurals occurring on the pattern فِعْلَى, al-Mutanabbī immediately mentioned حِجْلَى and ظِرْبَى, asserting that there was no third example.

verses.tr: But al-Fārisī did not obey him and continued searching throughout his life yet found nothing.

exp.en: Al-Fārisī was not satisfied with the answer. He continued searching for another example of the pattern فِعْلَى, but according to the account, he found none. The story further relates that he suffered from an eye ailment and that his prolonged scholarly search eventually led to severe deterioration of his eyesight.

verses.tr: Until he became blind. Then al-Damāmīnī added to them the word مِعْزَى, and found [a third].

exp.en:
The poem concludes with the later development of the story. Generations after al-Fārisī, بدر الدين الدماميني identified مِعْزَى as another word occurring on the pattern فِعْلَى, thus adding a third example to the two traditionally cited by al-Mutanabbī.

The later addition of مِعْزَى was itself versified by العلامة أجدود بن أقطوشني العلوي:

verses.tr: A third word has been added to the two, attributed to al-Damāmīnī — and it is مِعْزَى.

chapters.ar: أَسۡمَاءُ الضَّرۡبِ فِي العَرَبِيّة
chapters.en: The Names of Striking in Arabic
chapters.desc: A selection of the precise Arabic verbs for different forms of striking and the parts of the body a blow falls upon, drawn from Ibn al-Jawzī’s al-Mudhish and set in a single memorable scene in which Zayd strikes an oppressor with one blow after another.

verses.tr: Zayd struck the oppressor on the nape, slapped him, struck him on the crown, struck his face, and punched him.

exp.en:
Background

لَيْسَ العَجَبُ مِنْ فَصَاحَةِ اللُّغَةِ الْعَرَبِيَّةِ فَحَسْبُ، بَلْ أَعْجَبُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ أَنَّ شَيْخَنَا الدُّكْتُوْر المنيسي حفظه الله ورعاه أَخَذَ بَرَاعَةَ اللُّغَةِ وَأَلْبَسَهَا ثَوْبَ الشِّعْرِ حَيْثُ قَالَ:

This poem gathers a selection of the precise Arabic verbs used to describe different forms of striking and different parts of the body upon which a blow falls. Drawing from the terminology recorded by Ibn al-Jawzī in al-Mudhish, the poet places these expressions into a single memorable scene, in which Zayd strikes an oppressor with one blow after another, each verb naming a different target and technique.

Explanation

The poet begins by presenting several verbs for striking, each carrying its own specific meaning. Rather than repeatedly describing the action simply as “striking,” Arabic employs distinct verbs according to the manner of the blow and the part of the body affected.

sadrW.g: struck his cheek with both hands

verses.tr: He struck his cheek with both hands, struck his jaw, struck his chin, kneed him, kicked him, and struck his chest.

exp.en:
The sequence continues with further expressions, each adding another form of striking. The two verses therefore function as a compact lexical catalogue, while the continuous action makes the various terms easier to remember.

The poet’s purpose is not merely to describe a beating, but to demonstrate the precision and richness of Arabic vocabulary. A single general action — striking — may be expressed by different verbs depending upon where the blow lands and how it is delivered. By gathering these words into one continuous scene, the poet turns a list of difficult vocabulary into a memorable sequence.

The Forms of Striking

  • صَفَعَ To strike the nape/back of the neck
  • لَطَمَ To slap the face/cheek with the open hand
  • صَقَعَ To strike the head/crown
  • صَكَّ To strike the face
  • لَكَمَ To punch with the fist
  • لَدَمَ To strike the cheek with both hands
  • لَهَزَ To strike the jaw
  • وَهَزَ To strike the chin
  • زَبَنَ To strike or push with the knee
  • رَكَلَ To kick with the foot
  • وَكَزَ To strike or jab the chest/body

Thus, the poem gathers eleven different expressions for striking into a single scene, allowing the vocabulary to be understood not as isolated words, but through the place and manner of each blow.

chapters.ar: لا تفرك الورود... أدبُ اللطائف والحكم
chapters.en: Do Not Crush the Roses: On Handling Delicate Insights with Care
chapters.desc: Some subtle insights are like roses: their benefit is found in pausing to appreciate them, and whoever rubs and scrutinises their petals in the name of critique may destroy the very beauty he sought to examine.

verses.tr: Some subtle insights are like roses: you smell them, delighting in their fragrance and their sweet scent.

exp.en:
Background

إِنَّ لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ أَدَبًا، وَأَدَبُ اللَّطَائِفِ وَالْحِكَمِ أَنْ يَسْتَفِيدَ الْإِنْسَانُ منها، فَلَيْسَ كُلُّ مَا يُؤْخَذُ يُفَكَّكُ وَيُنْقَدُ، وَرُبَّ لَطِيفَةٍ إِذَا أَكْثَرْتَ فِي تَفْتِيشِهَا أَفْسَدْتَ جَمَالَهَا، وَإِلَى هَذَا الْمَعْنَى أَشَارَ الشَّيْخُ الدُّكْتُورُ وَلِيدُ الْمُنَيْسِيُّ حَفِظَهُ اللهُ وَرَعَاهُ فَقَالَ:

True understanding is not always about analysing every detail. Sometimes, it is about recognising the value of a subtle insight, benefiting from it, and allowing its beauty to remain intact.

Some wisdoms are like roses: their beauty lies in their fragrance, and their benefit is found in pausing to appreciate them. If one begins to rub and scrutinise their petals in the name of critique, one may destroy the very beauty one sought to examine.

Abyāt 1–2

The poet builds a single extended analogy across both verses: certain laṭā’if, delicate insights or graceful remarks, are like roses, meant to be enjoyed for the pleasure they give, their fragrance, rather than subjected to close physical handling.

The second verse turns the analogy into a warning: rubbing or crushing a rose between the fingers, the way an overly literal or overly critical mind might pick apart a delicate remark, does not reveal more of its beauty. It destroys it.

verses.tr: Do not crush those roses between your fingers in the name of critique, or you will destroy their radiance.

chapters.ar: الأُمُوۡرُ السَّبۡعَة مَحۡمُوۡدَةٌ فِيۡهَا الۡعَجَلَة
chapters.en: Seven Matters Exempted from the Blame Attached to Haste
chapters.desc: Haste is generally blameworthy and traced back to Satan, in contrast to deliberateness and measured calm; these verses name seven matters exempted from that blame, where acting quickly is in fact the praiseworthy course.

verses.tr: Haste is blameworthy, for it is from Satan; except seven, which my explanation gathers.

exp.en:
Background

لَيْسَتْ كُلُّ عَجَلَةٍ مَذْمُومَةً، وَلَا كُلُّ تَأَنٍّ مَحْمُودًا؛ فَرُبَّ عَجَلَةٍ مَحْمُودَةٌ، وَرُبَّ تَأَنٍّ مَذْمُومٌ، فَالْعِبْرَةُ بِمَوْضِعِ الْعَجَلَةِ وَالتَّأَنِّي، فَلِكُلِّ مَقَامٍ مَقَالٌ.

وَقَدْ جَمَعَ شَيْخُنَا الدُّكْتُورُ الْمُنَيْسِيُّ حَفِظَهُ اللهُ هُنَا سَبْعَةَ مَوَاضِعَ تُحْمَدُ فِيهَا الْعَجَلَةُ:

Haste, ta’ajjul, is generally considered blameworthy and traced back to Satan, in contrast to anā’ah, deliberateness and measured calm, which is attributed to Allah. This verse names seven matters exempted from that general blame, where acting quickly is in fact the praiseworthy course rather than the discouraged one.

Abyāt 1–4

The poet opens by stating the general principle that haste is blameworthy as a matter traced to Satan, before immediately carving out seven exceptions, gathered across the remaining three verses, where the opposite holds, and speed itself becomes the commendable course of action.

  1. Preparing the deceased for burial. Not delaying the washing, shrouding, and burial of the dead.
  2. Feeding a guest. Not delaying hospitality once a guest has arrived.
  3. The repentance of a regretful sinner. Not postponing tawbah once remorse is felt.
  4. Marrying off a daughter of age. Not delaying marriage once a young woman has reached maturity.
  5. Paying off a debt. Settling what is owed without procrastination.
  6. The prayer, once its time enters. Not delaying ṣalāh once its time has come.
  7. The battle cry of horsemen. The swift charge of the brave into battle.

verses.tr: Preparing their dead for burial; likewise feeding a guest; and the repentance of a regretful sinner.
Marrying off a young woman once she has reached maturity, and paying off a debt without delay.

verses.sadr: وَكَذَا الصَّلَاةَ إِذَا أَتَتۡ عَجِّلۡ بِهَا
verses.tr: and likewise, the prayer, hasten with it once its time comes; and the battle cry among horsemen, for the brave.

chapters.ar: مُخۡتَصَرُ خَلِيلٍ: مَكَانَتُهُ وَعَدَدُ مَسَائِلِهِ وَحُرُوفِهِ
chapters.en: Mukhtaṣar Khalīl: Its Scholarly Status, Number of Issues and Letters
chapters.desc: Praise of Mukhtaṣar Khalīl, a central text of the Mālikī school, told through a story transmitted by a chain of scholars: that it holds two hundred thousand legal issues, and how Muḥammad al-Ḥasan Būṣū counted its letters to verify an estimate of its length against the Qur’an.

verses.ajuz: عَنۡ يُوۡسُفٍ بَلۡحُوۡرِ عَنۡ سِي لۡعَرَبِي
verses.tr: The meticulous, brilliant Ibn Būṣū narrated from Yūsuf Balḥūr, from Sī l-'Arabī.

exp.en:
Background

The Mukhtaṣar of Imām Khalīl ibn Isḥāq al-Jundī is among the most celebrated works of Mālikī jurisprudence. Its concise wording brings together a vast range of legal rulings, making it a central text in the study and teaching of the Mālikī school.

The following poem by Shaykh Dr Waleed al-Meneese recounts a remarkable story transmitted through a chain of scholars. The account highlights the importance of memorising and understanding Mukhtaṣar Khalīl, reports that it contains more than 200,000 legal issues, and describes an attempt by Muḥammad al-Ḥasan Būṣū to verify an estimate of its length by counting its letters and comparing them with a corresponding portion of the Qur’an.

The poem combines praise of a foundational work with a story about scholarly transmission, memorisation and numerical verification.

Abyāt 1–2

The poem begins by naming the transmitters of the story.

The poet traces the report from Ibn Būṣū to Yūsuf Balḥūr and then to Sī al-ʿArabī. The expression حدَّثه مشافهةً indicates that the account was conveyed orally, face to face, rather than merely encountered in a written source.

By beginning with this chain, the poet presents the story as a transmitted report and highlights the importance of preserving scholarly accounts through narration.

verses.tr: Who told him directly a story recounted to him, a tale astonishing in every wonder.
Whoever has not memorized the Mukhtaṣar of Sayyidī Khalīl has not [fully] grasped

exp.en:
Abyāt 3–4

The poet emphasises the central position of Mukhtaṣar Khalīl in the study of Mālikī jurisprudence. His statement that one who has not memorised it has not fully grasped the jurisprudence of Imām Mālik is an expression of the work’s importance within the scholarly tradition, rather than a literal denial that Mālikī fiqh can be studied through other sources.

The comparison كالكوكب refers to Imām Mālik, whom the poet intended by this expression, drawing on the statement attributed to Imām al-Shāfiʿī:

إذا ذُكِرَ العلماءُ فمالكٌ النجمُ

“When the scholars are mentioned, Mālik is the star.”

Just as a star shines in the sky, Imām Mālik stands out among the scholars.

ajuzW.g: and he is the one who

verses.tr: The fiqh of Imām Mālik ibn Anas, and he [Imam Malik] is like a star among the jurists.
Khalīl's book contains two hundred thousand issues of a delightful, exquisite kind.

exp.en:
Abyāt 5–6

The poet then states that, according to the account, the work contains two hundred thousand legal issues. The expression سِفر الخليل refers to Khalīl’s substantial scholarly work, while من الطراز المطرب praises the remarkable quality of its contents and formulation.

The following verse divides these issues into two categories:

  • 100,000 transmitted issues (manqūl), based on transmitted reports.
  • 100,000 reasoned issues (maʿqūl), involving juristic reasoning and deduction.

The distinction highlights the two broad dimensions of Islamic jurisprudence: transmitted evidence and the scholarly reasoning through which legal rulings are understood and derived. These figures are those reported in the account transmitted by the poet.

verses.tr: Half of them are transmitted reports, and half are rationally derived; glory be to my Lord, the Bestower.
And the scholars have estimated its size at forty, counted in aḥzāb.

exp.en: The poet relates that scholars estimated the length of Mukhtaṣar Khalīl at approximately forty أحزاب (aḥzāb), using divisions of the Qur’an as a measure of its size. This is a striking comparison: a work renowned for its concise wording contains an immense body of jurisprudential material.

verses.tr: So, Shaykh Ibn Būṣū rose and set about counting the letters, calculating with a calculator.

exp.en:
Keen to verify the reported estimate, Muḥammad al-Ḥasan Būṣū undertook a letter count of Mukhtaṣar Khalīl. He obtained a digital Word copy from Shaykh Shukrī al-Majūlī and removed the commentaries and additions that were not part of Khalīl’s original text.

His calculation produced a total of 227,009 letters for the Mukhtaṣar. He then compared this figure with the number of Qur’anic letters counted from the beginning of Sūrat al-Fātiḥah up to a specific letter in Sūrat al-Kahf.

verses.tr: And behold, the count reached the hamzah of أَوْهَنَ, thus confirming the statement of the noble, virtuous scholar.

exp.en:
The poet reveals the result of Ibn Būṣū’s calculation. The Qur’anic count, beginning with Sūrat al-Fātiḥah and ending at the alif in أَوْهَنَ, in the verse in Sūrat al-Kahf, also amounted to 227,009 letters.

The two totals were therefore almost identical:

  • Mukhtaṣar Khalīl: 227,009 letters.
  • Qur’an, from the beginning of Sūrat al-Fātiḥah to the hamza in أَوْهَنَ: 227,009 letters.
  • Difference between Mukhtaṣar Khalīl and forty aḥzāb: 278 letters.

According to Ibn Būṣū’s account, the Mukhtaṣar fell short of forty aḥzāb by only 278 letters. He regarded this close correspondence as confirmation of the estimate transmitted by Shaykh Yūsuf Balḥūr, particularly the wording that the scholars had estimated its length at approximately forty aḥzāb.

The poem thus concludes with a remarkable attempt at numerical verification, linking the scholarly transmission of an earlier statement with a calculated comparison between the letters of Mukhtaṣar Khalīl and a corresponding portion of the Qur’an.

chapters.ar: المَوَاضِعُ السِّتّةُ الَّتِي يُكۡرَهُ فِيهَا الأَذانُ عندَ الۡمَالِكِيَّة
chapters.en: The Six Prayers for Which the Imām of the Abode of Hijrah Disliked the Adhān
chapters.desc: The adhān is ordinarily called for the five obligatory prayers; this poem lists six situations in which it is considered disliked (makrūh) according to Imām Mālik, the Imām of the Abode of Hijrah.

verses.tr: In six [cases]: one praying alone while resident, a confined prayer, a missed prayer, a prayer of necessity...

exp.en:
Background

This poem lists six situations in which the adhān is considered disliked (makrūh) according to Imām Mālik, whom the poet refers to as Imām Dār al-Hijrah, the Imām of Madīnah.

The adhān is ordinarily called for the five obligatory prayers. The poem highlights six situations in which this ruling differs from the usual practice.

Abyāt 1–2

The poet lists six situations in which the adhān is considered disliked according to Imām Mālik.

1. مُنْفَرِدٌ فِي حَضَرٍ

This refers to a person praying alone while resident. Since the adhān serves to announce the prayer and call people together, its purpose is not fully realised when a person prays alone.

2. مَحْصُورَةٌ

This refers to a prayer performed under restricted circumstances. The poet includes it among the situations in which the usual practice of calling the adhān does not apply in the same way.

3. فَائِتَةٌ

This refers to a missed prayer being made up (qaḍāʾ). Since its prescribed time has already passed, it differs from a prayer being performed when its time has newly entered.

4. ضَرُورَةٌ

This refers to a prayer performed under circumstances of necessity. Such a situation differs from the ordinary circumstances in which the adhān is called for the obligatory prayers.

5. جَنَازَةٌ

This refers to the funeral prayer (ṣalāt al-janāzah). Unlike the five obligatory daily prayers, the funeral prayer is not preceded by an adhān.

6. نَافِلَةٌ

This refers to a voluntary prayer. The adhān is prescribed for the obligatory prayers, not for voluntary prayers.

Through these six cases, the poet summarises the situations in which the adhān is considered disliked according to Imām Mālik, the Imām of Madīnah.

verses.tr: A funeral prayer, and a voluntary prayer. The adhān in these cases is disliked by the Imām of the Abode of Migration.

chapters.ar: المَوَاضِعُ التِّسۡعَةُ الَّتِي تَجۡعَلُ لَكَ حَظًّا فِي دَعَوَاتِ الۡمَلَائِكَةِ
chapters.en: The Nine Ways to Be Included in the Angels' Supplication
chapters.desc: The angels who bear the Throne and those around it seek forgiveness for the believers, and the ḥadīth names deeds through which a believer may receive their supplication; the poet gathers them into four concise verses presenting nine ways in total.

verses.tr: If you desire the supplication of the angels, here are nine; take a path and follow it.

exp.en:
Background

أَتُرِيْدُ أَنْ تَدْعُوَ لَكَ أَهْلُ الْمَلَإِ الْأَعْلَى؟ فَخُذْ هَذِهِ التِّسْعَةَ، مِنْ شَيْخِنَا الدُّكْتُورِ المنيسي الله رعاه وحفظه، اِعْمَلْ بِهَا وَفُزْ بِدَعْوَى الْمَلَائِكَةِ.

The Qur’ān mentions that the angels who bear the Throne and those around it seek forgiveness for the believers. The ḥadīth also identifies several deeds through which a believer may receive the supplication of the angels. These include praying in the first row, remaining in one’s place of prayer after ṣalāh, eating suḥūr, sleeping in a state of purity, visiting the sick, teaching people good, visiting a brother for the sake of Allah, and supplicating for a fellow Muslim in his absence.

The Nine Ways to Attain the Supplication of Angels

  1. The Qur’ān mentions that the angels who bear the Throne and those around it seek forgiveness for the believers.
  2. Praying in the first row.
  3. Remaining in one’s place of prayer after ṣalāh.
  4. Eating suḥūr.
  5. Sleeping in a state of purity.
  6. Visiting the sick.
  7. Teaching people good.
  8. Visiting a brother for the sake of Allah.
  9. And supplicating for a fellow Muslim in his absence.

The poet gathers these deeds into four concise verses, presenting nine ways in total.

Explanation

The poet opens with a direct offer to the reader, a path toward being included among those the angels supplicate for, then lists the nine ways to attain it.

verses.tr: They seek forgiveness around the Throne of our Lord, for everyone who repents and is a believer.

exp.en:
1. Repentance and Īmān

The poet begins with the Qur’ānic description of the angels who seek forgiveness for the believers. Their supplication includes those who turn back to Allah in repentance and remain upon faith. As Allah says:

﴿الَّذِينَ يَحْمِلُونَ الْعَرْشَ وَمَنْ حَوْلَهُ يُسَبِّحُونَ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّهِمْ وَيُؤْمِنُونَ بِهِ وَيَسْتَغْفِرُونَ لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾

Ghāfir 40:7

verses.tr: Pray in the first row, and remain seated after the prayer, and likewise eat suḥūr.

exp.en:
2. Praying in the First Row

The poet says: فِي أَوَّلِ الصُّفُوفِ صَلِّ. He encourages the worshipper to seek a place in the first row, a position for which the Prophet ﷺ informed us that the angels supplicate.

إِنَّ اللَّهَ وَمَلَائِكَتَهُ يُصَلُّونَ عَلَى الصَّفِّ الْأَوَّلِ

“Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the first row.” Ibn Mājah

3. Remaining in One’s Place of Prayer after Ṣalāh

The words وَاجْلِسَنْ بَعْدَ الصَّلَاةِ refer to remaining in one’s place of prayer after completing ṣalāh, provided one maintains the conditions mentioned in the ḥadīth. The Prophet ﷺ said:

الْمَلَائِكَةُ تُصَلِّي عَلَى أَحَدِكُمْ مَا دَامَ فِي مُصَلَّاهُ الَّذِي صَلَّى فِيهِ، مَا لَمْ يُحْدِثْ

“The angels continue to supplicate for one of you as long as he remains in the place where he prayed, provided he does not invalidate his wuḍūʾ.” al-Bukhārī

4. Eating Suḥūr

The poet says: وَكَذَا تَسَحَّرَنْ. Suḥūr is the meal eaten before dawn by the person intending to fast. Its virtue extends beyond physical nourishment, as the Prophet ﷺ mentioned the supplication of Allah and the angels for those who partake in it. The Prophet ﷺ said:

إِنَّ اللَّهَ وَمَلَائِكَتَهُ يُصَلُّونَ عَلَى الْمُتَسَحِّرِينَ

“Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon those who eat suḥūr.” Ibn Ḥibbān

verses.ajuz: وَزُرۡ أَخَاكَ وَادۡعُ لَهۡ حُزۡتَ الۡمِنَنۡ
verses.tr: Sleep in a state of purity, visit the sick, teach, visit your brother, and supplicate for him: you will have attained the blessings.

exp.en:
5. Sleeping in a State of Purity

The words نَمْ طَاهِرًا encourage the believer to perform wuḍūʾ before sleeping. A ḥadīth mentions an angel remaining with the person who sleeps in a state of purity and supplicating for his forgiveness. The Prophet ﷺ said:

مَنْ بَاتَ طَاهِرًا بَاتَ فِي شِعَارِهِ مَلَكٌ، فَلَا يَسْتَيْقِظُ إِلَّا قَالَ الْمَلَكُ: اللَّهُمَّ اغْفِرْ لِعَبْدِكَ فُلَانٍ، فَإِنَّهُ بَاتَ طَاهِرًا

“Whoever sleeps in a state of purity has an angel with him through the night. Whenever he awakens, the angel says: ‘O Allah, forgive Your servant so-and-so, for he slept in a state of purity.’” al-Ṭabarānī

6. Visiting the Sick

The poet says: وَعُدْ مَرِيضًا. Visiting an ill person is an act of compassion and brotherhood, and the ḥadīth describes a great reward for the one who undertakes it. The Prophet ﷺ said:

مَا مِنْ مُسْلِمٍ يَعُودُ مُسْلِمًا غُدْوَةً إِلَّا صَلَّى عَلَيْهِ سَبْعُونَ أَلْفَ مَلَكٍ حَتَّى يُمْسِيَ... الحديث

“No Muslim visits another Muslim in the morning except that seventy thousand angels supplicate for him until the evening.” al-Tirmidhī

7. Teaching People Good

The word عَلِّمَنْ calls the reader to teach others what is beneficial. The virtue of this deed is not restricted to those who study it; it also encompasses those who convey and teach beneficial knowledge. The Prophet ﷺ said:

إِنَّ اللَّهَ وَمَلَائِكَتَهُ وَأَهْلَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرَضِينَ، حَتَّى النَّمْلَةَ فِي جُحْرِهَا وَحَتَّى الْحُوتَ، لَيُصَلُّونَ عَلَى مُعَلِّمِ النَّاسِ الْخَيْرَ

“Indeed, Allah, His angels, the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth—even the ant in its hole and the fish—send blessings upon the one who teaches people good.” al-Tirmidhī

8. Visiting a Brother for the Sake of Allah

The words وَزُرْ أَخَاكَ refer to visiting a fellow Muslim out of love for Allah, rather than for a worldly benefit. Such a visit reflects sincere brotherhood and earns a special virtue.

The Prophet ﷺ related the story of a man who set out to visit a brother in another village. Allah placed an angel along his route, who asked him where he was going. When the man explained that he was visiting his brother solely because he loved him for Allah’s sake, the angel informed him:

فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ قَدْ أَحَبَّكَ كَمَا أَحْبَبْتَهُ فِيهِ

“Allah has indeed loved you just as you have loved him for His sake.” Muslim

9. Supplicating for a Brother in His Absence

The poet concludes with وَادْعُ لَهْ, encouraging the believer to supplicate for another Muslim without that person being present. This is a deed of sincerity, since the supplicant asks Allah to grant good to his brother without seeking recognition or praise from him.

The Prophet ﷺ said:

دَعْوَةُ الْمَرْءِ الْمُسْلِمِ لِأَخِيهِ بِظَهْرِ الْغَيْبِ مُسْتَجَابَةٌ، عِنْدَ رَأْسِهِ مَلَكٌ مُوَكَّلٌ، كُلَّمَا دَعَا لِأَخِيهِ بِخَيْرٍ قَالَ الْمَلَكُ الْمُوَكَّلُ بِهِ: آمِينَ، وَلَكَ بِمِثْلٍ

“The supplication of a Muslim for his brother in his absence is answered. An angel is appointed beside him; whenever he supplicates for good for his brother, the appointed angel says: ‘Āmīn, and for you the same.’” Muslim

The poet concludes with حُزْتَ الْمِنَنْ, meaning that the one who follows these paths has attained great blessings.

Conclusion of the book

As I bring this collection to a close, I cannot do so without expressing my gratitude for the immense benefit I have personally received from the works of Shaykh Dr Waleed ibn Idris al-Minisi, may Allah preserve him.

One of the qualities I have admired most in his poetry is his remarkable ability to take concepts that may initially appear complex or difficult and distil them into a few concise, memorable lines. His verses are not merely poetry for its own sake; they are carefully constructed vessels for knowledge. A ruling, a distinction, a list of words, or a subtle point of recitation can be gathered into a handful of lines that the student can understand, memorise and recall.

His skill in creating memorable patterns and mnemonic devices is equally remarkable. Where a student may struggle to retain a collection of details, the Shaykh is able to arrange them in such a way that the poetry itself becomes a key to unlocking them. This is one of the great strengths of the classical tradition of naẓm, and it is a quality that the Shaykh has demonstrated with mastery throughout these works.

Beyond this is his command of the Arabic language. His ability to select the precise word, construct the appropriate expression, maintain the demands of metre and rhyme, and at the same time preserve the intended meaning is a testimony to a deep familiarity with the language and its literary tradition.

I have personally benefited greatly from these works, not only from the knowledge contained within them, but from witnessing how knowledge can be taught: with precision, brevity, beauty and memorability.

It is my hope that this small collection will allow others to experience some of that benefit. What appears on these pages may be brief in length, but behind each line lies knowledge, thought and craftsmanship. I therefore encourage the reader not merely to read these poems, but to memorise them, study them, reflect upon them and return to them repeatedly. For that is where the true benefit of a manẓūmah is found.

I ask Allah to preserve my teacher, increase him in knowledge and benefit, accept his efforts, and allow his works to continue benefiting students long after they have been written.

And I ask Allah to make me a grateful student, faithful to what I have been taught, and worthy of carrying even a small portion of what my teachers have entrusted to me.

وَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ

— Abdullah Badat
